Paramount and the State AGs Meet Face to Face Monday Under a Court-Ordered Mediation
A status conference this week ordered the parties into mediation before a magistrate judge. Trial is set for March 2 in Oakland, with a $7 million-a-day fee running.
CEO Summary
Paramount representatives and state attorneys general offices are meeting face to face on Monday, August 24. A status conference earlier this week before Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin set future dates and stipulated mediation before a magistrate judge; an insider told Deadline the Monday meeting is mandated under that procedure. Separately, Gavin Newsom weighed in publicly on the merger for the first time on Friday, backing a settlement and saying he takes David Ellison's threat to move Paramount out of California "seriously."
Why This Matters
The court ordered the Monday meeting, so its occurrence carries no information about either side's willingness to deal. Newsom speaking is the new fact. He has now endorsed a settlement on the record, while Rob Bonta, the attorney general who actually controls California's posture, has said nothing since calling the relocation threat blackmail.

Newsom also named the constraint himself: Bonta is one of twelve attorneys general in the coalition, and a settlement requires all of them to accept the same package.
The Facts
  • Paramount representatives and state attorneys general offices are meeting face to face on Monday, August 24, per Deadline. The depth and scope of the meeting is unclear.
  • "This is mandated under the mediation procedure," an insider told Deadline. A status conference earlier in the week before Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin set future dates and stipulated mediation before a magistrate judge.
  • Trial is set for March 2 in federal court in Oakland.
  • Paramount is seeking a court order for a $1.88 billion bond and faces a $7 million-a-day ticking-fee deadline.
  • The suit is an antitrust action by a coalition of state attorneys general challenging Paramount's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
  • Newsom on Ellison's threat to relocate to Tennessee, Texas or Georgia: "We're hoping that doesn't happen. And I'm of the belief they don't want that to happen. It's not, I don't think, in the company's long-term interest, but I take it seriously." He added: "I'm concerned about the state, our reputation."
  • Echoing Bonta's line that the matter could be settled in the boardroom and not the courtroom, Newsom said: "I think there's some universal settlement there, if that's possible. The question is if that's possible and what's the best deal ... that has to be worked through."
  • On talks already underway: "I know there are many meetings that are going on, and there's a lot of conversation." He described the process as unfolding "in real time."
  • Per The Hollywood Reporter, Newsom noted Bonta "is also part of this coalition with a dozen other states. So we also have to be mindful of that coalition as well."
  • Bonta has called Paramount's relocation threats "blackmail." His office did not respond to Deadline's request for comment. Paramount had no comment.
  • Ellison's stated deadline for resolving the suit is October, per THR.
  • Newsom's position aligns him with gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, L.A. Mayor Karen Bass, the DGA and IATSE.

Karen Bass Wants the Paramount-Warner Merger Settled. Her Election Opponent Wants It Decided in Court.
Bass, who once opposed the $111 billion deal, now wants Bonta to settle it. Raman, her November opponent, backs the suit. WGA West called Bass's move a pressure campaign.
CEO Summary
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass called Thursday for Paramount Skydance and California Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle the 12-state antitrust suit against the $111 billion Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, reversing her earlier opposition. Her general-election opponent, Councilmember Nithya Raman, said the same day that the merger's legality should be decided in court. Cinema United, the DGA and IATSE have all recently called for a settlement; WGA West publicly criticized Bass for joining them.
Why This Matters
Cinema United, the DGA, IATSE and now Bass all represent people who earn money when productions run, and a year of corporate limbo costs them whether the case is won or lost. WGA West and Raman represent the other side of the table, where one fewer studio buyer permanently changes what a writer can ask for.

Bass named the price of her support: "meaningful and enforceable commitments" on headquarters location, jobs, shoots and California investment. That is a settlement built on behavioral undertakings, meaning promises about conduct rather than a forced sale of assets.
Specific Implication
Any organization whose members are paid per production is a candidate to shift toward settlement next. Organizations that sell into a buyer market are not, and their public position is a reasonable proxy for how contested the March trial date remains.
The Facts
  • Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass held a press conference on Thursday, August 20, calling on Paramount Skydance and California Attorney General Rob Bonta to reach a quick settlement in the antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 state regulators against the $111 billion merger.
  • Bass had previously opposed the deal unless it avoided job losses. Her press office said she was calling for the parties either to settle or to begin trial sooner.
  • Bass said any resolution must include "meaningful and enforceable commitments" to keep Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery based in Los Angeles and to maintain jobs, productions and investment in California.
  • L.A. Councilmember Nithya Raman, Bass's opponent in the November general election, restated her support for Bonta's suit the same day. "Serious questions about this merger's legality should be decided in court, not through corporate threats," Raman said.
  • WGA West, which has filed its own suit to stop the merger, rebuked Bass: "We are disappointed that Mayor Bass has chosen to join Paramount's pressure campaign on public enforcers to push through a merger that is being rightfully challenged as illegal."
  • Bass followed Cinema United, the movie theater trade organization once vociferously opposed to the merger, which called for a settlement on Tuesday. The DGA and IATSE made the same request the previous week.
  • IATSE's California political division has endorsed Bass for mayor. Raman's husband, Vali Chandrasekaran, was a writer-producer on "30 Rock" and "Modern Family," and her support base skews toward writers and comedians.
  • Both statements came one day after a report from the L.A. Department of Economic Opportunity and CVL Economics estimating 4,500 film and television jobs at risk, more than 10,000 jobs region-wide, $1.26 billion in lost wages and $2.78 billion in lost economic value.
  • The trial is currently scheduled for March.
· The Hollywood Reporter · Katie Kilkenny · 2026-08-20 · https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/nithya-raman-paramount-warner-bros-court-1236678117/ · Provenance: named-exec-quote source ↗
Fox Passed on Renegotiating the NFL Early, and an Analyst Put the Price of Waiting at $1.1 Billion a Year
Ampere estimates an early NFL renewal would have cost Fox another $1.1 billion a year, about 15% of its total content spend. Fox declined and kept 2029 pricing.
CEO Summary
Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch told investors this month that Fox will hold its current NFL deal and pricing through the 2029 season rather than renegotiate early. Ampere estimates a renewal at the roughly 50% increase the league has sought elsewhere would add about $1.1 billion a year to Fox's NFL bill. U.S. broadcasters will spend roughly $36.5 billion on sports rights in 2026, up 75% from $20.8 billion in 2021.
Why This Matters
Two analysts on the record connect the sports bill to everything else a network buys. Sam Nursall of Ampere says a broadcaster paying $3 billion a year for the NFL starts passing on cheaper competitions, and Daniel Cohen of Octagon says the same discipline now hits the tech bidders, whose capital is going to AI data centers. That combination undercuts the assumption that Amazon, Google or Netflix will absorb whatever traditional broadcasters drop.
Specific Implication
Fox's entertainment programming budget is protected by its own decision through 2029 and unprotected after it. Sellers with multi-year Fox commitments that extend past that window should price the renewal risk now, while the 2030 opt-out is still four years out.
The Facts
  • Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch said on the company's recent earnings call that Fox will keep its existing NFL deal and pricing through the 2029 season rather than renegotiate early. Murdoch said Fox had held "thorough and productive discussions" with the league before deciding against amending the agreement.
  • Fox's NFL agreement runs through 2033. The NFL holds a one-time right to terminate after the 2029 season, covering 2030 through 2033.
  • Based on the roughly 50% increase the NFL has reportedly sought in other rights talks, a similar jump would add about $1.1 billion per year to Fox's NFL spending, according to Ampere.
  • Ampere estimates Fox will spend roughly $7 billion on all content in 2026, including about $4 billion on sports. Another $1.1 billion for the NFL alone would be roughly a 15% increase in total content spending.
  • Fox pays roughly $2.03 billion annually in NFL rights fees, according to Octagon Media Rights Consulting, which estimates the package is around break-even to slightly profitable on a direct basis after amortizing the advertising lift from Super Bowl broadcasts.
  • U.S. broadcasters will spend roughly $36.5 billion on sports rights in 2026, per Ampere, up 75% from about $20.8 billion in 2021.
  • Annual NFL rights fees rose from roughly $7.7 billion in 2022-23 to $12.4 billion in 2023-24. The NBA's new agreements took its annual rights haul from $2.7 billion to $6.8 billion beginning with the 2025-26 season.
  • "If a broadcaster has to pay $3 billion annually for the NFL, they might tend to pass on less expensive competitions," Ampere analyst Sam Nursall told TheWrap. "I'm hard-pressed to imagine a world where Fox does not have NFL rights."
  • "The NFL is a need-to-have for many, and a want-to-have for all," said Daniel Cohen, EVP of Octagon Media Rights Consulting. Cohen also said AI spending is a competing priority for tech bidders: "Spending discipline is hitting the tech giants in a big way and Fox knows this."
  • Nursall pointed to Versant's post-NBC spinoff sports strategy, which has taken rights to the new Pac-12, the WNBA, League One Volleyball and Bundesliga, as an example of opportunities opening for midsized buyers.
  • Fox Sports declined to comment beyond the company's earnings remarks.

New Mexico's Production Spend Fell From $874 Million to $327 Million, and the Mid-Tier Feature Shrank by Half
State film office director Steve Graham says the mid-tier feature used to be $20 million to $40 million and is now $10 million to $20 million, with half as many people working as two years ago.
CEO Summary
New Mexico film and TV production spend fell from $874 million at its 2022 peak to $327 million in the past year. Film Office director Steve Graham told The Hollywood Reporter that the number of productions has risen while the average budget per production has fallen, and put the current mid-tier feature at $10 million to $20 million against a prior $20 million to $40 million. The state reports that 92 percent of its shoots would not happen without its incentive.
Why This Matters
The mid-tier feature did not disappear, it repriced, and a named state official put the new ceiling on the record at a number most buyers will not say out loud.
Specific Implication
That $10 million to $20 million band is a usable comp when a buyer describes a mid-tier budget as generous. It is also the band a project has to fit to attract the volume of buyers currently active at that level.
The Facts
  • New Mexico film and TV production spend fell from $874 million at its 2022 peak to $327 million in the past year, a drop of roughly 63%.
  • Steve Graham, director of the New Mexico Film Office and a producer ("Walker: Independence," "Black Summer"), told THR the number of productions has gone up while average budget per production has gone down.
  • Graham on the mid-tier: "Mid-tier used to be $40 million, right? $20 million to $40 million, and now they're $10 million to $20 million."
  • On employment: "It's half of the people working that were working two years ago."
  • The state's film office report says 92 percent of film and TV shoots in New Mexico would not happen without the incentive. Graham said he would stand by that figure.
  • California more than doubled its annual tax credit program from $330 million to $750 million in 2025; Graham said the effects are only starting to be seen this year.
  • Graham said every studio has reached out and many scouted over the summer for fall or spring projects.
  • New Mexico has formal production-hub partnerships with Netflix (Albuquerque, since 2018) and NBCUniversal. Graham said Netflix recently shot two series in the state and NBC is looking at a series later this year plus more features.
  • New Jersey has lined up three studio partners with long-term commitments: Netflix, Lionsgate and Paramount.
  • The state's "Uplift Zone" rural incentive adds 10 percent for productions shooting outside a 60-mile radius of Albuquerque and Santa Fe. Spend outside the two hubs hit a record $58.5 million last year, much of it around Las Cruces.
  • Titles shot in the state include "Breaking Bad," "Better Call Saul," "Oppenheimer," "Stranger Things," Vince Gilligan's Apple TV series "Pluribus," AMC's "Dark Winds" (five seasons) and Netflix's "Ransom Canyon."

Apple Music Is Making AI Disclosure Mandatory, and a Third of Its New Uploads Are AI-Generated
Apple Music told partners it will require AI Transparency Tags on any content where AI created a material portion. Apple head Oliver Schusser has said over a third of new monthly uploads are AI-generated.
CEO Summary
Apple Music told industry partners in an email obtained by The Hollywood Reporter that AI labels will launch later this year and that content providers will be required to tag any content where AI created a material portion. The company gave no launch date and no enforcement detail. Apple Music does not detect AI content itself and relies on labels and distributors to declare it. Spotify announced its own AI-artist labeling earlier in August.
Why This Matters
Apple put the duty on the supplier and kept none of it. Apple detects nothing, so whoever signs the declaration carries the exposure if the declaration turns out to be wrong, and the trigger phrase, "a material portion of the content," goes undefined in the announcement.

Apple and Spotify also chose different objects to label. Apple tags the work. Spotify tags the artist profile and excludes those profiles from editorial and algorithmic recommendation, which is a distribution penalty rather than a disclosure. The gap between a labeling regime and a demotion regime is where platform AI policy will actually be contested.
Specific Implication
A supplier-side AI declaration is now a live delivery requirement in one medium and transfers directly to film and television delivery schedules. Anyone likely to be asked to sign one should establish now who inside a production actually knows what tools were used.
The Facts
  • Apple Music told industry partners in an email on Thursday, August 20, obtained by The Hollywood Reporter, that it will launch labels on AI-created songs "later this year." No specific launch date was given.
  • The email states: "Content providers will be required to include AI Transparency Tags in any instance where AI was used to create a material portion of the content, including tracks that are AI platform generated." Apple defines AI-platform-generated content as "anything that is primarily derived from a generative AI service."
  • Apple Music launched Transparency Tags in March for labels and distributors to voluntarily disclose content "materially generated using AI." The upcoming change makes the tags visible and mandatory.
  • Apple Music did not include details on how the requirement will be enforced.
  • Apple Music does not detect AI content itself; it relies on labels and distributors to declare it.
  • The announcement follows an RIAA and IFPI-led initiative calling on streaming services to add AI labels in a manner similar to explicit-content disclosure.
  • Spotify said earlier in August it will label AI artists and exclude them from editorial and algorithmic recommendations. Spotify's labeling attaches to artist profiles, not individual songs. Its April song-level labeling feature is voluntary; Spotify says it sees tens of thousands of credits submitted daily.
  • Apple Music doubled its penalty fees for streaming fraud in January, with Apple Music head Oliver Schusser citing the proliferation of AI content as a factor.
  • Schusser subsequently told Billboard that over a third of Apple Music's new monthly uploads were AI-generated songs, while actual usage of AI songs was less than 1 percent.

An Exhibitor Asked Paramount to Extend Its 30-Film Pledge From Three Years to Five and Make It Enforceable
Phoenix Theatres owner Cory Jacobson wants Paramount's 30-releases-a-year pledge extended to five years and made enforceable. He prices the delay at nearly $7 million a day starting October 1.
CEO Summary
Cory Jacobson, who owns the 10-theater Phoenix Theatres chain, argued in a Hollywood Reporter guest column that Paramount's commitment to at least 30 annual theatrical releases should run five years instead of three and be concrete and enforceable. He notes that beginning October 1, Paramount owes Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders a ticking fee, meaning extra merger consideration for each day the deal stays open, of roughly $650 million per quarter. Paramount has estimated the obligation could reach about $1.3 billion by the end of post-trial briefing.
Why This Matters
Jacobson gives a reason for the specific number rather than asking for more on principle: a feature can take several years to move from development to release, so a three-year output pledge expires before the films it was meant to guarantee reach a screen. That test applies to any volume or output commitment, and most of them fail it.
Specific Implication
An output commitment should be measured against the production cycle of the thing it covers, not against the negotiating calendar. On a theatrical slate, three years guarantees the back half of nothing.
The Facts
  • Cory Jacobson is sole owner of Phoenix Theatres, which operates 10 first-run theaters and 93 screens across Michigan, Ohio, Iowa, Massachusetts and Tennessee. He spent two decades at United Artists Theatres and Marcus Theatres before founding Phoenix in 2000.
  • Paramount under David Ellison has publicly committed to at least 30 theatrical releases annually and "meaningful periods of exclusive theatrical exhibition." Jacobson writes that Ellison has made the 30-film pledge for three years.
  • Jacobson's ask: extend the commitment to five years and make it "concrete and enforceable," which he argues would protect the theatrical pipeline through the integration period.
  • On the cost of delay: beginning October 1, Paramount owes additional merger consideration to WBD shareholders, a "ticking fee" of approximately $650 million per quarter, or nearly $7 million per day the transaction remains unclosed.
  • Paramount has estimated the ticking-fee obligation could reach approximately $1.3 billion by the completion of post-trial briefing.
  • Jacobson on current exhibition performance: "We remain approximately 8 percent behind 2019, but I believe we can close that gap and finish the year ahead of 2019 if the production pipeline remains stable."
  • His core argument: "A movie that isn't put into production today becomes an empty spot on a future release calendar. An empty spot on the release calendar eventually becomes an empty auditorium."
  • He does not argue consolidation is safe: "Market power can be abused, and a transaction involving companies this significant deserves careful regulatory scrutiny."

Prime Video Committed $2 Billion to Latin America Through 2030 and Will Double Its Local Originals
Prime Video will spend more than $2 billion across five Latin American markets from 2027 to 2030, double its local originals against 2026, and carry 38 Mexico National Team home matches over four years.
CEO Summary
Prime Video announced at a Mexico City showcase that it will invest more than $2 billion in Latin America between 2027 and 2030 across originals, licensed content and live sports in Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Colombia and Chile. Local executives named 25 titles for 2027 and said the streamer aims to double its local originals output against 2026. Beginning September 26, Prime Video becomes the home of the Mexico National Team for 38 home matches over four years.
Why This Matters
Amazon funded the football rights and the scripted slate out of the same envelope, which is what makes the volume target credible: the national team acquires households and local originals keep them.
The Facts
  • Prime Video announced plans to invest more than $2 billion in Latin America between 2027 and 2030. Details were announced at a Prime Video showcase in Mexico City.
  • The investment spans original programming, locally produced and acquired content, and live sports rights across Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Colombia and Chile.
  • Prime Video will aim to double the number of local originals produced across those five countries compared with 2026.
  • Local executives announced 25 new titles set for 2027, including "La Oficina" Season 2, "Florence Cassez," "Tremembé" Season 2, "Marília," "Menem" Season 2, "Te Odio, Te Amo," "Rojo Corazón," "Catedrales" and "Valentina."
  • Kelly Day, vice president of international at Prime Video: "Today we're matching that energy with more than $2 billion through 2030 across original and licensed programming and sports. What excites me most is the breadth; this isn't a bet on one country or one genre."
  • Beginning September 26, Prime Video becomes the new home for the Mexico National Team, carrying 38 home matches over four years.

'Hadestown' Grossed $20.7 Million as a Filmed Stage Show and Drove Broadway Ticket Sales Up Instead of Down
Bleecker Street's West End capture took $20.7 million, past "Hamilton" at just under $17 million, on a five-night event dated July 24 between "The Odyssey" and "Spider-Man."
CEO Summary
"Hadestown: The Musical," a filmed capture of the West End production released by Bleecker Street's Crosswalk label, has grossed $20.7 million, making it the highest-grossing live theater capture and passing "Hamilton," which took just under $17 million domestically in 2025. Billed as a five-night event, the run extended four weeks. It goes on demand August 25 and to physical media October 20.
Why This Matters
Only one of the two claims here is proven. Bleecker Street can document the gross. The cannibalization answer comes from the show's own creative producer describing what she observed, and the fear it addresses has kept a lot of running shows off screens.

The reporting does establish a repeatable mechanic: tickets on sale six weeks out, trailer released the same day, scarcity in the messaging, and a date in the one open week between two of the year's biggest films.

Sanderson adds the part that outlasts this title. A theatrical run made buyers willing to pay for the disc later, which argues for the window on grounds other than box office.
Specific Implication
For a rights holder with a stage property, the capture is a separate revenue line with its own theatrical, transactional and physical windows. Bundling it into a streaming deal as a promotional asset gives away three of them.
The Facts
  • "Hadestown: The Musical," a filmed capture of the West End production, has grossed $20.7 million, making it the highest-grossing live theater capture ever. It surpasses "Hamilton," which took just under $17 million domestically when released theatrically in 2025 after a long run on Disney+.
  • Billed as a "five night only" event, the run was extended for four weeks on demand.
  • Bleecker Street released it through Crosswalk, a division the company launched in 2025 for "event cinema." Crosswalk has also distributed "Waitress: The Musical" and "Stray Kids: The dominate Experience," a concert film from SoFi Stadium. "George Michael: The Faith Tour" is next.
  • Bleecker Street CEO Kent Sanderson on the campaign: "We put tickets on sale about six weeks before the film actually came out, and released the trailer on the same day with messaging to go buy tickets now because it will only be in theaters for a few nights."
  • It opened July 24, 2026, between "The Odyssey" (July 17) and "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" (July 31). Sanderson: "People probably thought we were crazy to go between two record-breaking movies. But we found our lane and were able to create the room we needed to coexist."
  • Three performances were captured at London's Lyric Theatre by Steam Motion and Sound.
  • The film goes on demand August 25; DVD and Blu-ray follow October 20. Sanderson said that within a couple of hours of pre-sales opening it was the number three physical media product on Amazon.
  • Sanderson on why the theatrical run raises downstream value: "releasing it in theaters makes it a more premium experience and that allows people to justify renting or buying the film later in a way they wouldn't if it were a straight-to-streaming release."
  • Creative producer Mara Isaacs said the stage productions saw a surge in ticket sales after the film's release, as did streams of the Broadway cast recording. Some theater producers have resisted filming shows still running on Broadway and the West End for fear cheaper access would suppress live ticket sales.
  • "Hadestown" originated as a concept album by Anaïs Mitchell, was developed in regional workshops and off-Broadway with director Rachel Chavkin, opened on Broadway in 2019 and won the Tony for best musical.

A New Private Equity Firm Raised $1 Billion for Sports and Media and Is Targeting a $7 Billion Fund
BlackSun's announced ventures give players equity in a proposed football league and fighters a pension funded from a share of broadcast and streaming revenue.
CEO Summary
BlackSun Private Equity has raised $1 billion for its first fund, targeting professional sports and franchise ownership with a stated focus on community and stakeholder participation. Dubai-based Greenstone Equity Partners is placing a Mega Fund I with a $7 billion target. Announced ventures include a World American Football League in which players hold team equity and Knockout Fights, where signed fighters receive salary, lifetime healthcare and a pension funded by a direct share of broadcast and streaming revenue.
Why This Matters
A challenger with no incumbent relationships is competing on terms rather than on price, which is the only lever a new entrant has and the reason those terms are now publicly on the table.
The Facts
  • BlackSun Private Equity is launching its first fund with $1 billion raised so far, targeting professional sports and franchise ownership with a focus on community and stakeholder participation.
  • BlackSun was founded by Atonn Muhammad, who played college football at Miami and launched cable's Real Hip-Hop Network in 2008, and investment banker Nery Gomez.
  • Strategy and communications chief Nick Rathod was a Deputy Director in the Obama White House and a Special Assistant to the President, ran Beto O'Rourke's Texas gubernatorial campaign, and worked with Sen. Elizabeth Warren on setting up the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
  • Managing Director John Godina is a four-time world champion and two-time Olympic medalist in shot put and founder of ALTIS, an elite track and field training center in Phoenix.
  • Jason Kidd, Roy Jones Jr., Lawrence Taylor and Gary Clark are attached as investors and advisors.
  • Capital initiatives include a $100 million SPAC, a $500 million PIPE program and a $750 million acquisition bridge facility.
  • Dubai-based Greenstone Equity Partners is exclusive global placement agent for BlackSun's Mega Fund I, which has a target of $7 billion. CIO Changa Ingram spent 18 years at the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, most recently as Senior Manager of Enterprise Risk and Regulatory Compliance.
  • The firm notes Middle East sovereign wealth funds have "demonstrated sustained appetite for alternative investment platforms at the intersection of sports, media, and culture."
  • Early moves include forming a group to bid for the Seattle SuperSonics, which are targeting a return to the NBA. Partners include Native World Sports, a platform for tribal nation participation in professional sports and entertainment.
  • Planned ventures: the World American Football League, in which players would own equity in teams, and Knockout Fights, a boxing and martial arts platform where signed fighters get a guaranteed salary, lifetime healthcare and a retirement pension supported by a direct share of broadcast and streaming revenue.
  • A community equity program run through DealMaker Securities will open participation to fan and community investors. The first campaign, supporting the World American Football League, launches in October.
  • The fund will also look at media and entertainment, IP, fintech and commercial real estate.

Netflix carries the show exclusively outside the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Spain, and waits 90 days past the AMC finale for U.S. and Canadian rights.

Netflix has spent a decade refusing to premiere behind another outlet at home. AMC Studios holds the lead-studio position, so Netflix is funding and sharing a series it does not control.

A seller who wants a domestic linear premiere alongside Netflix's international reach now has a precedent to point at, with the lead-studio position and the length of the domestic gap as the negotiable terms.
The Facts

  • Black co-wrote the first episode and will executive produce and direct the first two, his first TV series. Silverstein will showrun, write and executive produce, retaining his EP credit on Disney+'s Percy Jackson and the Olympians. Greg Nicotero and Brian Witten also executive produce.

  • Netflix and AMC will jointly debut each episode in Australia, New Zealand and Spain. Netflix carries the show exclusively everywhere else.

  • Deadline frames the deal as opening "a new avenue for Netflix to collaborate with traditional studios," following the co-licensing model introduced roughly a decade ago by now-Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria.

Why This Matters
The contract permitted termination without cause, so the dispute is about what the payout provision obligated. Aronson's complaint quotes co-chair Josh Greenstein assuring him Paramount would "pay you everything you're owed under your contract." An executive papering a deal with a studio in the middle of an integration should confirm that the pay-on-termination obligation is a stated term of the agreement rather than a discretionary practice.

Three Companies Take 94 Percent of a $150 Billion Vertical Video Market

CEO Summary
Vertical media is projected to generate $150 billion in revenue in 2026 outside China, a 42 percent gain over 2025, according to Owl & Co.'s first-half report. The U.S. accounts for about 40 percent of that. Meta, ByteDance and YouTube together generate 94 percent of the total. Owl & Co. counts nearly 2,000 apps worldwide competing for the remainder, with vertical-app startups including ReelShort, DramaBox, PineDrama and MyDrama spending heavily on customer acquisition.
Why This Matters
New series launches rose 25 percent in the second quarter while total watch time for new series fell 4 percent, which is the oversupply curve subscription streaming took a decade to reach.

The Facts
  • Vertical media is projected to generate $150 billion in revenue in 2026 in global markets outside China, a 42% gain over 2025, per Owl & Co.'s "Vertical Economy Report 1H26: Mapping Consumption, Creation, Value Capture Across a $150B Audiovisual Language."
  • Hernan Lopez, founder and CEO of Owl & Co., is the report's author.
  • $131 billion of the total is expected to come from advertising via platforms including TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook. Variety notes the numbers are approaching the volume of revenue generated in the U.S. by subscription streaming platforms.
  • Meta (Instagram, Facebook), ByteDance (TikTok) and YouTube generate 94% of the $150 billion. Meta draws 27% of its total revenue from vertical media, YouTube 22%, ByteDance 72%.
  • The U.S. accounts for about 40% of the projected 2026 revenue.
  • Owl & Co. counts nearly 2,000 apps worldwide fielding content. New series introductions grew 25% in the second quarter while total watch time of new series declined 4%.
  • Lopez writes: "Traditional streaming learned years ago about the diminishing marginal returns of launching too many shows."
  • On customer acquisition: "Some creators and show producers are finding viewership organically. But the apps themselves are spending a significant share of their revenue in customer acquisition. It's a lot like what TikTok was doing in the year 2020 when it was becoming popular."
  • Lopez on studio participation: "I think it makes sense for every company to lean into this medium which really represents a new native-digital visual language. Disney has a brand that's so unique and it has a global fandom. It makes it obvious why they will be the first ones to do it, but I think the one step that nobody has taken at scale is to produce original verticals."
  • Romance and drama thriller remain the dominant genres. Business, finance and news programs accounted for 12% of vertical media views outside China.

A secret three-year AI group run by Kathleen Kennedy and AFI published its first framework
The group's document sorts AI use into three tiers and attaches a copyright status to each, calling purely prompted performances, voices and stories not copyrightable.
CEO Summary
Producer Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute dean Susan Ruskin have convened Oscar-winning filmmakers, actors, studio executives and Silicon Valley figures in private since November 2023. The Ankler, which attended off the record, published the group's first public document on Thursday. It proposes three categories of AI use in final footage: utility and embedded tools, Human Generative Workflows, and Machine Generative. The first two are described as copyrightable; the third is not. The group calls it an argument, not a standard.
Why This Matters
The tiers borrow their authority from the U.S. Copyright Office rather than from any body that could enforce them. That is what makes them usable: a production adopting the vocabulary is describing its chain of title, not making a marketing claim, which is why the language will show up in AI riders before it shows up in any formal standard.

The document also names what it declined to settle: training data, licensing, consent, labor transition, economic policy. Those carry the money.
Specific Implication
Anyone drafting an AI provision now has a published definition to point at instead of building one per deal. The tier a use falls into determines whether the output is claimed as copyrightable, which is a term worth specifying.
The Facts
  • The meetings began at artist Refik Anadol's Los Angeles studio in November 2023, weeks after the strikes ended, then moved to the AFI campus. Google VP of technology and society Mira Lane on the choice of venue: AFI "has all the heads of the big studios, all the guilds are part of the board of trustees."
  • Last weekend the group expanded to roughly 120 participants for sessions on authorship, standards, transparency and control.
  • The three tiers: Utility Techniques and Embedded AI (denoising, upscaling, rotoscoping, markerless mocap, wire removal), described as copyrightable. Human Generative Workflows (artist-controlled pipelines in Nuke, Unreal, Blender, ComfyUI and DaVinci Resolve using narrowly trained LoRA models and structured inputs), described as copyrightable. Machine Generative (purely prompted likenesses, voices, performances or stories), described as not copyrightable.
  • The document quotes U.S. Copyright Office guidance that "prompts do not alone provide sufficient control," and that protection extends only to human contributions.
  • Worked example: "Dear Upstairs Neighbors," a six-minute animated short directed by Connie He, produced by Marcia Mayer, made by roughly 45 people including Pixar and DreamWorks veterans with Google DeepMind engineers. It premiered at Tribeca in June 2026.
  • Jon Avnet, DGA AI Committee co-chair with Christopher Nolan, led a weekend panel: "The key thing was to start the conversation in light of day."
  • The document cites existing market positions: A24's "Heretic" (2024) credited "No generative AI was used in the making of this film"; Vince Gilligan's "Pluribus" (2025) closed "This show was made by humans"; DreamWorks' "Bad Guys 2" used credits to prohibit AI training on the work.
  • Proposed next steps: publish the vocabulary for response, open consent talks on machine-generative outputs of actors, engage with certification efforts, and extend to music, sound and the writing room.

YouTube Is Offering Creators Millions Not To Put Their Videos On Netflix
No deal is signed yet. YouTube has told creators that signing with Netflix costs them marketing placement, event slots, and a share of proceeds from some major brand campaigns.
CEO Summary
YouTube is offering millions of dollars to popular channels that upload to the site exclusively for a set period, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the conversations. The money would come as direct financing of programs or as an allotted share of major brand deals. Netflix has been paying creators including Alan Chikin Chow and Nick DiGiovanni to post the same videos on both services, and remains in talks with dozens more, including the talk show Hot Ones.
Why This Matters
What YouTube is buying is not content. It is order of release. Exclusivity for a period is normally a term inside a license, and here it stands alone as the whole of the bargain. A creator who declines breaches nothing. They simply receive less of what the platform hands out at its own discretion.

Neal Mohan's stated position until recently was that creator deals with Instagram or Amazon Prime Video send viewers back to YouTube. Bloomberg reports that in recent weeks he and his team concluded concurrent Netflix posting was the exception. The reason given is advertising: a video also running on Netflix is harder to sell against.
Specific Implication
A creator weighing a concurrent-posting deal with a streamer has one question to settle before signing, and it is not the fee. It is whether the platform carrying their primary audience treats that deal as grounds to withdraw promotional support. Nothing obliges that platform to keep providing it.
The Facts
  • YouTube has not finalized a deal with any creator but is close to an agreement with several partners.
  • Netflix requires videos delivered days in advance and has asked creators to remove certain brand sponsorships. Some creators have declined on those terms.
  • Netflix has more than 325 million subscribers.
  • YouTube has told creators that cross-posting hurts YouTube viewership and signals that channels are deprioritizing it as their primary outlet.

Discovery would settle only on "real, robust, structural" remedies, specifying "structural, not behavioral." He said a relocation out of California would not defeat the states' standing, because the lawsuit's geographic jurisdiction is the United States and twelve attorneys general brought it. It is his first extended public comment since Paramount began its pressure campaign.
Why This Matters
Behavioral remedies are conduct promises: release counts, window lengths, in-state production floors, job guarantees. Every commitment Paramount has made publicly falls in that category. Bonta's stated condition therefore does not describe a narrower version of the announced transaction. It describes a different one, in which Warner Bros. assets are sold to a third party before any close.

That position held through a week in which three industry groups moved toward settlement. The DGA and IATSE wrote asking for talks, and Cinema United reversed its opposition. Bonta characterized the exhibitor group's shift as "neutral" and read the guild letters as stakeholders seeking certainty rather than as pressure on his office.
Specific Implication
A buyer or financier evaluating Warner Bros. assets should treat a pre-trial divestiture package as a live possibility before the March trial date, not only as a post-verdict outcome.
The Facts
  • Bonta gave the interview on Tuesday, August 18. It published August 19 at 12:08 AM.
  • Twelve state attorneys general, led by California, sued last month to block the acquisition. The Northern California District Court has allowed the case to proceed with little impediment.
  • On Paramount's motion asking the states to post a bond of nearly $2 billion against ticking fees: "There's no basis for it." Bonta noted the judge already declined a bond at the temporary restraining order stage.
  • Bonta said Paramount entered the ticking-fee agreement with Warner Bros. voluntarily and agreed not to close until 2027. "We had absolutely nothing to do with it."
  • On standing if Paramount relocates: "Anywhere he goes in the United States of America he cannot flee accountability."
  • Guild and industry positions: the WGA has sued to stop the merger; SAG-AFTRA and the Teamsters oppose it; the DGA and IATSE wrote asking for settlement talks; Cinema United shifted Tuesday to favor talks.
  • On the timeline: Bonta said Paramount was "foot-dragging and slow in responding to our requests for information in the investigative phase," and that "the time issue is Paramount's issue." He noted the case runs from complaint to full trial in under a year.
  • He declined to characterize his conversations with Governor Gavin Newsom, and said former Attorney General Xavier Becerra's pro-settlement comment was "aligned" with his own views.

A Los Angeles County Study Puts The Paramount-Warner Merger At 4,500 Jobs And $2.78 Billion

CEO Summary
A CVL Economics and Los Angeles County Department of Economic Opportunity analysis, obtained exclusively by TheWrap, estimates the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger could cost nearly 4,500 film and TV jobs in the county over three years. The report puts the associated loss at $1.26 billion in wages and $2.78 billion in economic value. It was ordered by and submitted to the county Board of Supervisors on Tuesday, after a 120-day study.
Why This Matters
The load-bearing figure in the report is not the job count. It is roughly $6.7 billion in identified annual cost reductions across overlapping operations, which CVL and the county tie to management's stated goal of reaching investment-grade leverage metrics within three years. That framing turns the job losses from a discretionary corporate choice into a financing requirement. The report adds that if revenues underperform or savings prove harder to reach, pressure for further reductions increases.

The county's own production data complicates the simplest version of its argument. Between 2023 and 2025, 8.2% of the two companies' films shot in California, against 8.1% for the rest of the market. Television is where they ran above market, at 30.3% of series with an identified production location versus 25.4%, and 85.4% of that California television work sat in Los Angeles County.
Specific Implication
The creators holding exclusive deals across the two companies are the population whose paper converts first if development shrinks. Anyone holding one should establish which of the two entities their agreement actually sits with, and what a change of control does to it.
The Facts
  • The report estimates 10,360 total job years at risk, including 2,661 indirect jobs at supporting small businesses and 3,204 induced jobs from local spending.
  • Full impact estimate: $4.06 billion in total business output and $547 million in tax revenue, of which $78.6 million is local and 63% of that is property taxes.
  • The county's creative economy supports more than 312,000 workers, including roughly 171,155 entertainment sector jobs.
  • The 4,500 direct jobs equal nearly 9% of the 52,016 film and TV jobs California has lost since 2022. 99.6% of those losses were in Los Angeles County.
  • An earlier 60-day interim report found roughly 2,500 local and 6,000 global jobs at risk.
  • A Paramount spokesperson said the report underscores an industry "in decline," and cited a plan to invest $30 billion annually in production and release at least 30 films a year.
  • A spokesperson for California Attorney General Rob Bonta called the report "one snapshot of the potential impact of the proposed merger."
  • The merger is on hold pending litigation from 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America, headed to trial in March. The final closing deadline is June 4, 2027.
  • David Ellison has threatened to move Paramount out of California if Bonta does not negotiate by Oct. 1, when a 25 cent per share ticking fee begins. That runs to $7 million per day.

CEO Summary
ABC filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission on Tuesday, arguing that the agency's investigations and regulatory orders were part of a Trump administration effort to punish the network for its coverage. The suit asks the court for a temporary restraining order barring the FCC from further action in the early renewal proceedings. An FCC spokesperson said all broadcasters have a legal obligation to operate in the public interest and that the commission has been examining claims of illegal DEI discrimination at Disney for over a year.
Why This Matters
The hard element in any retaliation claim is causation, and this complaint is built to prove it with the regulator's own words rather than with timing and inference. It quotes Chairman Brendan Carr telling the network's stations "we can do this the easy way or the hard way." It cites his warning that stations airing "fake news" had "a chance now to correct course before their license renewals come up." Most directly, it records Carr stating that the commission would weigh ABC's decision not to carry a July 16 presidential address when reviewing the stations' renewal applications.

The filing also puts the network's own editorial judgment into evidence. ABC's lawyers wrote that it returned Kimmel to air with full awareness that doing so was likely to invite further reprisal. Framing a business decision as a knowingly accepted cost is unusual in a regulatory dispute, and it is what turns an abstract chilling-effect argument into a documented one.
Specific Implication
Broadcast station buyers and affiliate groups now have a live instance of renewal timing used as leverage on licenses that still had two years to run. That belongs in transaction diligence and affiliation negotiations as a priced item rather than a routine administrative step.
The Facts
  • The FCC tied the early renewal order to an ongoing investigation of the network's diversity, equity and inclusion practices.
  • The complaint's third paragraph reproduces a Trump Truth Social post calling for license termination over "100% negative" newscast and late-night coverage.

  • The same inquiry demanded a list of every political donation by employees and co-hosts over the past four years, with dates.

  • ABC argues The View qualifies for the bonafide news programming exemption, and that the FCC affirmed as much in 2002.
  • Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the commission, has said the FCC is using an "undefined" concept as a "roving mandate to police speech."

The studio's 2027 slate consists of a "Minecraft" sequel, a "Superman" sequel, a Bradley Cooper and Margot Robbie "Ocean's" prequel, and "The Hunt for Gollum."
Why This Matters
The pattern inside the ledger is narrower than the year's headline. "Lee Cronin's The Mummy" returned $90 million on a $22 million budget and "Evil Dead Burn" returned $71 million on $20 million. Both are cheap New Line horror. Between $80 million and $180 million, the studio has four consecutive losses, including "Supergirl" at $126 million worldwide against a $180 million budget.

A studio coming off a year like this normally corrects by committing capital to an aggressive development cycle. Warner cannot do that while the Paramount acquisition is contested. The correction available to a company being bought is a freeze, and a 2027 slate assembled entirely from pre-sold franchises is what that looks like on paper.
Specific Implication
A filmmaker taking an original, non-franchise feature to Warner Bros. in the next six months should expect the budget conversation to anchor near the New Line horror band rather than near the studio's 2025 comparables.

The February deferral is the fact to hold onto. What arrives Sept. 1 is a baseline reset, not a change in direction. Nielsen states the overall trend line holds, with streaming still commanding the largest share of TV use by a wide margin. The reference point against which next season's numbers get compared is what moves.

Any compensation, bonus, or renewal threshold keyed to a Nielsen share should be checked for whether it names a methodology or simply references whatever Nielsen publishes. Season-over-season comparisons that cross Sept. 1 will rest on different universe estimates.

The complaint does not date the injury to the film's 2025 release. CEO Summary
Jason Statham's "Mutiny" opens in theaters on August 21. On August 19 it was available to stream in full on the US version of Amazon Prime Video for at least an hour. Neither production company, Punch Palace Productions and MadRiver Pictures, nor US distributor Lionsgate is owned by Amazon, and The Verge reported nothing to suggest the release was intentional or a marketing stunt. Amazon was contacted for comment.
Why This Matters
Anti-piracy provisions are written against unauthorized copying by third parties. Theatrical exclusivity covenants bind the distributor. This incident was neither. A platform holding no rights to the film served it at full quality through its own retail storefront, which is a failure mode that sits outside both instruments.

The parties absorbing the loss had no relationship with the system that caused it. Punch Palace and MadRiver produced the film and Lionsgate is releasing it. The reporting identifies no mechanism by which any of them would be made whole.
Specific Implication
Producers and distributors whose talent compensation is tied to theatrical performance should confirm, before the next release, whether their agreements name a remedy for a window broken by a platform they do not control.

The change is structural rather than personal. CEO Summary
Alamo Drafthouse will reopen the Cinerama Dome, closed since Arclight Cinemas folded after the pandemic, under a lease from Decurion Corp. Alamo CEO Michael Kustermann told TheWrap that talks with Decurion "picked up significantly after Sony acquired the chain in 2024, providing the financial backing for refurbishment and operation that Decurion was looking for." Kustermann named the mechanism directly, and it was a studio balance sheet that unlocked the lease. It gives Sony an asset to offer in a premiere or distribution negotiation that it did not hold in 2023.

ABC's own complaint says the FCC "cannot lawfully grant renewal this early in the license terms," so "the only outcomes on the table are adverse to Plaintiffs." The first station licenses were not due until 2028.
CEO Summary
ABC filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the FCC on Tuesday in federal court in Washington, D.C., naming the agency, chairman Brendan Carr and both commissioners. It seeks a temporary restraining order to halt the proceeding requiring ABC's eight owned stations to seek early license renewal, plus an order barring the FCC from acting to coerce the network over editorial decisions. No network had previously sued the agency.
Why This Matters
The complaint's central argument is procedural, and that is what makes it unusual. ABC is not asking a court to declare the FCC's motives unlawful in the abstract. It argues that the agency cannot lawfully grant an early renewal at all, which means every available outcome inside the FCC process is adverse, and the only remaining question is whether the harm arrives as years of litigation or as revocation. On that reading, participating in the agency proceeding is itself the loss, which is why the relief sought is an injunction against the proceeding rather than a ruling on the merits.

Timing supports the urgency claim. Bloomberg reported the FCC may issue a hearing designation order this month, which would open the adjudication ABC is trying to prevent.
Specific Implication
Owned-station groups now have a documented case that an early-renewal proceeding, on its own, constitutes the injury. Broadcasters facing similar FCC action have a filed template for seeking injunctive relief before a hearing designation order issues rather than after.
The Facts
  • The suit names the FCC, Carr, and commissioners Olivia Trusty and Anna Gomez, and was filed in federal court in Washington, D.C.
  • From the complaint: "Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts."
  • ABC on the range of outcomes: the FCC may "intentionally prolong the adjudicative process, miring ABC in years of costly litigation," or "use the hearing to deny license renewal or immediately revoke the Stations' licenses."
  • The first of the eight station licenses was not due for renewal until 2028.
  • The FCC cited an investigation of The Walt Disney Co.'s DEI policies when ordering early renewals. ABC calls it "pretextual," saying cooperation "simply begat increasingly aggressive demands."
  • The complaint cites Carr's September podcast remark, after a Jimmy Kimmel joke tied to the Charlie Kirk assassination investigation, that "we can do this the easy way or the hard way." Two station groups declined to air the show and ABC pulled Kimmel for several days.
  • Also cited: Carr's statement that ABC's decision not to air a Trump primetime address last month would factor into the license review, and an FCC review of whether The View retains its equal-time exemption.
  • ABC ran an on-air campaign soliciting comments: more than 153,000 filed on the licenses, more than 78,000 on The View.

  • The FCC under Carr has also investigated Comcast and NBCUniversal over DEI and CBS over a 60 Minutes edit.
  • Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA), quoted in the complaint, told an FCC official the agency is "getting into the foothills of violating the First Amendment."

Tom Holland Will Clear $100 Million On Spider-Man With An Uncapped Backend
Holland made $250,000 for his first Spider-Man appearance in 2016 and at least $20 million up front for this one, with a backend bonus that carries no cap.
CEO Summary
Three individuals with knowledge of the deal told TheWrap that Tom Holland took a base salary of at least $20 million on "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," up $10 million from "No Way Home," with an uncapped backend bonus that one source said will pay him at least $100 million. The film crossed $2 billion worldwide over the weekend in its third week of release. The deal was negotiated fresh after Holland's original six-picture contract expired. Sony said it does not comment on cast salaries.
Why This Matters
The term that distinguishes this deal is the absence of a ceiling, not the size of the guarantee. Every comparable in the reporting is a fixed negotiated outcome on a known quantity: Robert Downey Jr. cleared roughly $50 million on "Iron Man 3" and over $100 million across "Infinity War" and "Endgame," and Scarlett Johansson took $20 million up front on "Black Widow." An uncapped escalator converts the studio's exposure into a variable that only grows when the studio is already winning, which is how it clears business affairs when a raised guarantee would not.

Contract expiry is what created the opening. Holland's six-picture deal ended with "No Way Home," so the negotiation started from zero on a dated release with no substitute performer available.
Specific Implication
Performers reaching the end of an option ladder on a proven franchise should treat the expiry itself as the leverage event, and should press for an uncapped escalator rather than a larger fixed guarantee, since the studio prices the two differently.

  • Negotiated by WME agents Andrew Dunlap, James Farrell and Liam Buckley, and attorney Robert Offer.

Netflix Outspent The MPA In Washington For The First Time In 2025
Netflix spent $3.1 million lobbying Washington in 2025 against the MPA's $2.7 million, while also paying the MPA roughly $10 million a year in dues.
CEO Summary
Stephen Follows compiled every federal lobbying disclosure filed by the major Hollywood players since 1999: 3,437 filings containing 8,218 individual items through June 2026. In 2025 Netflix outspent the Motion Picture Association for the first time, $3.1 million to $2.7 million. Netflix's top lobbying subject is telecommunications, not copyright, which has been the MPA's number-one subject in 19 of the past 27 years. The dataset also dates the arrival of AI as a lobbying issue to the quarter ChatGPT launched.
Why This Matters
The studio side files roughly twice the AI lobbying volume of the guilds: 48 items to 22 in 2025, and 32 to 14 in the first half of 2026. Both camps publicly support the No Fakes Act, which cleared Senate Judiciary unanimously in June, and Follows notes that the two sides "do not want the same thing" on the underlying question of building with AI versus protecting against it.

That volume gap matters because statutory language is where the ambiguity gets resolved. A likeness right established by federal statute becomes the floor beneath every digital-replica clause currently negotiated deal by deal, and the party filing twice as often is the party in the room more often while the text is drafted.
Specific Implication
Performers and their counsel negotiating digital-replica terms should not assume the No Fakes Act will settle the question in their favor by default. The provision-level drafting is being shaped in a forum where the studio side is filing at roughly twice the guilds' volume.
The Facts
  • Dataset: 3,437 federal lobbying filings containing 8,218 individual items, covering the MPA, Netflix, Paramount, the other legacy studios, the cinema chains and the major guilds since 1999, through June 2026.
  • 2024: MPA $3.1 million, Netflix $1.9 million. 2025: Netflix $3.1 million, MPA $2.7 million. First time a single filmed-entertainment company outspent the trade body.
  • Netflix pays the MPA roughly $10 million a year in dues, judging by MPA tax filings. The MPA does not disclose the figure.
  • H1 2026: Netflix $2.15 million, $1.28 million in Q1 alone, while pursuing Warner Bros. Discovery's studio and streaming division. On pace to break its own record.
  • Netflix outside firms: three in 2024, six in 2025, nine in H1 2026. It hired Ballard Partners, whose quarterly Netflix retainer nearly doubled to $150,000 at the start of 2026. Paramount also retained Ballard during the bidding war.
  • Netflix's bid failed after Paramount pledged $31 a share for the whole company.
  • Paramount's in-house lobbying hit $6.2 million in 2025, its highest in 27 years of filings; $2.9 million in H1 2026. Figures cover the whole company including CBS News.
  • Netflix's top subjects are telecommunications, then communications and broadcasting. Its own disclosures rank "content delivery" first and "intellectual property protection" second. It funds Incompas and, since 2024, the Alliance for the Open Internet.
  • Copyright has been the MPA's top subject in 19 of 27 years and every year since 2018. Total MPA lobbying spend since 1999: $59.2 million.
  • Disney's top subject across 490 items since 1999 is broadcasting at nearly four in 10, with tax second and copyright third at about one in 10. Alone among the studios its top subjects include travel and tourism.
  • Federal tax was a fifth or more of MPA lobbying in the early 2000s, fell below a tenth by the early 2020s, and is back at 17% in 2025 and 19% in H1 2026. Recent entries name the CREATE Act and the Section 181 film deduction.
  • Trade peaked at 26% of MPA lobbying in 2019 and is at 14% in H1 2026. China mentions peaked 2019 to 2021.
  • AI first appears in Q4 2022, the quarter ChatGPT launched, on a bill criminalizing faked explicit images. Zero mentions ever before that. Both quarters of 2026 hit 23 items, the highest on record.
  • Of 215 AI items, the MPA's own team accounts for 41; Paramount, the DGA and Sony Pictures are the next largest in-house voices. Busiest outside firm on AI is the Goodlatte Group.
  • Comcast, Apple and Amazon are excluded from film-industry totals because a filing reports one figure across all topics.

California will exempt indie film credits from its $5 million tax cap but not studio credits
Independent film credits are transferable and can be sold to buyers offsetting state tax. Studio credits are not, and the deal gives studios only faster refunds inside the cap.
CEO Summary
California lawmakers are close to a deal easing the effect of Senate Bill 122, the June budget measure that caps annual corporate tax credits at 70 percent of liability or $5 million, whichever is greater, for three years. Per Variety's sources, the agreement would exempt independent film production credits outright while creating a mechanism to accelerate refunds on studio projects, and would extend the expiration date on old non-refundable credits by five years. Lawmakers face an August 31 deadline to pass bills this session.
Why This Matters
The split follows the instrument, not the industry. An indie credit is collateral: it is sold to a third party and banked before a frame is shot, so a cap on the buyer's annual claim destroys its value at the moment of financing. A studio credit is an accounting entry against a large liability, and delay costs interest rather than access to capital. Lawmakers protected the financeable one.

The Entertainment Union Coalition memo makes the financing point directly, warning the cap would make it harder for independent productions "to sell their tax credits to buyers or even get financing from banks."
Specific Implication
Producers financing California independents can continue to price a transferable state credit into the capital stack. Studio-side budgets shot in California should model the credit as a multi-year receivable rather than a near-term offset when comparing against New York, Illinois, Canada or the United Kingdom.
The Facts
  • Gov. Gavin Newsom signed SB 122 on June 29 as part of the budget package. The cap was written to stop companies, particularly in tech, from erasing state tax liability through research and development credits.
  • The legislative fix is led by Assemblyman Rick Chavez Zbur and Sen. Ben Allen, who had sought a full carveout. Newsom's office is in the negotiations; the Office of Business and Economic Development declined to comment.
  • The cap lands one year after California raised its production incentive from $330 million to $750 million, a program that has qualified more than 110 film, television and animation projects.
  • The Entertainment Union Coalition says more than 350,000 letters have been sent by union members to Sacramento lawmakers over SB 122.
  • ProdPro reported a 5 percent year-over-year rise in California production spending last quarter.
  • Lawmakers have been mindful that a full film carveout would prompt tech companies to demand one of their own.
  • A separate bill, AB 2319, would create a 35 to 50 percent refundable credit for post-production work. A $150 million soundstage-construction incentive has been fully depleted; reauthorization is expected next session.
  • One person involved told Variety: "There was a lot of fanfare over the expansion. It feels like there was a commitment that was made and that was rescinded."
  • Zbur told TheWrap: "we are in the process of building out a fix that would mitigate the impacts that SB 122 has on this program."

Broadcast Viewing Rose 118 Percent In June And Still Finished Behind YouTube
A World Cup and an NBA Finals in the same month more than doubled broadcast viewing, and YouTube still finished first among all distributors at 13.8 percent.
CEO Summary
Nielsen's June Gauge report shows broadcast viewing up 118% to a 19.8% share of TV time, its first June increase since the report launched in 2021, driven by the FIFA World Cup and the NBA Finals. Cable fell 2% to 19.5%. Streaming was 48.5%. Fox and NBCUniversal, the World Cup's broadcast and streaming homes, were the only distributors to post viewing increases, drawing over 84 billion minutes combined.
Why This Matters
The month is a controlled test of what live sport can do to the distribution split, because the inputs were close to maximal: a World Cup and an NBA Finals inside the same four weeks. Broadcast doubled and landed at 19.8%, against streaming's 48.5%, with YouTube alone at 13.8%.

The narrower reading is about proportional lift versus absolute position. Fox Sports 1 viewing rose 232% and Fox affiliate viewing 73%, and Fox finished fifth. Telemundo, holding exclusive Spanish-language rights, posted the largest proportional gain in the report at 143% affiliate growth with Hispanic viewing up nearly 200% month over month. Exclusivity produced the sharpest movement; it did not produce a ranking change.
Specific Implication
Rights holders negotiating language-exclusive carve-outs have a measured comparable: exclusive Spanish-language World Cup rights delivered Telemundo a 143% affiliate lift and a near-200% increase in Hispanic viewing in a single month.
The Facts
  • Broadcast: +118% to a 19.8% share, its first June increase since the Gauge launched in 2021.
  • Cable: down 2% to a 19.5% share, with cable sports viewing down 10% month over month absent the NBA and NHL playoffs.
  • Streaming: 48.5% of TV viewing, up about 3% from May, just under the 3.1% rise in total TV usage.
  • Distributor ranking: YouTube 13.8%, Disney 9.6% (4.6% from Disney+, Hulu and ESPN+), NBCU and Versant combined 9.1% (NBCU 7%, Versant 2.1%), Netflix 7.9%, Fox 7.4%, Paramount 6.8% (2.3% streaming), Warner Bros. Discovery 5.3% (1.4% streaming), Amazon 4.3%, The Roku Channel 3%, Scripps 1.6%, Weigel 1.4%, A&E Networks 0.9%, Hallmark 0.8%, AMC Networks 0.6%.
  • Fox and NBCUniversal were the only distributors to post increases. The World Cup drew over 84 billion minutes across their properties combined.

Higgsfield Published The Prompts Behind Its Cannes AI Feature And Made Certification Free
Higgsfield's CEO says the $100 million exclusive contracts other AI companies pitched to studios "completely overpromised and underdelivered," so his company is giving its prompts away instead.
CEO Summary
Higgsfield AI launched Higgsfield Academy in August, publishing the prompts used to make "Hell Grind," its 95-minute AI-generated feature that premiered at the Marché du Film at Cannes in May, and offering free certification in its Cinema Studio platform. The company reports a $500 million annual run rate reached within 14 months, over 26 million users, and use by 390 of the Fortune 500. Co-founder and CEO Mahi de Silva said the company is "not in the content creation business" but "in the tools distribution business."
Why This Matters
De Silva stated the switching cost on the record: "You can cut and paste a prompt right out of our system and play it somewhere else, but you're likely not to get the visual coherence, the visual fidelity from scene to scene. That's part of our magic." Publishing the prompts is therefore not a giveaway of the product. It distributes the part that ports and retains the part that does not, while building a pool of filmmakers trained on one company's workflow.

The likeness detail sits underneath. Higgsfield's second feature, "The Cully Hill Boys," used the likenesses of Israel Adesanya, Quinton "Rampage" Jackson and the creator N3on in a film the company describes as a teaching tool rather than content. That is a use case standard digital-replica language was not drafted around.
Specific Implication
Anyone granting likeness rights to an AI platform should establish whether the resulting material will function as a production, a product demonstration, or training data, since those three carry different reuse and duration terms.
The Facts
  • Higgsfield Academy launched in August, publishing the prompts behind "Hell Grind" and offering free platform certification.
  • "Hell Grind" is 95 minutes and premiered at the Marché du Film at Cannes in May. It was criticized for its plot and praised by some viewers for its visuals.
  • The company surpassed a $500 million annual run rate within 14 months, claiming to be the fastest-growing generative AI company in history. Higgsfield.ai reports over 31 million monthly visits and over 26 million users.
  • Its platform is used by 390 of the Fortune 500 and more than 170,000 corporate accounts.
  • De Silva on the prior vendor approach: companies told studios "you can sign an exclusive deal with us. You have to commit $100 million to a contract, and trust us, we're going to make it work for you... And I think the companies that did that have completely overpromised and underdelivered."
  • De Silva on positioning: "I think it sends mixed signals to studios if they think we're going to try to compete with them... We are not in the content creation business. We're in the tools distribution business."
  • De Silva declined to characterize the company's Hollywood customer base in detail, but said Higgsfield has supported filmmakers on reshoots and visual effects.
  • A single shot's prompt can require instructions covering characters, environments, camera movement, lighting, action and continuity, plus assets already built inside Cinema Studio.
  • Second feature "The Cully Hill Boys" used the likenesses of two-time UFC champion Israel Adesanya, MMA veteran Quinton "Rampage" Jackson and livestream creator N3on.
  • Content lead Adil Alimzhanov on the first Academy lesson, identifying AI artifacts: "The plastic look, where the skin is too smooth, the lighting is too perfect, and then the uncanny valley effect, where everything is too symmetrical, too perfect."
  • De Silva: "machines are not going to be a substitute for humans... giving them access to realizing their creative talent at a tiny fraction of what it used to cost."

Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" is now the highest-grossing film in the history of BFI IMAX, the UK's largest cinema screen, with more than 101,000 admissions and £2,683,987 in ticket sales from a single auditorium at 95% occupancy. The presale record is the transferable number. Distributors negotiating premium-format guarantees should treat single-venue capacity as the binding constraint on titles with this demand profile, since the venue ran at 95% occupancy and sold out weeks ahead.

Australia's Screen And Games Sector Produced $7.9 Billion And 40 Percent Of Games Firms Own No Rights
Australia's screen and games sector exported $1.1 billion in FY2023/24, and 40 percent of its games businesses own no rights at all to the titles they release.
CEO Summary
Screen Australia's "Screen Currency 2026" study puts the sector's gross value added at AUD11.1 billion ($7.9 billion) in FY2023/24, with 68,844 people directly employed in FY2024/25 and exports of AUD1.6 billion ($1.1 billion). Games exports grew at 15.4% a year since 2016/17, more than three times the screen rate. The study also found that 45% of games businesses retain full rights to their titles at first release, 15% hold partial rights, and 40% own none.
Why This Matters
Export growth and rights ownership are separate measurements, and this study reports both. A sector can post 15.4% annual export growth while 40% of its companies own nothing they ship, which describes work-for-hire volume rather than a rights position.

The screen side shows the same structure one level up. The study's own case study reports that "MasterChef Australia," an adaptation of a British format, generates an estimated AUD700 million a year in licensing and commercial revenue for Banijay, its French-owned rights holder. Endemol Shine Australia COO Scott Howard said on the record that the country's success adapting formats has not been matched by investment in original local IP.
Specific Implication
Buyers and financiers evaluating a production territory should ask for the rights-retention split alongside the output and export figures, since this study shows the two can move in opposite directions inside the same sector.
The Facts
  • Sector gross value added: AUD11.1 billion ($7.9 billion) in FY2023/24. Screen AUD10.8 billion, games AUD317 million.
  • Direct employment FY2024/25: 68,844, split 66,080 screen and 2,764 digital games development.
  • Exports FY2023/24: AUD1.6 billion ($1.1 billion), comprising AUD1.3 billion screen and AUD323 million games. Royalty exports rebounded to AUD415 million in FY2024/25.
  • Games exports grew 15.4% annually between 2016/17 and 2023/24, versus 4.7% annually for screen exports since 2008/09. Games are roughly a fifth of total sector export earnings.
  • 188 registered digital games businesses in FY2021/22, growing 15.3% annually since 2015/16.
  • Rights: 45% of games businesses hold full rights at first release, 15% partial, 40% none.
  • "Bluey" is named the country's most effective cultural export, cited as the most-streamed show in the U.S. in 2025.
  • Audience gap: 84% of Australians rate local screen content as important to access and 75% want more, but only 36% consider it easy to find, and nearly two-thirds watch it for under 30% of total viewing time.
  • Government funding, direct and indirect, is now the leading finance source behind Australian narrative drama, documentary and children's television.
  • Arts Minister Tony Burke pointed to new legislation requiring streaming services to carry a minimum amount of Australian content.
  • International recognition of 11 recent Australian titles: U.K. and New Zealand 88%, India 80%, U.S. 67%, China 65%, Canada 61%, Singapore 60%, Germany 46%.
  • Screen Australia CEO Deirdre Brennan said future success depends on "businesses building durable intellectual property, strengthening audience relationships and improving discoverability in a market increasingly shaped by algorithms and platform recommendations rather than active search."
  • "MasterChef Australia," in its 18th season on Network Ten since 2009, is estimated by the Australian Financial Review to generate AUD700 million a year for Banijay. It airs in more than 120 countries with roughly 60 localized adaptations.
  • ESA COO Scott Howard said format success has not been matched by investment in original local IP and the industry needs more support to develop homegrown intellectual property.
  • The study drew on more than 40 stakeholder consultations, 18 research partners and 13,750 participants including 13,550 survey respondents across six surveys.

The variable here is renewal timing, not relationship quality. Producers and showrunners whose studio deals expire before the Warner transaction closes hold unusually strong renewal leverage, because the incumbent cannot make forward slate commitments and rival buyers know the expiration date.

Round Hill Music sued Suno and Anthropic and asked for a jury instead of a license
The complaint lists 500 songs and says it will be amended to at least 10,000. Round Hill's counsel is Richard S. Busch, who won the "Blurred Lines" verdict for the Marvin Gaye estate.
CEO Summary
Independent music publisher Round Hill Music sued Suno and Anthropic in federal court in California, alleging both companies scraped its songs to train models without permission in violation of the Copyright Act. Round Hill owns rights to Bonnie Tyler's "Total Eclipse of the Heart," the Goo Goo Dolls' "Iris" and more than 10,000 other compositions and recordings. It puts damages in the "hundreds of millions of dollars" and says they "may ultimately approach or exceed $1 billion," and it is demanding a jury trial.
Why This Matters
Every prior music action against these two defendants has ended in a rate. Warner Music settled with Suno. BMG sued Anthropic and then licensed to Suno inside the same year. Round Hill is asking for a verdict instead, and a verdict produces a number the whole market can see, where a settlement produces one only the parties know.

The choice of counsel is consistent with that. Busch's record is built on taking a music copyright question to a jury and getting a figure, not on negotiating a rate.
Specific Implication
Rights holders currently negotiating AI training licenses should track this docket as a pricing event rather than a legal one, because a jury figure would become the first public benchmark against which private rates are measured.
The Facts
  • Round Hill CEO Josh Gruss: "We are not against artificial intelligence. We are against the idea that you can build a business worth billions on top of other people's creative work and pay the creators nothing. Licensing isn't an obstacle to innovation, it is there to protect the legal owners of the raw material, their property."
  • Busch: "Copyrighted works have been used to build multi-billion dollar businesses, and in the case of Anthropic a company now valued at more than a trillion dollars, while the songwriters and publishers who created the foundations of that value have received nothing. There is nothing fair about that use."
  • Suno has been sued by Warner Music Group, Universal Music Group and Sony Music. It settled with WMG last year and struck a licensing agreement with BMG last week.
  • BMG sued Anthropic earlier this year over alleged use of its recordings in training, describing it as "widespread and systematic infringement."
  • Representatives for Suno and Anthropic did not respond to Variety's immediate requests for comment.
