Roughly $1 trillion in undeployed U.S. private equity capital is sitting on the sidelines, and the recurring thesis among firms circling entertainment is that sports, live events and scarce real-world experiences are valuable precisely because generative AI cannot easily replace them. Apollo argued this in a December 2025 white paper and launched Apollo Sports Capital in September. Private equity now holds stakes across the representation business, including WME (Silver Lake), UTA (EQT), Independent Artist Group (Yucaipa), Gersh (Crestview), Innovative Artists (Coral Tree) and Excel Sports Management (Goldman Sachs), plus management firms Entertainment 360 (Carlyle), Initial Group (TPG) and Brillstein Entertainment Partners via The Team (Providence).
Why This Matters
Apollo published its sports-as-AI-hedge thesis in a December 2025 white paper and launched Apollo Sports Capital in September. The same reasoning is cited by The Ankler as underlying private equity's broader move into sports and representation assets rather than into scripted libraries or studios. Those assets include stakes in WME, UTA, Excel Sports Management and other agencies. Firms in this space typically target 18 to 20 percent annual returns on a five-to-seven-year exit horizon, a structure the reporting says pushes deployment decisions on a fixed timeline regardless of asset quality. Providence Equity's reported buyout of the remainder of The Team at a $3.4 billion valuation, following a months-long shopping process of the company's individual divisions, is cited as a specific instance of this dynamic.
Specific Implication
A representation or management company with private equity ownership operating on a five-to-seven-year fund horizon is a more likely candidate for divisional carve-out than for a whole-company sale, based on the Providence Equity/The Team precedent.

The reversion structure concentrates the cost of failure on the corporate parties while leaving the creative team's position intact. Two Hollywood Unions Break With the WGA and Ask California to Let the Paramount-Warner Merger Through

CEO Summary
The Directors Guild of America and IATSE jointly wrote to California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison on Wednesday, urging them to settle the antitrust suit over the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger on conditions rather than fight to a March 2, 2027 trial. The letter puts both unions at odds with the Writers Guild, which sued to block the deal. It sets out nine conditions, including keeping the two studios operationally separate, minimum theatrical output with a 45-day exclusive window, and keeping Paramount headquartered in Los Angeles.
Why This Matters
The letter's substance is a behavioral consent decree, the category of remedy Bonta has publicly ruled out, so its practical function is pressure rather than a settlement blueprint. It aligns two guilds with Paramount's timing problem without endorsing the deal. Its fallback request for an earlier trial date targets the delay itself, the variable the unions say is already costing their members work. A regulator holding out for structural relief now faces labor on the other side of the courtroom aisle. That changes the political cost of running the clock to trial even if it changes nothing in the legal posture.
Specific Implication
The 45-to-60-day theatrical window figure in the unions' letter gives any negotiation over exclusivity terms a specific number to cite. It was offered to win labor support during a contested merger process rather than negotiated as a standalone distribution term. Its durability depends on a settlement Bonta has indicated he is not inclined to accept.
The Facts
  • The letter was signed by DGA national executive director Russell Hollander and IATSE international president Matthew Loeb, and sent to Bonta and Paramount leadership on Wednesday.
  • The Writers Guild filed its own antitrust suit to block the merger.
  • Nine conditions, per TheWrap. The most prominent: Paramount and Warner Bros. maintained as separate studios with their own distribution, marketing and production divisions; Paramount's headquarters kept in Los Angeles. Others as written: each studio produces and distributes a minimum of 15 theatrical films per year with an exclusive theatrical window of at least 45 days, preferably 60 or more, before PVOD and 120 days before SVOD; third-party theatrical licensing held at no less than the five-year average percentage, excluding 2020 and 2023; the same separate structure for the television studios; HBO maintained as a linear pay-television channel available on third-party platforms; US production held at no less than the five-year average; third-party original-content licensing held at no less than the five-year average.
  • From the letter: "While we have been consistent in our view that mergers, such as this one, historically offer few benefits to workers, we are also particularly concerned about the negative impact a delay in the decision regarding the proposed merger will have on our members and the industry at large." And: "We are aware of productions that have been put on hold or canceled altogether."
  • Bonta led a 12-state coalition suing in July over consolidation in basic cable and theatrical distribution. Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin issued a temporary restraining order and set trial for March 2, 2027. Paramount had sought November; Bonta asked for April 2027.
  • Bonta has said he is not interested in behavioral remedies, including a 30-films-a-year pledge with a 45-day window, and will only accept structural remedies.
  • Exhibition is split: AMC's Adam Aron and Regal's Eduardo Acuna have endorsed the merger; the trade group Cinema United opposes it; Cinemark's Sean Gamble has not endorsed. More than 90% of Cinema United members operate fewer than 75 screens. Cinema United has balked at Paramount's three-year exhibitor contracts, pushing for a longer commitment.
  • Per LightShed: the merger agreement expires June 4, 2027; a loss would trigger a $7 billion breakup fee, which the firm calls the largest in US corporate history; Paramount's 30-film pledge was first put to Bonta's office in May inside a 12-point behavioral consent decree that went unanswered; Bloomberg reported three-year contracts with AMC and Regal guaranteeing 30 films a year, a 45-day minimum window and a 90-day streaming holdback on close.
  • The combined company is expected to carry a debt load of roughly $79 billion to $80 billion.
  • If no settlement is reached, the unions ask both sides to agree to an earlier trial date.

The structural change is in who originates. Toyota conceiving a talk show and pitching it to creator Kareem Rahma reverses the customary direction of the pitch. YouTube announced on August 10 that new applicants to its Partner Program will need 8,000 qualified watch hours over the past year or 20 million qualified Shorts views over the past 90 days, double the current 4,000 hours and 10 million views. The change takes effect February 1, 2027 and does not apply to creators already in the program. It converts Partner Program membership into an incumbency asset, since established channels keep terms new entrants must now clear at far higher cost. It lands in the same week X restricted creator payouts to original content and Meta is spending to lure creators away. A platform tightening terms while its rivals loosen theirs is making a statement about relative position: YouTube is pricing its distribution as scarce, and the value of an already-monetized channel rises accordingly.

  • New YPP thresholds effective February 1, 2027: 8,000 qualified watch hours over the previous 365 days, or 20 million qualified Shorts views over the previous 90 days. Current thresholds are 4,000 watch hours or 10 million Shorts views. The 1,000-subscriber requirement is unchanged.

  • Premium Lite expands to all countries where YouTube Premium is available. Subscription revenue share to creators is based on member watch time and views, 55 percent to long-form video creators and 45 percent to Shorts creators.

BMG becomes the second significant rightsholder to settle with Suno after Warner Music Group, while Universal Music Group and Sony Music litigation against the company continues.
Why This Matters
BMG settling with one AI company while continuing to litigate against another shows identical claim types being priced by counterparty. Where the defendant offers forward revenue and product participation, infringement exposure converts into a license; where it does not, the claim stays in court. Training-data claims are functioning as negotiable assets whose market price is being discovered one settlement at a time, not as principles to be vindicated. The German ruling against Suno last month sits in the background as the pricing pressure that makes forward licenses cheaper than verdicts.
The Facts
  • The agreement is a global strategic alliance covering BMG's recorded music and music publishing repertoire, announced August 12, 2026.
  • Suno pays for BMG's repertoire and the deal covers use of BMG songs in training Suno's past models.
  • BMG artists and songwriters must opt in before their music is used for inputs (training) or outputs (works generated by Suno users); those who opt in are compensated.
  • BMG joins Warner Music Group in settling with Suno. WMG's alliance was announced roughly nine months earlier.
  • Suno CEO and co-founder Mikey Shulman: "We believe the future of music will be more participatory, creating entirely new ways for artists and fans to connect. Building that future responsibly means working directly with the people who make music and the companies that represent them."
  • Celine Joshua, BMG EVP global marketing and streaming: "Choice is the guiding principle. This agreement establishes strong protections, clear economics, and new creative possibilities for artists and their fans."
  • Still outstanding: Universal Music Group and Sony Music copyright suits against Suno; a German court ruling last month that Suno violated US and German copyright law; BMG's own suit against Anthropic.
  • Suno began watermarking downloaded songs last week and limited downloads across its three usage tiers.

A Combined Warner-Paramount Would Still Earn Most of Its Profit From Linear TV
Linear produced $2.5 billion of adjusted EBITDA on revenue down 14 percent, while the combined studio business earned $132 million, down 84 percent, on revenue down 26 percent.
CEO Summary
Combining the just-reported Q2 numbers from Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery produces a pro-forma view of the merged company. Revenue would have been $15.6 billion, down 6.2 percent year over year, with net profit of $190 million, adjusted EBITDA of $2.98 billion, up 5.8 percent, and free cash flow of $830 million, essentially flat. Linear television would have supplied about 46 percent of revenue at $7.12 billion, down 14 percent, but $2.5 billion of adjusted EBITDA, up 3.5 percent. Streaming revenue would have been $5.55 billion, up 10 percent, with $878 million of adjusted EBITDA, up 60 percent. The studio business would have been the weak leg: $3.64 billion of revenue, down 26 percent, and $132 million of adjusted EBITDA, down 84 percent.
Why This Matters
The pro-forma exposes the merger's central structural bind. The segment generating most of the combined profit is the same declining asset regulators are most likely to demand the merged company address. Management's promise to bring leverage down within three years of closing depends on exactly that cash flow. A structural remedy would not merely shrink the company; it would strip the earnings that make the debt serviceable. That is why the remedies fight is existential for the capital structure rather than a negotiation over conditions. It is also why the studio segment's collapse matters: it removes the alternative profit engine that would make a linear divestiture survivable.
Specific Implication
An output commitment or overall deal negotiated against either studio currently sits against a company whose studio segment, by this pro-forma measure, contributed a small and declining share of adjusted EBITDA relative to linear television.
The Facts
  • Pro-forma combined Q2 2026 (PSKY plus WBD, no combined earnings call): revenue $15.6 billion, down 6.2 percent; net profit $190 million; adjusted EBITDA $2.98 billion, up 5.8 percent; free cash flow $830 million, up $14 million.
  • Linear TV: about 46 percent of total revenue. Revenue $7.12 billion, down 14 percent. Adjusted EBITDA $2.5 billion, up 3.5 percent.
  • Streaming: about 36 percent of total revenue. Revenue $5.55 billion, up 10 percent. Adjusted EBITDA $878 million, up 60 percent.
  • Studios: about 23 percent of total revenue. Revenue $3.64 billion, down 26 percent. Adjusted EBITDA $132 million, down 84 percent.
  • Percentages do not total 100 because internal licensing revenue and corporate costs are deducted.
  • Reporting caveat: Paramount books its CBS Media Ventures syndication arm inside linear TV, while Warner books syndication inside its studio business.
  • Q2 comparisons absorb the loss of the NBA in its largest annual revenue quarter and no Final Four for CBS.
  • Warner and Paramount collectively wrote off $15 billion from the value of the cable business in 2024.
  • David Ellison has reportedly obtained board approval for a corporate headquarters move out of California as of October 1, when the ticking fee begins; a move is reported to save an additional $500 million a year in corporate taxes.
  • Management has promised Wall Street it will bring leverage down to reasonable levels within three years of closing.

ByteDance's New Model Blocks 80 Percent of Copyright Prompts After Hollywood Complained
Seedance 2.5 blocked 80 percent of copyright prompts and 100 percent of attempts to generate video from copyrighted images, but it blocked them at the output stage after rendering, and it still produced Shark Tale's Oscar unprompted by name.
CEO Summary
ByteDance's new video generator Seedance 2.5 is successfully blocking most attempts to reproduce Hollywood intellectual property, according to research shared with Deadline by VN.ai, a startup that stress tests generative AI tools for copyright infringement. The predecessor model, Seedance 2.0, produced a wave of infringing videos including a viral Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt fight clip and drew cease-and-desist letters from Disney and Netflix over titles including Stranger Things and The Avengers. VN.ai found Seedance 2.5 blocks around 80 percent of prompts involving copyrighted material and 100 percent of attempts to create video from copyrighted images, but does so by moderating the rendered output rather than refusing the prompt.
Why This Matters
Because the blocking happens only after a faithful render, the improvement is evidence for the studios' core claim, not against it. The protected works remain in the model, and what changed is ByteDance's willingness to serve them. That leaves the training-data cause of action, the basis of rightsholder leverage, fully intact while removing the viral outputs that generated public pressure. It is a compliance posture that lowers ByteDance's visibility as a defendant without lowering its exposure.
Specific Implication
For a rights holder pursuing enforcement against AI-generated reproductions of well-known characters, VN.ai's findings indicate that output-stage detection is currently more consistent for famous IP than for lesser-known characters. Prompt variations were still shown to bypass the guardrail on the latter.
The Facts
  • Seedance 2.5 launched in late July 2026. VN.ai stress tested it and shared findings with Deadline.
  • VN.ai found Seedance 2.5 blocks around 80 percent of prompts involving copyrighted material, described as far more consistent than Seedance 2.0 or the Seedream 5 image generator, and 100 percent of attempts to create videos from copyrighted images.
  • The block happens at the output stage: the model renders the video, moderates it, and refuses to serve it.
  • VN.ai produced a faithful video of Shark Tale's Oscar without using the character's name or the DreamWorks title.
  • Seedance 2.0 produced a viral Tom Cruise versus Brad Pitt fight video and reproductions of titles including Stranger Things and The Avengers; Disney and Netflix sent ByteDance cease-and-desist letters, and ByteDance said it had "heard the concerns."
  • ByteDance spokesperson: "ByteDance launches models with AI transparency measures and guardrails designed to prevent the unauthorized use of intellectual property, which we continually work to strengthen in collaboration with creative communities as AI technologies evolve."
  • Deadline reported last week that MiniMax H3, another Chinese model, was being used to create remixed videos of The Office, Friends and Star Wars; MiniMax did not respond to a request for comment.
  • In the same reporting, VN.ai generated bootleg images of Elsa, Shrek and Buzz Lightyear via Seedream 5.0 through a third-party API, and found that tweaking prompts to specify exact pixel sizes defeated character-name denials.

CEO Summary
Spotify-owned The Ringer began live-streaming its sports gambling show Ringer Wise Guys on Amazon-owned Twitch on Monday, its first video podcast on the platform and the first activity on a Ringer Twitch account dormant for roughly eight years. Episodes still post to YouTube, Spotify and other feeds later the same day, so only the live window moved. Twitch has 150 million average monthly visitors against YouTube's more than 2.5 billion monthly active users, and its entire Talk Shows and Podcasts category accounted for under 1% of live viewers on the morning of publication.
Why This Matters
Dan Clancy's on-record sorting of formats defines the actual contested ground: shows that riff and respond suit Twitch, and guest-driven interview shows do not. Twitch is not bidding for podcasting's on-demand catalog but for the live premiere hour of a specific interactive subset. That narrows the challenge to YouTube while making it more precise, since the premiere is where chat, polls and live monetization operate. It is the one piece of an established show a rival platform can take without asking the audience to move its library habits.
Specific Implication
Splitting a live premiere window from same-day on-demand distribution, as done here, creates two distribution rights that can be licensed to different platforms rather than one. The audience scale on the live side here, 670 viewers, is a fraction of the show's existing on-demand reach.

CEO Summary
"Lanterns" premieres Sunday on HBO after a nearly seven-year path involving at least four takes and two creative teams, the first live-action scripted DC series developed under James Gunn and Peter Safran. DC and HBO also passed on Poison Ivy and Catwoman pitches, and "Booster Gold" is searching for a new writer. The pattern locates DC's television problem in governance rather than economics. The regime whose first move was to cancel the five series it inherited has now killed or stalled most of the slate it announced to replace them. The 2023 reset installed a taste bottleneck where a pipeline was promised. A label that discards a fully scripted season over a creative disagreement, with cost never raised, is exercising a veto that operates after delivery. That is the stage at which it is most expensive for every party involved.
Specific Implication
An overall or series commitment tied to franchise television at a major superhero label carries a reported risk of extended, multi-regime development delay or cancellation independent of budget. Both the WBD and Disney examples in this reporting show that risk.
The Facts

And: "It wasn't a note that was borne or driven by budget. No one ever said, 'Listen, we can't afford to make the version of the show you're talking about.' I never got that note."
  • Berlanti took three stabs at Green Lantern, then approached David Zaslav, who blessed his exit from DC entirely. He remains at Warner Bros. Television on an overall deal. His 2011 Green Lantern feature grossed $237 million worldwide on a $200 million budget.
  • A season-two writers room for "Lanterns" has been working more than a month without an official HBO renewal. Lindelof will not return, having signed for one season. Reviews are embargoed until Friday, and HBO wanted to see reception before deciding.

  • The DC IP is described as among the most consequential assets at stake in Paramount Skydance's $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery.

CEO Summary
David Ellison told Paramount's 12-member Executive Leadership Team last Wednesday that he will move the company to Tennessee, Texas, Georgia or another state if California Attorney General Rob Bonta does not negotiate a settlement in the 12-state antitrust suit against the $110 billion Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition. He set an October 1 deadline, the date a $7 million-per-day ticking fee to WBD shareholders begins, and said the board has already approved the move. The relocation threat fails its own arithmetic. The deadline reads as a measure of Paramount's cost of delay rather than a moving timetable. That inversion weakens the threat as leverage, because the party bleeding the larger daily amount in a stalemate is Paramount, and Bonta's office can price the October date accordingly.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Tuesday he would consider structural remedies to settle the 12-state antitrust suit against Paramount Skydance's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, defining them as "keeping certain corporate entities separate" in the challenged markets. He rejected behavioral remedies including David Ellison's pledge of 30 films a year, calling it "an old stale promise," and separately ruled out a CNN divestiture on the grounds that the complaint has "little, if any, mention of CNN." Hours later at the same Politico conference, Paramount Chief Legal Officer Makan Delrahim said "everything is on the table" while predicting the states' cable claim "will fall apart because of the market definition."
Why This Matters
The consequential move is the CNN carve-out. By taking the one politically convenient divestiture off the table while insisting on structural relief, Bonta narrowed the settlement space to the assets covered by the three markets the complaint pleads. That points any remedy at studio output or basic cable channels. Those are the assets the merger exists to combine, so the settlement Bonta says he will accept is priced close to the cost of not merging at all.
Specific Implication
An output commitment a studio puts in writing to an exhibitor or regulator carries weight only to the extent the relevant enforcer classifies it as structural rather than behavioral. Bonta's rejection of the 30-film pledge is the on-record test of that distinction.
The Facts
  • Bonta spoke at Politico's California Agenda conference in Sacramento. He leads 12 states in the suit, filed last month.
  • The complaint alleges harm in three markets: wide-release theatrical film distribution, anticipated big-budget blockbusters, and basic cable channel licensing.
  • On settlement: "I think they're eager to enter those talks. And we are very happy with where we are. Literally, on in every development in this case, we have won and they have lost."
  • On Ellison's framing of the suit as political: "What Mr. Ellison has posited is false. Yesterday, false. Today, false. Tomorrow, false."
  • Delrahim on the relocation threat: "I heard the attorney general say that this was some kind of blackmail attempt for the lawsuit. It is not." He noted the merger has been approved in roughly 67 countries.
  • Delrahim said he takes Bonta "at his word" that the case is not about CNN.
  • Bonta declined to comment on a Wall Street Journal report that Governor Gavin Newsom had urged him to settle.
  • The Writers Guild of America said Ellison's exit threat "proves the danger of its outsized power."

An AI series costs $14,000 to $28,000 against over $100,000 for comparable live action, with the cheapest productions now under $2,800, and production teams have compressed from six people to one.

The structural feature beneath the cost collapse is vertical integration. ByteDance owns the production software, the distribution app, and the ad network, so the margin removed from performers and crews is recaptured inside a single company's stack. That same company acts as the de facto enforcer against unauthorized likeness use. A market in which the chief beneficiary of synthetic supply also adjudicates misuse of real faces leaves performers without an independent enforcement layer, which matters more to likeness-deal risk than the per-episode rate.
Specific Implication
The $15-to-$74-per-episode licensing rate reported here applies to volume-tier microdrama production. Actors and representatives negotiating likeness rights in that specific bulk-licensing tier should treat this as the current comp for that tier only, not as a benchmark for prestige-format deals.

CEO Summary
Paramount Skydance is offering exhibitors written contracts pledging 30 theatrical releases a year for at least three years, each with a 45-day window to premium on demand and 90 days to streaming, plus an unspecified financial penalty for missing the count. AMC, Regal and Vue have publicly backed the Warner Bros. Discovery merger on those terms; Cinemark decides at a board meeting this week. Cinema United and multiple regional chains have refused, objecting to the three-year term, the penalty severity, and what would count as a film.
Why This Matters
The detail that explains the split is Paramount's approach to independent film companies about counting acquisitions toward the total. A pledge that can be satisfied with acquired titles costs the studio far less than one requiring its own wide releases. The chains that can prosper on any product mix can accept that, while regional operators dependent on tentpole traffic cannot. The definitional fight is the real negotiation; the headline count has already been conceded.

  • Terms per three individuals with knowledge of the talks: 30 films a year, three years minimum, 45-day PVOD window, 90-day streaming window, penalty attached. Bloomberg reported the written-contract offer over the weekend.

  • Regal CEO Eduardo Acuna and Vue CEO Tim Richards issued supporting statements last week. AMC's Adam Aron endorsed at CinemaCon in April. Paramount sends the offer to smaller chains this week.

  • Paramount has approached independent film companies about contracting how many of the 30 would be indie acquisitions, which carry more favorable exhibitor splits.
  • Any settlement version would take the form of legally binding consent decrees, the instrument behind the 1948 Supreme Court ruling the DOJ phased out in 2020. Bonta has signaled behavioral decrees are insufficient.
  • Paramount stands to pay over $1 billion in ticking fees before the March trial.

Doug Shapiro argues the last decade's value migration in media went not to distribution but to the coupling of distribution with coordination, meaning control over the moment of consumer choice. Citing Morgan Stanley data, he shows the enterprise value of a representative set of media companies roughly doubled from 2018 to 2025 with virtually all gains accruing to digital consumer platforms, while conglomerates, MVPDs and broadcasters declined. His forward claim is that AI partially uncouples the two by inserting an agent-mediated decision layer above platforms, which he calls one of the biggest battles in media over the next decade.
Why This Matters
The load-bearing element in Shapiro's history is the blackout-era mechanism: the side without the consumer relationship blinked first. Leverage belongs to whoever sits at the moment of choice, not to whoever owns the pipe or the library. Run forward, that mechanism puts the decade's platform winners in the losing seat if an agent layer forms above them. That leaves Netflix and YouTube in the structural position cable occupied when carriage standoffs began going against it.

  • Media conglomerates and networks, MVPDs and broadcasters declined in value over the period. Newspapers and music labels were, in Shapiro's phrasing, a rounding error.

The instructive choice is the penalty Spotify did not use. It has removed more than 75 million spam tracks in a year, so takedown is a proven instrument. Selecting recommendation exclusion instead classifies AI Personas as a legitimate catalog segment being ring-fenced rather than abuse being purged. That preserves optionality: the inventory stays on the platform and monetizable, and the ring-fence can be relaxed the moment listener behavior makes AI Personas commercially useful.
Specific Implication
The badge functions as a distribution penalty rather than a disclosure label, since AI Personas are excluded from all recommendations unless followed. Artists and representatives should treat verified-human status on Spotify as a discoverability asset distinct from the badge itself.

CEO Summary
The State of Creators 2026, from CreatorIQ and Influencers.club, surveyed 5,095 creators across 100 regions and found that 67% earn less than $10,000 annually from content creation, with 62% saying it is not their primary income. Earnings correlate more strongly with follower count and views than with engagement metrics, contradicting a year of industry guidance. Half of creators have launched or plan to launch their own brand, and 42% report tension between what their audience wants and what brands ask for, rising to 53% among those with 500,000 or more Instagram followers.
Why This Matters
The line that reorders the category is that creators above $250,000 report building structurally different businesses from those under $10,000. The survey is describing two industries sharing one label: a small ownership-and-equity business at the top and a large unpaid audience-building layer beneath it. Averages drawn across that split describe nobody, and the brand-launch wave reads as the lower tier attempting to cross into the top tier's business model, not as expansion of a healthy middle.
Specific Implication
The survey's own split runs TikTok for near-term branded-content volume and performance, and Instagram as the platform higher-earning creators cite as sustaining a durable business. That distinction, not interchangeability, is what a creator deal or platform-exclusivity negotiation should be built around.
The Facts
  • Survey base: 5,095 creators across 100 regions. 67% earn under $10,000 a year from creation; 62% say it is not their primary income.
  • Earnings correlate more with follower count and views than with engagement metrics.
  • 50% have launched or plan to launch their own brand. Creators above $250,000 a year report building structurally different businesses from those under $10,000.
  • 42% report tension between audience-wanted and brand-requested content, rising to 53% at 500,000-plus Instagram followers.
  • Among creators earning $250,000-plus, 60% name Instagram their primary branded-content platform, versus 30% for TikTok.
  • TikTok ranks first for where creators post most branded content (52%), monetization (48%) and performance (51%). Instagram ranks first for long-term sustainable business potential (38%), ahead of TikTok (35%) and YouTube (23%).
  • 72% use AI for brainstorming, writing or editing; 4% for strategy; 1% to automate workflows. Most report no pressure to use AI to stay competitive.

CEO Summary

He argues the merger creates illegal concentration in three markets and would leave four distributors controlling more than 90% of anticipated blockbusters, which account for 88% of box office revenue over the past four years. The procedural detail carries the leverage read. Both companies agreed to pause the merger rather than contest preliminary injunction hearings, which handed the states a trial calendar without forcing them to prove likelihood of success first. A defendant confident that the blockbuster-specific market definition would collapse under scrutiny had an early, cheap chance to test it and declined. The pleaded market has therefore already survived the first practical stress point before trial.
The Facts

  • Claimed concentration: nearly one-third of theatrical motion picture distribution; nearly one-third of basic cable channels, including 50 of the most popular cable channels.
  • Four distributors would control more than 90% of anticipated top-grossing films. Blockbusters account for 88% of box office revenue for films released over the past four years.
  • Statutory basis: the Clayton Act.
  • Bonta on remedies: the case "seeks to prevent the long-term structural impact from the loss of competition. An impact that can't be remedied with a few one-off, piecemeal promises."

  • Closing line: "And we intend to win."

The projections in the filing carry the read. Fox underwrote Roku growing adjusted EBITDA from $650 million to $2.2 billion by 2030. A founder or CEO raising succession with the board, even as a limited proposal like a co-CEO recommendation, can prompt the board to initiate a sale process rather than the succession plan itself. Roku's own S-4 documents that sequence.

Producers Say a Finished Series Sells 100% of the Time and a Pitch Sells 5%, and Private Equity Is Funding the Difference
Amplify's Joe Lewis, formerly head of originals at Amazon Studios, puts a pitch at a 5% chance of getting made, a pilot at 50-50, and a finished series at 100% in his company's experience. No streamer has a team that buys finished series.
CEO Summary
Former Amazon Studios original programming head Joe Lewis, now running Amplify Pictures with backing from private-markets investor Great Mountain Partners, told The Ankler that self-financing changes the odds at each stage: roughly 5 percent for a pitch, 50-50 for a pilot, and 100 percent for a completed series in his company's experience. Amplify has fully financed Mt. Mystic and The Earliest Show, both wrapped. Lewis says no streamer has a dedicated team for acquiring finished outside series, so every buy runs through an originals executive and a licensing executive together.
Why This Matters
The branding detail carries the structural read. Acquired shows are presented as originals, and "100 Foot Wave" runs as an HBO original, so the audience-facing product already treats a finished acquisition as interchangeable with a commission. What has not caught up is the buy side's org chart, and that gap is the actual arbitrage. A de-risked completed series is priced by executives whose mandates and budgets were built for pitches. That is why private capital can fund the difference and expect the spread to persist until a dedicated acquisitions desk closes it.
Specific Implication
Producers or creators with access to independent financing for a pilot or completed season have a documented path to a sale that does not depend on a streamer greenlighting a pitch. Lewis's stated pickup rates and the cited Gillis and Duplass outcomes are the record.
The Facts
  • Joe Lewis, Amplify Pictures (Emmy winner for Fleabag, former Amazon Studios head of original programming): "If someone pitches the show, there's a 5 percent chance it gets made.   • Amplify is backed by Great Mountain Partners, which took a minority stake in 2023 at a reported $50 million valuation.
  • Lewis' two market buckets: "premium series" at low-seven-figure budgets that must license to a traditional distributor, and "emerging series" budgeted to recoup on YouTube alone.
  • Amplify and Stay Tuned (Kenny Neibart, Douglas Banker, Barry Kotler) fully financed Mt. Mystic (Johnny Knoxville added post-shoot, changing episode one "about 20 percent") and The Earliest Show (Ben Schwartz directing and starring; guests Chris Pratt, Lamorne Morris, Sarah Silverman, Nicole Byer). Both wrapped.
  • Lewis on the buy side: "As far as we know, none of the streamers have a team specifically dedicated to this." Buys need an originals exec and a licensing exec in the room. Acquired shows are still branded originals; 100 Foot Wave is an HBO original.
  • Shooting in L.A. can be cheaper at low budgets: the 10-20 percent savings elsewhere are outweighed by access to department heads and local cast.
  • Mark Duplass: "I'm willing to fund an entire first season of shows so that I can then take it to the executives and say, 'I know you weren't willing to buy this on a pitch, but here it is, right in front of you.'" Penelope went to Netflix; The Creep Tapes season three to Shudder this fall.

Spotify Is Testing a Podcast Ad-Skip Button for Paying Users, and Advertisers Are Not Pulling Spend
The skip button covers baked-in sponsorships creators sold themselves but does not apply to ads Spotify sells. Acast's CEO says about 10 percent of users actually skip, and no advertiser has pulled spend.
CEO Summary
Spotify began testing a "skip ahead" button last week for some paid subscribers, surfacing when they reach ads, promotions, intros, outros and baked-in sponsorships in podcasts. As Semafor first reported, the feature does not apply to ads Spotify sells itself. Oxford Advertising CEO Dan Granger says he has seen no advertiser pullback and expects minimal impact; Acast CEO Greg Glenday says some creators are unhappy and that Acast's own data shows roughly 10 percent of users skip, already priced into the ecosystem. Ads still register as delivered when skipped. Spotify says the test may or may not become a permanent feature.
Why This Matters
The design of the exemption carries the judgment. A skip control that spares only the platform's own inventory makes Spotify-sold placements the sole format guaranteed a listen. That operates as structural pressure on sponsors to route spend through Spotify's sales channel whether or not the test becomes permanent. Advertiser calm at the current skip rate does not change that direction; it only sets the pace.
Specific Implication
Podcast sponsorship deals structured around baked-in, creator-sold ad placements carry exposure to platform-side delivery changes that sit outside the creator's contract, as demonstrated by Spotify's unilateral rollout of this test.
The Facts
  • Spotify began rolling out the test last week for some paid subscribers; the "skip ahead" button surfaces at ads, promotions, intros, outros and baked-in sponsorships.
  • The feature does not apply to ads sold by Spotify itself. First reported by Semafor.
  • Ads are still technically delivered when skipped, so ad-delivery reporting is unchanged.
  • Dan Granger, CEO, Oxford Advertising: "Ad skipping is maybe scarier in theory than in practice, and so I don't think this is going to have major material direct impact on the brands that advertise." No advertiser pullback observed; most are taking a wait-and-see position.
  • Greg Glenday, CEO, Acast: some creators "are not happy about this and we will support them completely as they evaluate any recourse." Acast is working privately with Spotify on the rollout.
  • Acast internal metrics: about 10 percent of users choose to skip ads, already priced in.
  • Granger: the highest advertiser value is in host-read ads; excluding those from the skip while allowing other promos to be skipped would leave advertisers satisfied.
  • Spotify statement: "We regularly conduct tests at Spotify — some tests become permanent features, while others help inform future product development... We'll continue to evolve the experience as we learn."

Ellison Runs Short Of Moves, Time And Money On The $111 Billion WBD Merger
The antitrust trial starts March 2027. The merger agreement expires June 4, 2027. A $650 million quarterly ticking fee to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders begins next month.
CEO Summary
David Ellison lost the fight over the trial start date in the antitrust suit brought by state attorneys general and the WGA, and Deadline reports his $111 billion Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery is in serious peril for the first time since he outbid Netflix. Trial is set for March 2027 against a June 4, 2027 merger expiration, with a $650 million per quarter ticking fee starting next month and a $7 billion termination fee if the deal fails on regulatory grounds. More than 60 jurisdictions including the UK and the US have now approved the transaction.
Why This Matters
None of the remedies Deadline's sources describe involves divesting an asset. The remedies are a Los Angeles production announcement, a personnel change at CBS News, and input from a former state attorney general. That is the tell: the plaintiffs' price is political and reputational rather than structural, which means Ellison cannot buy back the calendar by selling anything. Paramount's own filings concede it must refile merger materials with the DOJ if the deal is not finalized by February 19. The binding constraint is now time, and every lever under discussion operates on goodwill rather than on the clock.

A production seeking a Los Angeles shoot commitment from Paramount has a concrete comparison point in the Clueless sequel series and Ascent, both cited as part of the company's regulatory approval case.

  • Merger agreement expires June 4, 2027. A $7 billion termination fee is owed if the deal fails for regulatory reasons.
  • A $650 million per quarter ticking fee to WBD shareholders begins next month.
  • Combined company would carry roughly $80 billion of debt.
  • Paramount conceded in filings that if the deal is not finalized by February 19 it must refile merger materials with the DOJ.

The territory table is the structural point. CEO Summary
Speaking at Locarno, Olivia Wilde said streaming buyers pay a premium to keep a film out of theaters, that the premium goes to financiers rather than filmmakers, and called it a bribe. She credited Annapurna's Megan Ellison with accepting A24's theatrical offer over higher streaming bids on The Invite. The film has grossed $23.5 million domestically since June 26 and $18 million across roughly 30 international territories.
Why This Matters
The misalignment Wilde is describing is structural. The premium is paid to the financier, but the cost of a skipped release falls on the filmmaker, whose next negotiation is priced partly on theatrical performance. On her account the correction ran on Ellison's goodwill, not on any contractual right, which is what made the outcome exceptional enough to recount from a festival stage. The film's seventh week in 342 theaters is the asset the declined premium purchased, and it accrues to the filmmaker's side of the ledger rather than to the financier who turned the money down.
Specific Implication
A director on an independently financed film has no guaranteed say over a theatrical-versus-streaming decision unless distribution-path approval is negotiated into the financing agreement.
The Facts

The financiers will get a lot more money to go to streaming, and you can take that bribe and give that up if that's where your priorities lie."

Chinese AI Models Are Still Generating 'The Office' Clips While Three Studios Sue
MiniMax withheld Hailuo 3 from the U.S. over the pending Disney, Universal and Warner Bros. suit, and a U.S. venture investor generated a Dwight-and-Jim clip through an aggregator on MiniMax's own servers.
CEO Summary
MiniMax released Hailuo 3 this week without direct availability in the U.S. or European Union, citing "ongoing copyright-related legal proceedings specifically concerning generative video AI." Andreessen Horowitz partner Justine Moore then generated a recognizable clip of Dwight and Jim from The Office using a simple H3 prompt through Krea, an aggregator, with the prompt routing back through MiniMax's servers. Separately, the startup VN.ai produced bootleg images of Elsa, Shrek and Buzz Lightyear through ByteDance's Seedream 5.0 via a third-party API.
Why This Matters
The ByteDance comparison isolates what actually changes model behavior. Guardrails arrived at Seedance only after cease-and-desist letters followed the Tom Cruise-Brad Pitt deepfake. MiniMax, facing litigation rather than a commercial relationship it needs to protect, responded by restricting distribution and leaving the model itself unchanged. Enforcement pressure produces model-level restraint only where the developer has U.S. market exposure at stake; where it does not, legal action redraws distribution maps without touching outputs.
Specific Implication
Rights holders negotiating AI licensing or enforcement terms with a model provider should require that restrictions bind third-party aggregators and API resellers directly, not only the provider's own first-party product. MiniMax's withholding of Hailuo 3 from the U.S. did not prevent a recognizable clip from being generated through the aggregator Krea on MiniMax's own servers.
The Facts
  • MiniMax released Hailuo 3 (H3) this week; it is not directly available in the U.S. or EU but has gone viral outside China through third-party access.
  • Justine Moore, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, generated a clip of Dwight and Jim from The Office with a simple H3 text prompt in Krea. The prompt routed through MiniMax's servers.
  • Disney, Universal and Warner Bros. allege in their suit that Hailuo "pirates and plunders copyrighted works on a massive scale," citing MiniMax's own YouTube promotion using Deadpool, Wolverine and The Joker videos. Those videos have been removed. MiniMax denies the allegations and did not respond to a request for comment.
  • At launch, a MiniMax representative said the full model would not be available in the U.S. because of "ongoing copyright-related legal proceedings specifically concerning generative video AI."
  • ByteDance released Seedance 2.5 the same week without comparable IP reproduction. Seedance 2.0 had produced the viral Tom Cruise versus Brad Pitt deepfake, drawing cease-and-desist letters from Netflix, Disney and others.
  • VN.ai generated bootleg images of Elsa, Shrek and Buzz Lightyear through Seedream 5.0 via a third-party API, per research reports seen by Deadline. Character prompts were often denied; specifying exact pixel sizes produced a recognizable Buzz Lightyear.
  • ByteDance statement: "ByteDance launches models with safeguards designed to prevent unauthorized use of intellectual property, and continually works to expand and strengthen these in collaboration with rightsholders and creative communities."
  • U.S. studios and the Motion Picture Association were approached for comment.

Commissioner Anna Gomez, the lone Democrat, called the move "unlawful on its face" because Congress set the cap in 2012, citing agreement from former FCC Commissioner Mike O'Rielly, former House Majority Leader Tom DeLay and Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz. That makes the real closing risk on any repeal-enabled deal a post-signing state court action rather than the FCC's own vote count.

  • Gomez cited O'Rielly ("unequivocal that the FCC lacks authority"), DeLay (Congress wrote the cap to keep the FCC from changing it) and Cruz (skeptical a change can be made absent an act of Congress).
  • Carr: "Repealing the national cap will provide essential relief for local broadcasters by restoring a healthy counterbalance to the growing leverage of national programmers."
  • Nexstar-Tegna would reach 80% of U.S. television households. A court enjoined merger integration in April 2026 in a suit by eight state attorneys general; trial is set for July 6, 2027. Nexstar's Ninth Circuit appeal seeking to narrow the injunction is expected to be argued in Q4 2026.

Nielsen Is Buying DoubleVerify for $2.15 Billion to Fix the Thing Advertisers Stopped Trusting It On
Nielsen is paying $2.15 billion, a 30% premium, for DoubleVerify in an all-cash deal closing by Q1 2027, taking both the measurement and verification layers of the ad market private under one owner.
CEO Summary
Nielsen agreed to acquire ad-verification firm DoubleVerify for approximately $2.15 billion in an all-cash transaction, a 30% premium to DoubleVerify's 60-day trading average. The deal, approved by both boards, is expected to close by Q1 2027 and takes DoubleVerify private under Nielsen, which has itself been privately held since 2022. Providence Equity Partners, holding roughly 11.8% of DoubleVerify's shares, has agreed to vote in favor and will exit its stake at closing.
Why This Matters
DoubleVerify's commercial value to advertisers rested on being structurally independent of the measurement firms it checks. Folding it into Nielsen removes that independence, converting a third-party check on Nielsen's own data into a subsidiary of the company being checked. The "single currency" both CEOs describe only holds credibility with advertisers if the scoring stays separable from the measurement it grades, which common ownership makes harder to demonstrate, not easier.
Specific Implication
Counterparties with ad-based bonus, threshold, or revenue-share terms tied to Nielsen measurement should specify the underlying methodology and add a change-of-control or methodology-change clause to future contracts. The verification function historically cited to support those terms will no longer sit with an independently owned company.
The Facts

Sook benefits from any regulatory friction that slows a competitor's scale even as he seeks the same kind of scale for Nexstar.

Producers, financiers, or filmmakers planning a 2027 theatrical release tied to either studio should treat the 30-films-per-year figure Paramount has committed to post-merger as the planning ceiling if the deal closes. Netflix Spends 5 Percent of Its Content Budget on 1 Percent of Its Viewing Because Live Cannot Be Faked

Producers behind recent Netflix live events, including Plimsoll's Skyscraper Live and Done+Dusted, describe a broader industry shift toward live formats as the one content category that cannot be synthetically generated.

Whisper TV hiring native speakers to dub the Fury-Makhmudov fight for each international feed, instead of using AI translation on a marquee live event, shows the AI-proof premium on live extends past production into localization. Even the category treated as immune to synthetic generation is being kept manually produced end to end for its highest-value broadcasts, not just at the point of capture.
Specific Implication
Producers capable of delivering complex live formats, spanning multiple time zones, insured, and multilingually produced, are operating from a narrower supply base than Netflix's spending growth alone would suggest. Banijay has been building its dedicated live division since 2023.
The Facts

CEO Summary
Gareth Edwards will not return to direct the next Jurassic World film after creative differences with Universal, TheWrap reports, despite his 2025 film Jurassic World: Rebirth grossing $869 million globally. David Koepp has already written the follow-up script, and stars Scarlett Johansson, Mahershala Ali and Jonathan Bailey are expected to return; a new director search is underway. A Universal-side insider described the franchise as having rotated through five different core casts and directing teams across seven films, with producers Steven Spielberg and Frank Marshall as the constant.

An $869 million global gross did not secure Edwards a renewed mandate. Box office return on the prior entry is therefore not itself the qualifying criterion for keeping a director on this franchise. Alignment with the producers who hold actual continuity, Spielberg and Marshall, functions as the higher bar. A director weighing a future Jurassic assignment should read a strong opening for the franchise as necessary but not sufficient for a second film.
Specific Implication
Directors accepting an assignment on an established franchise where script and cast are set independently of them should negotiate first-position or script-input terms before signing. Box office results on a prior entry did not carry over into creative continuity on this franchise.
The Facts
  • Gareth Edwards will not return to direct the next installment in the Jurassic World franchise, citing creative differences, TheWrap reported.

The Facts

  • Ordinary-course deals are restricted to lasting only two years past deal close; anything longer requires giving Paramount first rights to negotiate.
  • Separate limits apply to deals involving undefined "key property" IP (THR notes franchises like Harry Potter, Game of Thrones and DC likely qualify) and to HBO Max bundle agreements, both capped at two years post-closing.

The Paramount-WBD antitrust trial starts March 2, 2027, and the $7 million a day clock starts October 1
Paramount wanted November, the attorneys general wanted April. The merger agreement expires June 4, and a spring trial forces Paramount to refile with a Justice Department that already cleared it.
CEO Summary
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín set the trial over Paramount Skydance's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery for March 2 to March 19, 2027, closer to the April date sought by twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America than the November start Paramount requested. Paramount owes Warner shareholders a ticking fee of 25 cents per share per quarter, roughly $7 million a day, for every day the deal does not close after September 30, which the trades put above $1 billion by the time trial opens. The merger agreement expires June 4, 2027, and carries a $7 billion regulatory termination fee.
Why This Matters
Paramount's refiling exposure extends beyond the Justice Department, to the 65 jurisdictions worldwide it says have already cleared the deal or declined to challenge it. A trial date that slips past any of those regulators' own clearance windows could force Paramount to redo approvals it has already banked. That makes the March 2027 date a multi-jurisdiction risk rather than a single US antitrust question.
Specific Implication
Anyone planning around Paramount's stated ramp to 30 films a year should treat the trial calendar, not the ramp date itself, as the operative schedule until the merger closes.
The Facts
  • Trial set for March 2 to March 19, 2027, before U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in Oakland. Court hours 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m.; dark March 8 and March 15.
  • Paramount sought a November 2026 start. The state attorneys general and the WGA proposed April 2027.
  • Ticking fee: 25 cents per WBD share per quarter for every day past September 30 the deal has not closed, roughly $7 million per day, more than $1 billion by trial.
  • Merger agreement expires June 4, 2027. Regulatory termination fee: $7 billion.
  • A Justice Department waiting period expires February 19, 2027; Paramount told the court a later trial forces refiling in the United States and other cleared jurisdictions.
  • California Attorney General Rob Bonta leads 11 other state AGs. Suit filed July 13, followed by a temporary restraining order.
  • Initial case management conference August 19; joint statement due August 13. No timeline given for a post-trial ruling.
  • Paramount statement: "We respect the court's decision and continue to believe a trial on the merits is the best and most direct way for us to prove what we've said from the start."
  • On the same day's earnings call, CEO David Ellison said he is "absolutely open" to settling but expects to win at trial.
  • Paramount told the court it plans to raise output to 30 films per year and that the later date prolongs uncertainty for the creative community.

Participation and bonus structures written against a three-day opening-weekend threshold would not have captured the scale of this film's post-opening performance, since a meaningful share of its gross accrued after the weekend closed.

Private equity is sitting on about $1 trillion and buying the parts of entertainment AI cannot copy
Apollo argued in a December white paper that sports hedges AI because the seats are finite and the games run live. KKR has $53 billion to deploy, Blackstone $43 billion.
CEO Summary
Roughly $1 trillion in uncommitted U.S. private equity capital is looking for somewhere to go, and reporting across lawyers, financial advisers and dealmakers found one thesis recurring: sports, live events and other scarce real-world experiences are being underwritten specifically because generative AI cannot replicate them. Private equity already holds positions across the representation and management business and in production, from a $25 billion Endeavor take-private to the $8 billion Banijay-All3Media merger. Firms target 18 to 20 percent annual returns on five-to-seven-year holds, and continuation vehicles that let original investors stay past a fund's expiry are now routine in media.
Why This Matters
That capital overhang functions as a driver independent of the AI-hedge thesis. Fund structures force deployment before an expiration clock, so dry powder needs a home whether or not a given target actually resists AI substitution. One dealmaker put the dynamic bluntly: "Money has to be invested, whether that money is a useful investment or not." A seller courted under the sports-and-scarcity narrative should weigh whether the buyer's real motive is thesis conviction or capital that simply has to move.
Specific Implication
A talent business or media asset acquired by a private-equity-backed platform should expect the platform's ownership horizon, typically five to seven years or extended via a continuation vehicle, to shape deal terms. The underlying thesis prices scarcity and live, in-person value specifically for eventual resale.
The Facts
  • Midyear estimates put uncommitted U.S. private equity capital near $1 trillion. One corporate dealmaker: "Money has to be invested, whether that money is a useful investment or not."
  • Typical targets: 18 to 20 percent annual returns, five-to-seven-year exits. Continuation vehicles, single-purpose funds letting original investors stay in, are increasingly common in media and entertainment as an alternative to expiry-driven fire sales.
  • Apollo Global Management: $67 billion in private equity; holds HarbourView, Legendary Entertainment and Wrexham AFC; launched Apollo Sports Capital in September; a December 2025 white paper argued sports hedges AI disruption because seats are finite and games are watched live. Took a minority Legendary stake for $760 million in 2022.
  • Silver Lake: $114 billion. Completed a $25 billion Endeavor take-private last year and is part of the $55 billion EA leveraged buyout with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and Affinity Partners, cleared by EU regulators July 23.
  • KKR: $255 billion, about $53 billion available. Holdings span Mediawan, Simon & Schuster, Epic Games, ByteDance and Superstruct. Acquired Arctos this year; the only firm approved by all five major U.S. leagues to hold multiple team stakes.
  • Blackstone: $174 billion in private equity, $43 billion available as of June 30. Its $1 billion Candle Media bet has struggled since acquisitions of Hello Sunshine, Moonbug and ATTN.
  • RedBird Capital: $14 billion, dry powder about $965 million. Put $1.8 billion into Skydance's $8 billion Paramount purchase and committed $250 million toward the Paramount-WBD deal. RedBird IMI merged All3Media with Banijay for about $720 million in cash, creating the world's largest independent producer.
  • Providence Equity Partners is buying the remaining stake in The Team; at a reported $3.4 billion valuation the balance costs about $1.36 billion against just under $2 billion of dry powder.
  • EQT: $335 billion total; lost the auction for The Team and told Bloomberg it plans to invest $250 billion in the U.S. over five years. Shamrock Capital raised more than $800 million after selling its Excel stake.
  • Named new entrants circling the sector: Permira ($91 billion), Warburg Pincus ($105 billion, which hired a former major-label chief AI officer last year), Bluestone Equity Partners ($440 million).
  • One dealmaker on the consensus: "Everyone has dry powder for sports."

The WBD merger agreement forces Warner to sue over a departing executive, and California law punishes it for trying

CEO Summary
Warner Bros. Discovery has sued Amazon over its hiring of HBO Max marketing executive Pia Barlow before her fixed-term contract expired, calling Amazon a "digital bull in a china shop." The Paramount merger agreement bars WBD from failing to enforce employees' restrictive covenants, and a failure to enforce could hand Paramount an argument against paying the $7 billion regulatory termination fee if the deal is blocked, so WBD is pushed toward aggressive enforcement. California's 2024 amendments to Business and Professions Code §16600 cut the other way, requiring courts to read the noncompete prohibition broadly and giving an employee subjected to attempted enforcement of a void restraint their own claim for an injunction, damages and attorney fees.
Why This Matters
The merger agreement bars WBD from failing to enforce restrictive covenants, and non-enforcement could support a Paramount argument against paying the $7 billion termination fee. Together those supply a contractual reason for WBD to bring this suit independent of the underlying relationship with Barlow. The complaint's structure suggests an awareness of the risk on the other side: it does not name Barlow as a defendant, attach the employment agreement, disclose its termination terms, or seek emergency relief. That caution is consistent with California's 2024 amendments to Business and Professions Code section 16600, which let an employee facing enforcement of a void restraint sue for an injunction, damages and attorney fees. A comparable case last year, Disney's attempt to block Justin Connolly's move to YouTube, was denied emergency relief by a California judge and later settled.
Specific Implication
An executive departing a company mid-merger, where covenant enforcement may be contractually required rather than discretionary, should seek an explicit release as a condition of exit rather than rely on an assessment that the restriction is unenforceable.
The Facts
  • WBD sued Amazon over the hiring of HBO Max marketing executive Pia Barlow before her fixed-term contract expired; her restriction would run to October 2027.
  • The Paramount-WBD merger agreement prohibits WBD from waiving or failing to "enforce the restrictive covenant obligations" of current or former employees. Non-enforcement could support a Paramount argument against the $7 billion regulatory termination fee.
  • California's 2024 amendments to §16600 require courts to invalidate noncompetes "no matter how narrowly tailored" and remove the assumption that an unenforceable restraint carries no downside. Whether the statute voids a bona fide fixed-term contract is unsettled.
  • The same legislation lets an employee or former employee facing attempted enforcement of a void restraint sue for an injunction, actual damages and attorney fees.
  • Precedent: 20th Century Fox and Viacom defeated Netflix on executive poaching a decade ago. Last year Disney failed to block former ESPN executive Justin Connolly from joining YouTube; Judge James Chalfant refused emergency relief, found no probability of success, faulted Disney's showing of urgency, and held the balance of harms favored Connolly. Disney appealed; the parties settled before an appellate ruling.
  • Connolly's argument: because Disney could terminate him without necessarily paying the remainder, the deal looked less like security exchanged for a term commitment and more like a one-way noncompete.
  • WBD is represented by Proskauer partner Anthony Oncidi, who represented Viacom in the earlier case. He has not named Barlow as a defendant, attached the agreement, disclosed its termination provisions, or moved for emergency relief, and has emphasized Amazon's conduct, including its promise to absorb the legal consequences of her departure, its selection of counsel for her, and its alleged pursuit of other WBD executives.
  • WBD frames its interest as workforce stability and business planning; Amazon's position is that WBD is preparing to change owners, reporting structures and job definitions.

Ellison's essay answers a question the antitrust case is not formally asking. The state attorneys general's and WGA's suit turns on market concentration, a competitive-effect standard. The essay's silence on President Trump points the same way, toward a fight being waged as much in Washington and public opinion as in the courtroom.

A judge threw out Terrence Howard's 'Empire' pay suit because his loan-out company would have been paid, not him
Fox contracted with Howard's loan-out, Universal Bridges, which paid him a fixed salary. The judge held that a higher fee would have raised the entity's revenue only, making damages too speculative for trial.
CEO Summary
Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Cherol Nellon dismissed Terrence Howard's 2023 suit against CAA on July 31, ending a case that had targeted packaging fees and alleged that conflicted advice cost him market-rate pay across six seasons of Fox's "Empire." The ruling turned on structure rather than conduct: Fox contracted with Howard's loan-out company, which paid him a fixed salary, so the court found that a successfully negotiated increase would have raised the loan-out's revenue without necessarily reaching him, making the alleged damages too speculative for trial. The court also found the agency did push Fox to renegotiate in 2018 and that Fox "rejected all attempts at renegotiation."
Why This Matters
The court's rationale does not touch Howard's core allegation, that CAA represented him alongside "Empire" co-creators Lee Daniels and Danny Strong and producer Imagine Entertainment without disclosing the conflict. The dismissal rests on the loan-out structure making damages too speculative. An artist with the same alleged multiple-representation conflict, but paid directly rather than through a fixed-salary loan-out, would face a different damages analysis. The merits question this ruling never reached would also be live for that artist.
Specific Implication
An artist compensated through a loan-out on a fixed internal salary, rather than one that passes through negotiated increases, should confirm which structure applies before pursuing a claim tied to underperformance of a deal. This ruling shows the structure itself can determine whether damages can be established.
The Facts
  • Judge Cherol Nellon, Los Angeles Superior Court, dismissed the suit on summary judgment in a ruling issued July 31, 2026.
  • Howard sued in 2023, alleging conflicted advice led him to accept below-market pay across six seasons as Lucious Lyon on "Empire," and targeting packaging fees, the commission paid for bundling writers, directors and actors into one project.
  • He alleged his agents did not disclose developments undermining his leverage, or that the agency also represented co-creators Lee Daniels and Danny Strong and production company Imagine Entertainment.
  • Fox contracted with his loan-out, Universal Bridges, which paid him a fixed salary as an employee. Judge Nellon: "The immediate economic result of an increase in compensation would have been an increase in revenue to Universal Bridges only."
  • The court found alleged damages too speculative for trial, and separately found that the agency pushed to renegotiate while Fox held final say and "rejected all attempts at renegotiation."

Spider-Man: Brand New Day opens to $927M worldwide and drives the biggest weekend in box office history
Sony's own public projection was $425M worldwide and roughly $200M domestic; the film did $927M worldwide and $355M domestic, about double the studio's guidance in each case.
CEO Summary
Sony and Marvel Studios' Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened to $355M domestic and $927M worldwide, the second-biggest global debut ever behind Avengers: Endgame. The entire North American market hit a record $428.99M for the weekend per Rentrak, the first all-time domestic weekend record since 2019. Sony's own public projection had been $425M worldwide, and Universal's three-week-old The Odyssey held at -43% alongside it rather than being crushed.
Why This Matters
The 24.1M domestic tickets sold represent about 20% more admissions than Spider-Man: No Way Home on a 27% larger nominal gross. That indicates the record reflects real audience growth rather than ticket-price inflation carrying the number. Admissions growth is the stronger signal for whether Marvel and Sony can sustain an audience this size at comparable pricing across future entries in the franchise.
The Facts
  • $355M domestic opening, second-best all time, roughly $2M behind Avengers: Endgame's $357.1M record. $927M worldwide across 90,000 screens, second-best global debut ever.
  • North American marketplace: record $428.99M weekend for all titles per Rentrak. Variety reported ~$430M and TheWrap $434M; the Rentrak figure is the measurement-of-record number. Prior all-time record was $402M (final weekend of 2019); best post-Covid weekend was $311.3M (July 2023).
  • Weekend was +246% against the same frame a year ago. YTD domestic box office is $6.19B through August 2, +15% year over year.
  • Sony's public global projection was $425M; The Ankler reports domestic guidance around $200M.
  • International: $572M from 66 markets. China $121.0M, UK $49.0M (#3 all time), Mexico $38.3M (#2), India $31.8M (best ever for a Hollywood picture there, sixth-biggest opening in Indian history), South Korea $25.0M, Australia $21.4M, Germany $20.0M, Italy $18.2M, Japan $10.0M. All-time like-for-like opening records also set in France, Brazil, Spain, Peru, Colombia, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Chile, Turkey, Ecuador and Belgium.
  • Production budget $225M (The Ankler). 24.1M US tickets sold per Entelligence against ~20M for Spider-Man: No Way Home — about 20% more admissions for a 27% larger nominal gross.
  • CinemaScore A. Opening-night audience 63% aged 18-34, 60% male; 36% White, 28% Latino, 20% Black, 10% Asian, 6% Native American/other.
  • Universal's The Odyssey took $51M in its third domestic weekend, -43%, for a $911M global cume.
  • MCU lifetime grosses now $33.3B across 38 films.
  • Rentrak's Paul Dergarabedian: "the likelihood of a $4 billion summer and a $10 billion year just went up exponentially."

Ellison may have built himself an exit from his own $111 billion Warner deal
Walking away costs Ellison $9.8B, a $7B breakup fee plus $2.8B to Netflix. Closing costs $113B, including $80B of fresh debt, against a standalone Paramount Skydance carrying $12B in net debt.
CEO Summary
David Ellison bypassed settlement talks with the state attorneys general and took the Paramount Skydance / Warner Bros. Discovery merger straight to trial, absorbing potentially $1B or more in ticking fees to do it. William Cohan's read is that the move is optionality rather than confidence: with a June 4, 2027 drop-dead date, Ellison now has eleven months in which he can decide the deal is no longer worth doing. The walk-away math is a $9.8B mistake, the $7B breakup fee to WBD plus $2.8B to Netflix, against a $113B one if he closes.
Why This Matters
Even fully combined, Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery would carry roughly $113B in market value, against Netflix's roughly $300B and Disney's roughly $167B. The transaction that resolves the antitrust trial does not by itself close the scale gap that made WBD a takeover target in the first place. That positions the combined company as a plausible acquisition target of its own once litigation clears.
Specific Implication
A counterparty transacting with Paramount Skydance during the pendency period should weigh the company's balance sheet, not the trial's outcome, as the constraint most likely to determine whether Ellison closes or walks.
The Facts
  • Drop-dead date in the merger agreement: June 4, 2027. Ellison chose trial over settlement, absorbing potentially $1B+ in ticking fees.
  • Walk-away cost: $9.8B ($7B breakup fee to WBD, $2.8B to Netflix). Close cost: $113B, including a fresh $80B of debt and $42.5B of equity at risk.
  • Standalone Paramount Skydance carries $12B of net debt; market capitalization roughly $8B. PSKY closed at $7.96 on July 31 and continues to hit fresh lows.
  • Comparative scale cited: Netflix ~$300B, Disney ~$167B. Combined PSKY+WBD ~$113B.
  • WBD shareholder outcome: $31.75/share ($31 offer plus 25 cents per quarter of ticking fees, September through June). Zaslav personally receives an additional $550M on close.
  • Sale-process sequence: Ellisons' first bid $19/share, declined; Revlon mode; Netflix merger agreement signed; Ellisons raised to $31/share cash, a 63% increase. Largest breakup fee ever, plus a personal Larry Ellison backstop on equity and debt.
  • Cohan's read on a broken deal: Zaslav would take the $7B fee, pay down debt to investment grade, and revert to the June 2025 split-up plan.
  • Paramount reports Q2 on August 4. Trial-date positions are far apart: Paramount seeks November, the state AGs and WGA seek April.

IMAX posted its second-best weekend ever without the biggest opening in history
Shot entirely for ScreenX from set through exhibition, Brand New Day opened domestic ScreenX at $7M, 2.6 times the format's prior record, while IMAX stayed locked to The Odyssey through mid-August.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened to $355M domestic on zero domestic IMAX screens, because Universal's The Odyssey holds the entire domestic IMAX network into mid-August and the 70mm screens into September. IMAX still posted $68M globally, its second-best weekend in history, with the format supplying 43% of The Odyssey's $51M domestic third weekend. Denied IMAX, Brand New Day drew 24% of its domestic opening from other premium large formats, including a record $31M global start in 4DX and ScreenX, a format it was shot for end to end.

In the international markets where Brand New Day did have IMAX access, China, Japan and Korea, the format still captured 16% to 18% of each territory's opening despite carrying The Odyssey's continuing run at the same time. That indicates the domestic IMAX blackout was a contractual allocation choice rather than evidence that a market the size of North America cannot support both titles in the format at once.
Specific Implication
A release whose date lands during a competing title's premium-format exclusivity window can still recover a meaningful share of premium-format revenue by shooting natively for an alternate format, as Brand New Day did with ScreenX.
The Facts
  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day opened on zero domestic IMAX screens. The Odyssey holds the domestic network until The End of Oak Street on August 14, and keeps the 70mm IMAX screens into September.
  • IMAX network weekend: $68M globally, second-highest-grossing weekend in its history.
  • IMAX supplied **43% of The Odyssey's $51M domestic third weekend ($22.1M) and 26% of its $85.2M international weekend ($22.6M). IMAX cume on the title is $221M**, the No. 3 IMAX title of all time and the fastest any film has reached $200M in the format. 70mm locations did $5.1M this weekend for a $27.6M cume, about 12% of the IMAX total.
  • Brand New Day drew 24% of its $355M domestic opening from premium large formats (~$85M): roughly 17% of the total in 3-D, $10M+ Dolby Cinema, $7M ScreenX, $5.2M 4DX, plus undisclosed D-BOX records.
  • 4DX and ScreenX combined for a record $31M global opening across 1,111 screens ($17M 4DX, $14.4M ScreenX), against a prior combined record of $15.7M (Jurassic World: Rebirth).
  • Brand New Day was shot entirely for ScreenX, CJ 4DPLEX's first collaboration running from on-set production through exhibition. Domestic ScreenX opened at $7M, 2.6x the previous format record ($2.7M, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie).
  • Where Brand New Day had IMAX (China, Japan, Korea): $23M combined. China $19M, 16% of the territory opening and a franchise IMAX record there; Japan $2.2M, 18% of that market's debut; Korea $2.4M, 9%.

Oliver extended by exercising an existing option rather than negotiating a fresh term. Other WBD talent holding similar option-based renewals may already have this contingency available to them without having to reopen negotiations.
Specific Implication
Talent renegotiating a contract at a company with an unresolved change of control can match the contract term to the transaction's expected resolution date. That avoids committing to a multi-year term with an ownership group that is not yet fixed.
The Facts
  • Oliver picked up an option to extend by one year, through the end of 2027. His prior contract was due to expire at year's end. Typical renewals for the show have run three years.
  • The Paramount / WBD $110B merger is paused for up to 11 months pending the federal antitrust suit brought by state AGs.
