A festival backup file left in production exposed 13,535 industry contact records
The cause was a plain-text backup left in the production environment, found via a public IoT search engine. A separate file held roughly 135,000 contacts Fowler says could seed phishing at scale.
CEO Summary
Cybersecurity researcher Jeremiah Fowler found 666,369 Tribeca Festival records exposed online, spanning 2019 to 2026, after a plain-text backup file was left inside the production environment. One folder held 13,535 contact entries with names, addresses, phone numbers and emails for filmmakers and actors including Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Guillermo del Toro, Robert De Niro, Jennifer Lawrence and Angelina Jolie. The festival disputes the characterization, saying no talent had personal contact information disclosed and the records were largely public-facing business contacts; Fowler says he saw consumer email accounts in the file.
Why This Matters
Fowler's own base rate is that an organization rarely suffers a second incident within three to five years once one becomes a remediation priority. That suggests Tribeca is now the safer property in this category. The greater exposure sits with comparable festivals and markets that have not yet had a plain-text backup surfaced by a public search engine and so have not yet been forced to fix the underlying practice.
Specific Implication
A festival, market or submission platform that stores industry contact data typically does not carry standard breach-notification terms in its participation agreements. A party that routinely shares contact information with such platforms may want that language addressed at signing rather than after an incident.
The Facts
  • 666,369 exposed records, timestamps spanning 2019 to 2026, found via a publicly available IoT search engine.
  • Root cause per Fowler: "a human error of leaving the backup file in the database, and the backup file was in plain text, unencrypted."
  • One folder, "contacts," held 13,535 entries — names, addresses, phone numbers, emails. Cited: Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, Guillermo del Toro, Ron Howard, Robert De Niro, Jennifer Lawrence, Angelina Jolie, Morgan Freeman, Rami Malek, Eva Mendes, Michael J. Fox.
  • A separate document held roughly 135,000 contacts, which Fowler assumes are mailing-list and event signups.
  • Festival statement: "None of the talent referenced in recent reporting had personal contact information disclosed. The vast majority of the information consisted of public-facing business contact information, including PR representatives, talent representatives, front office email addresses, information from the Festival website, and other information that was already publicly available. All information was removed promptly upon discovery."
  • Fowler's response: some contacts were managers or assistants, "but I saw a lot of consumer email accounts, like Google or Yahoo."
  • Fowler found no evidence anyone else accessed it, and credited the festival with responding "very fast and professionally."
  • Fowler on the AI multiplier: "you can feed it information and ask it to create a phishing email... and send it to 135,000 people, and somebody's going to open it."
  • Fowler's base rate: organizations that suffer a data incident "statistically don't have another one for three to five years since it becomes a primary focus."
  • Tribeca was co-founded in 2002 by De Niro, Jane Rosenthal and Craig Hatkoff. Its 25th-anniversary edition ran June 3-14, 2026.

Writer-producer Simon Afram and his company Op-Fortitude sued Netflix in California federal court for at least $105 million after an unencrypted master of their unreleased WWII thriller "Fortitude," directed by Simon West and starring Nicolas Cage, was stolen from Netflix's Los Angeles office during an acquisition screening. Netflix says it does not bear the risk of loss for a film "delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards," and that it withheld investigation details after a demand for $165 million. The producers say they paused sales because any buyer must now be told the film was compromised before release.
Why This Matters
The producer delivered an unencrypted master to Netflix for an acquisition screening on verbal instructions to delete it afterward; ten days later it was stolen from Netflix's office along with other drives. Both sides agree the file was unencrypted and that it was stolen, per the complaint and Netflix's public statement. No written delivery, encryption, or risk-of-loss terms governed the handoff, and each side disputes who bears the resulting loss.

The producers' damages claim does not allege the film has leaked. It rests on the disclosure obligation the theft now creates with every future buyer, and the producers say they have paused sales as a result.
Specific Implication
A seller delivering an unreleased master for a buyer's internal acquisition screening should secure written delivery, encryption, and risk-of-loss terms before the material leaves its custody. Neither party in this dispute had such terms in writing.

  • Suit filed Thursday in California federal court by Simon Afram and Op-Fortitude, seeking at least $105 million.

  • The suit says Netflix would not disclose whether it filed a police report and declined to involve the LAPD after the filmmakers filed their own.

  • Netflix statement: it "disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards," notes it does not own the rights, and says it offered to monitor piracy sites.
  • The producers say they paused sales despite domestic and international interest.

California's COMPETE Act Would Put Theatrical Windows And Multi-Picture Deals Under Antitrust Law
AB 1776 extends the Cartwright Act to single-firm conduct for the first time in its 119-year history, and adds monopsonization liability that has passed the Assembly and Senate Judiciary Committee.
CEO Summary
California's AB 1776, the COMPETE Act, has passed the Assembly and the Senate Judiciary Committee and now sits with Senate Appropriations. It would extend the Cartwright Act to single-firm conduct for the first time in the statute's 119-year history, creating state liability for monopolization and, critically, monopsonization. Puck's Eriq Gardner reports the practices exposed run from theatrical windows to multi-film talent contracts to refusing to license content to competitors.
Why This Matters
Because AB 1776 would create state-law claims, they would sit outside the federal case law that has made monopsonization theories difficult to win in federal court. A buyer-side claim already rejected under federal antitrust doctrine could be refiled and survive under California law if the bill passes. That gives plaintiffs a second track around unfavorable federal precedent rather than a stronger version of the same track.
Specific Implication
If enacted, AB 1776 would expose standard theatrical-windowing and multi-picture contract structures to state antitrust claims in California regardless of the outcome of the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger review. The bill's monopsonization provision, aimed at buyer-side conduct, is not limited to studios or distributors.
The Facts
  • AB 1776, the Competition and Opportunity in Markets for a Prosperous, Equitable and Transparent Economy (COMPETE) Act, introduced by Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry on 2026-03-23.
  • Status: passed the Assembly, passed the Senate Judiciary Committee, referred to Senate Appropriations.
  • Would create state-law liability for monopolization, attempted monopolization, maintenance of monopoly power, and monopsonization.
  • Extends the Cartwright Act to single-firm conduct for the first time since its enactment 119 years ago.
  • Puck reports exposed conduct includes theatrical windows, multi-film talent contracts, and refusals to license content to competitors.
  • Bonta is separately leading the multi-state challenge to the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, alongside the WGA.

Newsom's push for a settlement relies on a jobs estimate that is itself provisional pending the state's deeper Department of Economic Opportunity analysis due Aug. 18. The administration is thus weighing in on employment grounds ahead of its own office completing the underlying data. The governor's office is pressing Bonta toward settlement while Bonta continues to seek a later trial date and remedies beyond a CNN sale. The political and legal tracks inside California's own government are not yet aligned on this merger.
Specific Implication
A counterparty with pending business tied to either company should treat Paramount's Sept. 30 fee trigger and the contested trial date, not the parties' public settlement posture, as the operative near-term calendar.
The Facts
  • Newsom has warned that blocking the merger could hurt state employment and his office has encouraged Bonta toward an out-of-court settlement (WSJ). Representatives for Newsom, Bonta and Paramount declined to comment.
  • Trial dates: Paramount filed for a 12-day trial starting Nov. 4, 2026. The state AGs and WGA filed for April 5, 2027, running 12-15 days, allowing a merits decision by June 2027.
  • Paramount called the April request "nothing more than a stonewalling tactic." The states and WGA called a compressed schedule "unworkable, unfair and unjustified."
  • Bonta: "This challenge deserves careful and thorough review and today my office and attorneys general across the country asked the court for a trial date next spring."
  • Cost of delay: past Sept. 30, WBD shareholders receive 25 cents per share quarterly, roughly $650M per quarter or $7M per day. A regulatory failure triggers a $7B termination fee. Closing is deferred to five days after the trial outcome or June 1, 2027, whichever is earliest.
  • Remedy preference: Bonta has said the states want structural remedies, explicitly beyond a CNN sale: separate cable channels, a separate streaming service, a separate news channel or TV studio, a separate film studio.
  • Alleged concentration: 27% of wide-release theatrical distribution, 30% of anticipated blockbuster films, 27% of the basic cable bundle.
  • Jobs: LA County Board of Supervisors analysis found roughly 2,500 local and 6,000 global jobs at potential risk. A deeper Department of Economic Opportunity analysis on production workers is due Aug. 18.
  • Cleared: DOJ, WBD shareholders, the European Commission (conditioned on a UIP exit), plus Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, China, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, South Africa, Ukraine, Montenegro, New Zealand, North Macedonia, and FDI authorities in Spain, Germany, Slovenia, Belgium, Czechia, Italy, France and Romania. The UK CMA decides by Aug. 7.

Netflix And Prime Video Take France's Windowing Rules To Court
ARCOM offered Prime Video $103M a year for a window beyond 12 months or $126M a year for a window at 12 months, meaning roughly $23M buys several months of exclusivity.
CEO Summary
Netflix and Prime Video have each filed separate challenges at the Conseil d'État, France's highest administrative court, against the country's streaming windowing and investment rules. Netflix's industry agreement lapsed at the end of 2025, pushing its release window from 15 months back to the default 17 while its obligation to invest 20% of French revenue in local production continues. Prime Video's convention with regulator ARCOM expired days ago and was extended six months while talks continue.
Why This Matters
Canal+'s $1.1B agreement contains a clause that reopens its own terms if any rival streamer secures a window inside 12 months. That means ARCOM's negotiating position with Netflix and Prime Video is not limited to their windows individually. Any concession to either American streamer forces the regulator to also reopen and likely worsen its existing Canal+ contract. That raises the true cost of a settlement well past the price quoted directly to Prime Video. It also gives the streamers a court venue where that linked liability does not constrain the outcome.
Specific Implication
A streamer or broadcaster with a windowing agreement tied to a competitor's window length, as Canal+'s is, should treat any regulatory concession to Netflix or Prime Video in this proceeding as a potential trigger for its own contract to reopen.
The Facts
  • Since January 2022, SVOD services must invest 20% of annual French revenue in local production under France's implementation of the EU AVMS Directive.
  • Netflix's industry agreement expired end-2025, not renewed. Window slipped from 15 months to the default 17. Free-to-air broadcasters get films at 22 months, leaving Netflix five months of exclusivity.
  • Netflix invests $287M+ annually in French content, including roughly $68M in theatrically released films.
  • Source close to Netflix: "For us, it's an unsustainable equation: more obligations, a less favorable release window, and the latest Canal+ agreement locks in the current system."
  • Netflix argues U.S. streamers could fund nearly half of all French production by 2030 (estimates cited by Le Monde).
  • ARCOM's proposal to Prime Video: $103M/year for a window beyond 12 months, or $126M/year at 12 months.
  • Prime Video wants Disney's nine-month slot; ARCOM refused, noting Disney directs 14% of French revenue to cinema, above the minimum.
  • Canal+: $1.1B over five years buys a six-month window; any streamer inside 12 months triggers a three-month renegotiation.
  • Netflix skips Cannes annually because Palme d'Or competition requires French theatrical release.
  • Netflix, Prime Video and Disney+ have jointly filed a further challenge to amendments to France's SMAD decree.

CEO Summary
LightShed published nine questions for Disney ahead of its August 5 fiscal Q3 earnings, and correctly predicted a day early that Disney would sell its 50% A&E Networks stake to Hearst at a low single-digit EBITDA multiple. Its lead question: if a low multiple justifies exiting A&E, what multiple would justify the same logic on ESPN and ABC. The note points out that new CEO Josh D'Amaro said last quarter Disney has no interest in separating them, and that Comcast said the same about NBCUniversal in January before reversing.
Why This Matters
LightShed's framing turns Disney's own logic against it. If a low single-digit EBITDA multiple was sufficient reason to sell A&E, the firm's question forces D'Amaro to defend the specific multiple gap between ESPN/ABC and a hypothetical buyer, not the general principle of holding legacy linear assets. That shifts the burden from whether Disney will separate ESPN and ABC to what price would make separation the same trade Disney already made on A&E.
Specific Implication
A counterparty valuing Disney's linear assets ahead of the August 5 earnings call should treat management's current no-separation position on ESPN and ABC as unconfirmed, given the Comcast precedent cited in this reporting.
The Facts
  • Disney reports fiscal Q3 2026 on Wednesday, August 5.
  • LightShed predicted on July 30, before it was announced, that Disney would sell its 50% A&E Networks stake to Hearst, all-cash, at a low single-digit EBITDA multiple.
  • Lead question: what multiple would justify applying the A&E exit logic to ESPN and ABC, "especially if separating them leads to a far higher multiple on studio, theme parks, consumer products and streaming."
  • D'Amaro said last quarter Disney has no interest in separating ESPN and ABC. Comcast "was equally clear about NBCU as recently as January."
  • Other questions raised: whether new U.S. parks discounting is defensive against macro weakness or offensive share-taking from Universal; a possible free ad-supported Disney+/Hulu tier; what ESPN pays for certainty on the NFL's 2030 Monday Night Football opt-out; Roblox as an IP pipeline and whether the Epic Games partnership constrains it; whether Disney+ should open as a platform; whether Disney needs to buy a large games publisher outright; the absence of an original vertical-video strategy while time spent on Disney+ underperforms; and whether Disney should have a Sphere strategy.

Private Equity Has Repriced the Representation Business Into the Mid-Teens
EBITDA multiples for talent agencies have moved from low double digits into the mid-teens. One investor puts the EBITDA bar for a public listing at $300M.
CEO Summary
EBITDA multiples for talent agencies have risen from the low double digits to the mid-teens, according to a financial source cited by The Ledger, and nearly every major agency is now controlled by an investment firm. Recent marks include Silver Lake's $25B take-private of Endeavor, Artemis buying a CAA minority stake from TPG at a $7B valuation, Goldman Sachs Alternatives taking majority control of Excel Sports Management for about $1B, and Providence Equity Partners buying out Casey Wasserman's stake in The Team at a reported $3.4B valuation. Investors interviewed name sports exposure as the driver.
Why This Matters
Cassidy and Michael both describe the shift as investors buying leveraged exposure to athlete and creator monetization rather than to agency fee income itself. That means an agency's valuation now tracks the sports and creator business it can build on top of its client roster more than the roster's traditional packaging and commission revenue. That reorients what a sponsor is actually underwriting when it buys into a firm like CAA, Endeavor or The Team: less the representation business as historically practiced, more the sports-rights and influencer infrastructure layered onto it.
Specific Implication
Talent evaluating their representation firm's ownership structure should identify which private equity sponsor holds it and where that sponsor sits in its hold period. Cassidy's own account describes further sponsor-to-sponsor sales as the expected path for firms below the $300M EBITDA threshold he named for a public listing.
The Facts
  • A financial source tells The Ledger that talent agency EBITDA multiples have moved from the low double digits to the mid-teens.
  • Ownership map: Endeavor (WME) taken private by Silver Lake, $25B. CAA minority stake sold by TPG to Artemis, $7B. Excel Sports Management majority stake to Goldman Sachs Alternatives, about $1B. UTA stake bought by EQT Private Equity from Investcorp and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board. Gersh owned by Crestview Partners, which previously owned ICM before selling it to CAA.
  • The Team (formerly Wasserman): Casey Wasserman's stake sold to Providence Equity Partners, which already owns 60%. Closing in the second half of the year, terms undisclosed. Puck previously reported an estimated $3.4B valuation, up from roughly $3B when the process began in February.
  • Brian Cassidy, president and head of media investing, Crestview Partners: "Investing in talent agencies was a more diversified, downside-protected way of investing behind the growing value of content and talent... Today, the investment thesis is more about getting exposure to the growth trends in sports."
  • Alex Michael, global head of sports and entertainment, LionTree: agencies "give investors levered exposure to athlete and influencer monetization and the growth in sports rights, without the price tag or scarcity of owning a team outright."
  • Cassidy on exits: "I think you will probably see another agency go public in the next few years, but I think it's got to be of scale. It would take a firm to have EBITDA of at least $300 million for an IPO to make sense." He also expects more sponsor-to-sponsor stake sales.
  • Davis Noell, Providence co-head of North America: "The robust interest in the company throughout this process only reinforced our belief in the business."
  • On Crestview's 2023 Gersh investment: it issued equity to key agents and employees, then funded acquisitions building the sports, digital and brands businesses.

A Munich Court Says It Can Hear AI Training Cases No Matter Where the Training Happened
GEMA's general counsel said Munich can hear the claim regardless of where Suno's training took place. It is GEMA's second German win in nine months, after November's ruling against OpenAI.
CEO Summary
A regional court in Munich ruled Friday that AI music service Suno violated copyrights by training on works covered by the German licensing agency GEMA, ordering it to disclose illicit revenue and pay unspecified damages. Suno disputes the ruling and is weighing an appeal. GEMA's general counsel said the decisive point was jurisdictional: the agency can sue in Munich regardless of where the training took place. It is GEMA's second German win in nine months, after a November ruling against OpenAI over song lyrics.
Why This Matters
The German ruling rests on a jurisdictional finding rather than a substantive fair-use holding. A US court's eventual conclusion in the Midjourney case or similar litigation would therefore not disturb this result or the damages and disclosure order against Suno. Every AI company operating in Europe now faces training-liability exposure that resolves on Germany's own timeline, regardless of how the parallel American fair-use question is decided.
Specific Implication
A rights holder whose work was used to train an AI model reaching European users has a venue, under this ruling's jurisdictional finding, to bring a claim before a German court regardless of where the training occurred. That venue is independent of the outcome of any parallel U.S. fair-use litigation.
The Facts
  • A regional court in Munich ruled Friday that Suno violated copyrights when it used music covered by GEMA. Suno must disclose any "illicit revenue" and pay unspecified damages, and can appeal.
  • GEMA filed the suit in January 2025.
  • Kai Welp, GEMA general counsel: the ruling was "very gratifying to see the assessment of the legal situation in the USA and the fact that we can sue in Munich regardless of where the training takes place."
  • Tobias Holzmüller, GEMA CEO: "AI models based on the theft of intellectual property do not enjoy legal protection. AI providers must acquire licenses and cannot simply help themselves to our members' works for free... If systems are operated in Europe, legal action can be taken before European courts."
  • Suno spokesperson: "From the beginning, we trained our models to create new songs, not reproduce existing ones... We disagree with today's ruling — which rests on a fundamental mischaracterization of how Suno's technology works, how it is used and how U.S. law applies." Suno does not expect the decision to affect its US cases.
  • Wolfram Weimer, Germany's minister of state for culture and media, called it an "important signal for strengthening the rights of creatives in the digital music market."
  • Second German win: a German court ruled for GEMA against OpenAI over song lyrics in November.
  • US comparison: Warner Bros., NBCUniversal and Disney are suing Midjourney over unauthorized use of copyrighted works including Star Wars and Superman IP. Midjourney argues fair use.

Snapchat Bars Fully AI-Generated Video From Spotlight as Meta Promises Infinite Content

CEO Summary
Snap said Friday it will ban wholly AI-generated videos from Spotlight, the product that surfaces trending and original content from creators and studios. Content enhanced or edited with Snapchat's AI creative tools remains eligible. The announcement came one day after Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg promoted the company's Muse image and video models as producing a "nearly infinite universe of personalized content," and the same morning the major music labels proposed rules to keep AI-generated tracks off the charts.
Why This Matters
Snap's ban targets wholly AI-generated video specifically while leaving Snapchat's own AI editing tools untouched, which protects Snap's proprietary AI features from the same restriction it applies to outside generative-video tools. The distinction draws the line at platform-controlled AI assistance versus third-party AI generation, not at AI use itself.
The Facts
  • Snap will ban wholly AI-generated videos in Spotlight, which surfaces trending and original content from creators and studios.

  • AI-assisted content stays eligible. Creators who have "enhanced or edited using Snapchat's AI creative tools" remain eligible; Snap says "for some, AI plays an important part of the creative process, and we believe it can unlock incredible new forms of expression."
  • The target is prompt-driven output, increasingly common as video models such as Google's Nano Banana and Seedance improve.

Angel Studios Polls Its Audience Before It Buys, and SK Global Sold Into It
Angel's guild members vote on projects before acquisition, and that same feedback data then sets the film's P&A spend. The Brink of War opens Aug. 14 as the first test.
CEO Summary
Angel Studios, the Provo, Utah-based faith-based distributor, acquired SK Global and 2521 Entertainment's The Brink of War, starring Jeff Daniels as Ronald Reagan and Jared Harris as Mikhail Gorbachev, for an Aug. 14 release. SK Global head of film Elizabeth Haggard says the film went through Angel's guild program, in which members vote on the projects the company takes on, and that the resulting data also informs how it sets P&A.
Why This Matters
Angel's guild-vote data functions as both a greenlight gate and a marketing budget input: the same feedback that decided whether to acquire The Brink of War also shapes how much Angel commits to promoting it. A project that scores well on guild feedback effectively pre-qualifies for a larger P&A commitment before a single ticket sells. That ties distribution spend to a pre-release proxy for demand rather than to the film's own box office track record or comparable-title data most majors would use.
Specific Implication
A producer with a targeted mid-budget project that does not fit a major studio's global-scale slate math has an alternative acquisition path through Angel Studios' pre-acquisition audience-voting process. The mechanism's actual box office return is untested until The Brink of War opens Aug. 14.
The Facts
  • Angel Studios acquired rights to **SK Global's co-financed production The Brink of War, produced with 2521 Entertainment, starring Jeff Daniels as Ronald Reagan and Jared Harris as Mikhail Gorbachev, set during the 1986 Reykjavík Summit. Release date Aug. 14.
  • Elizabeth Haggard, SK Global EVP and head of film, on the mechanism: Angel runs a guild program that allows members to vote on the projects the company makes**, and "if they're excited about distributing a movie, they look at the data coming out of [guild feedback] to see if their core audience responds." The Brink of War received "a lot of love."
  • Haggard: "It almost has that early tech company feel; their data is really sound and really exciting. You see that carry through the way that they market the movie, the way that they make decisions about P&A."
  • On the market gap: "It may be harder for a major studio to release a film at this level with a targeted audience that can satisfy that audience, but Angel is able to do that."
  • On audience definition: "it's not even just the faith-based audience, but there's an adjacent audience that is folks who want to watch movies that are family-friendly, that are values-friendly."
  • Haggard was promoted earlier this year. Prior: assistant to Donna Langley at Universal, then Ramona Films (produced A24's Zola), then SVP of narrative film at Participant Media.
  • SK Global, formerly Sidney Kimmel Entertainment, has a slate history including Crazy Rich Asians, Anyone But You and Hell or High Water.

CEO Summary
Disney is selling its 50% stake in A+E Global Media, parent of A&E, History, Lifetime and FYI, to co-owner Hearst Communications for north of $1 billion in cash. The deal is being finalized and is expected to be announced at Disney's earnings call next week. It is the first linear asset Disney has actually sold, and it comes after CFO Hugh Johnston reaffirmed in May that the company does not plan to spin off or sell linear TV networks.
Why This Matters
Disney CFO Hugh Johnston's May statement that the company does not plan to spin off or sell linear networks preceded this sale by roughly two months. The transaction differs structurally from a divestiture of a wholly owned network: A+E Global Media was a 50-50 joint venture, and Hearst was already the co-owner. The sale closed without a stated management change, with A+E President and Chairman Paul Buccieri expected to continue under Hearst CEO Steven R. Schwartz. Disney's other linear networks, including FX, Freeform and National Geographic, are wholly owned, so no equivalent co-owner buyer exists for those assets under the structure used here.
Specific Implication
A buyer or partner evaluating access to Disney's wholly owned linear networks should not treat this sale as a signal of imminent divestiture there.

  • Management: A+E President and Chairman Paul Buccieri expected to continue under Hearst CEO Steven R. Schwartz.
  • Financial profile: still profitable, no debt, credited to Buccieri's early FAST adoption. A&E Networks owns a large portion of its content, rare in cable.

All 55 UEFA Members Vote to Boycott the World Cup Over FIFA's Stake Sale
UEFA's 55 members voted to sit out FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, unless FIFA drops its plan to sell roughly 20% of a $20 billion entity to private investors.
CEO Summary
All 55 UEFA member associations voted Thursday at an emergency meeting to boycott FIFA competitions, including the men's and women's World Cups, if FIFA proceeds with selling roughly 20% of a new entity called FIFA Forward Enterprise, valued at about $20 billion, to private investors. Joshua Kushner's Thrive Eternal is among the reported potential buyers. Concacaf has also objected. The first test arrives in October, at the Women's World Cup play-offs.
Why This Matters
UEFA's 55 members represent fewer than half of the 211 national associations required to ratify the stake sale, so the boycott vote targets participation rather than the approval process itself. UEFA's statement said "the moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever" and that "commercial return becomes a permanent obligation." That frames the objection around competition governance rather than the sale price or buyer identity. Concacaf separately cited a "lack of due process," saying the plan was disclosed before discussion with governance bodies. The first test of the boycott threat is scheduled for October, at the Women's World Cup play-offs.
Specific Implication
An investor evaluating a minority stake in a competition-owning entity should treat member-federation consent as a condition that can delay or block a deal of this structure. That consent operates here as a point of leverage distinct from board or ownership approval.
The Facts
  • All 55 UEFA member associations voted to boycott FIFA competitions, including the men's and women's World Cups and the Club World Cup, if the plan is approved. Reported by BBC Sport following Thursday's emergency meeting. FIFA announced the plan Tuesday.
  • Vehicle: FIFA Forward Enterprise, valued at about $20 billion. FIFA would sell roughly a 20% stake.
  • Potential investor named: Thrive Eternal, led by Joshua Kushner, per the Financial Times.
  • Use of proceeds: raise annual member payments from $2 million to $5 million, plus a one-off $20 million payment to each association.
  • Approval requires ratification by FIFA's 211 national member associations. UEFA has 55, Concacaf has 41.
  • Concacaf cited a "lack of due process" and said the plan was revealed before any discussion with governance bodies.
  • UEFA statement: "The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product." And: "The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever. Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation."
  • UEFA said no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition "for so long as these proposals remain alive," absent binding assurances FIFA will never again open governance or competitions to private ownership.
  • FIFA president Gianni Infantino has framed the plan as "the democratization of [soccer] worldwide."
  • First test: October, Women's World Cup play-offs.

An AI Question Killed a $2.4 Million Book Deal and Its Film Rights
Hodgman withdrew the book after writing she could no longer authenticate how the manuscript evolved, once the author's assurance that no AI was used could not be substantiated.
CEO Summary
The unpublished debut novel Call Me, I'll Hide the Body sold to Minotaur/Macmillan for a reported $2.4 million across two books, with international rights selling and film and TV interest building. On Thursday the foreign-rights agent withdrew it, writing that she could no longer authenticate how the manuscript evolved from origin to completion after the author had assured her no AI was used. UTA and Europa Content, who were selling the rights, are no longer involved.
Why This Matters
The withdrawal followed the agent's stated inability to verify how the manuscript was produced, not a stated objection to AI use itself. Hodgman's email, quoted by Deadline, said the agency had trusted the author's earlier assurance that no AI was used in the writing or editorial process. It said the agency could no longer substantiate that claim once international rights sales were underway. Deadline reports the underlying commercial concern as a chain-of-title issue. Publishers and film companies may be unable to register copyright or establish clear title on a work that incorporated AI-generated material. Such material can be treated as an amalgamation of other copyrighted works. UTA and Europa Content, who had been selling the rights, are no longer involved.
Specific Implication
A literary or film rights buyer evaluating an option on unpublished material has a reported precedent in this deal's collapse. An author's AI-use assurance can be treated as insufficient on its own, with documentation of the drafting record requested before acquiring rights.
The Facts
  • Sale: Call Me, I'll Hide the Body to Minotaur/Macmillan for a reported $2.4 million covering the novel and a follow-up. Deadline has withheld the author's name.
  • Withdrawal: Sandy Hodgman of Hodgman Literary, selling foreign rights for Europa Content, pulled the submission Thursday. Her email, obtained by Deadline: "we are no longer able to authenticate how the manuscript fully evolved from origin to completion. During the submission process we vetted the manuscript with [the author] for AI and felt trusting in his reassurance that it was written without utilizing AI as a resource in the writing or editorial process. We can no longer substantiate that, and we are withdrawing the book."
  • UTA and Europa Content had been selling the rights; Deadline reports both are no longer involved. Momentum had accelerated after a large U.S. offer was set.
  • Deadline reports it is routine for publishers and reps to ask authors about AI use, and that all parties proceeded in good faith on the author's assurance. Questions arose once rights began selling worldwide.
  • The commercial mechanism: publishers and film companies may be unable to register copyright or establish a clear chain of title with AI elements in the mix, because AI-aided copy is an amalgamation of many other copyrighted works.
  • The book: protagonist Femi Johnson trades "cleaner" origins in Lagos for a chemistry PhD in Houston; his ability to make bodies disappear leads to work for a cartel operator.

CEO Summary
Producer Simon Afram and Op-Fortitude Limited sued Netflix in federal court in Los Angeles seeking at least $105 million, claiming an unencrypted digital cinema package of the $45 million World War II thriller Fortitude, starring Nicolas Cage, was stolen from a Netflix desk after being delivered for an acquisition screening. Netflix says it does not bear the risk of loss on a film delivered "without the proper industry-standard safeguards" and alleges the producers demanded $165 million rather than work with the company in good faith.
Why This Matters
The complaint's timeline anchors the claim to a specific gap: Netflix screened the DCP around June 16, and the internal "Stolen PCP" email cited in the filing is dated June 25. The producers' claims of conversion and breach of bailment turn on that internal gap between screening and disclosure, not on the theft itself. That is why the case tests custody and notification duty rather than simple loss.
Specific Implication
This dispute shows no settled industry standard exists for who bears the loss when an unencrypted master or DCP delivered for a buyer's acquisition screening goes missing before a distribution agreement is signed. The submission agreement's custody and breach-notification terms are the specific point at issue in this case.
The Facts
  • Filed Wednesday in U.S. District Court, Los Angeles, by Simon Afram (producer, writer, financier) and Op-Fortitude Limited. Damages sought: at least $105 million.
  • Claims: conversion, breach of bailment contract, breach of implied contract.
  • The unencrypted DCP was delivered to Netflix for screening and possible purchase, with instructions to delete the files after screening.
  • Per the complaint, Netflix screened around June 16, then "failed to provide the promised instructions for picking up the unencrypted DCP for over a week." On June 25 a Netflix executive emailed with the subject line "Stolen PCP": "someone stole a good amount of drives from our office desks this past week."
  • The executive said security teams had "no luck" and piracy teams were "on high alert," and that the drive would likely be "sold for scrap given that they require" a key. The complaint alleges Netflix knew the DCP was unencrypted and openable without a key.
  • The film cost over $45 million to make. The complaint says Netflix refused to disclose whether it filed a police report and, on Tuesday, refused to involve the LAPD in its private investigation.
  • Netflix statement: it "disputes any claim that it bears the risk of loss for a film delivered without the proper industry-standard safeguards," says it does not own the rights to Fortitude, has conducted a thorough investigation and offered piracy-site monitoring, and declined to share details "given their hostile attempts to extort money from Netflix over this situation, including immediately demanding $165 million for the film."
  • A Netflix source says there is no evidence the film has leaked.
  • Fortitude: directed by Simon West, with Nicolas Cage as double agent Dusko Popov, plus Matthew Goode, Ben Kingsley, Ron Perlman and Michael Sheen.

The Writers Guild of America East ended a 12-year sponsorship of Urbanworld, the BIPOC-focused New York film festival, over the festival's new "AI Sidebar," which will screen AI-generated films and host tech demos in partnership with the New School. Founder Stacy Spikes learned of the decision through a forwarded email; the guild declined to comment and said its decision stands. Cannes banned AI films from its official lineup this year; Tribeca screened one last month.
Why This Matters
The WGA East's decision addressed the festival's new AI-focused sidebar, not a specific AI-generated film in competition, per Spikes' account of the guild's communication. Spikes said he learned of the decision through a forwarded email rather than direct conversation, and the guild declined to comment beyond confirming the decision stands. Festival treatment of AI-generated work is not consistent across venues this year: Cannes excluded AI films from its official lineup, directing them to an adjacent marketplace, while Tribeca screened the AI-generated Dreams of Violets last month.

A festival adding an AI-focused section should expect a guild sponsor's exit to arrive as a done decision rather than a negotiation. Urbanworld learned of the WGA East's withdrawal through a forwarded email, and the guild said the decision stands.
The Facts

  • The WGAE declined to comment or make anyone available. It has run an #AINeedsHumans campaign and made AI a pillar of its 148-day 2023 strike.
  • The AI category has not been an issue for other Urbanworld sponsors, whom Spikes declined to name.
  • Festival context: Cannes banned AI films from this year's official lineup, sending projects like Hell Grind to its adjacent marketplace. Tribeca screened the 75-minute AI-generated Dreams of Violets last month.
  • Spikes owns Urbanworld and is co-founder and CEO of MoviePass, which he took back over in 2021.

Jason Cloth, Financier Behind Joker And Longlegs, Charged In A $100 Million Ponzi Scheme
The Ontario Securities Commission alleges Cloth raised more than $500 million from over 500 investors between 2013 and 2022 and diverted at least $70 million.
CEO Summary
Jason Cloth, the film financier behind Joker, Longlegs, Babylon and Judas and the Black Messiah, was arrested Tuesday and charged with seven counts of wire fraud in a federal indictment alleging he and his Creative Wealth Media Finance Corp. fraudulently obtained more than $100 million from investors. Creative Wealth was the principal financier of Bron Studios, which went bankrupt in 2023. A parallel Ontario Securities Commission proceeding alleges Cloth raised more than $500 million from over 500 investors between 2013 and 2022 and diverted at least $70 million; final arguments there are set for August 4.
Why This Matters
The $12.25 million forfeiture sought in the federal case is a small fraction of the $100 million-plus alleged in that same indictment and the $500 million-plus the Ontario Securities Commission alleges Cloth raised over 2013-2022. Even a conviction and asset seizure would therefore recover only a portion of the money at issue for investors and creditors.
Specific Implication
A party owed deferred fees or backend participation tied to a Creative Wealth or Bron Studios financed title has exposure to recovery through a bankruptcy estate or a federal forfeiture proceeding rather than direct payment.
The Facts
  • Cloth, 60, of Beverly Hills, was arrested Tuesday and arraigned in Los Angeles. A 12-page indictment was filed the same day in US District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.
  • Seven counts of wire fraud, each punishable by up to 20 years in federal prison.
  • Prosecutors allege Cloth and Creative Wealth obtained more than $100 million from an Illinois investment adviser, that adviser's clients and other investors on false representations, while intending to use funds for other purposes including a Canadian real estate development, and used some investor funds to repay prior investors.
  • Forfeiture sought: at least $12.25 million.
  • Credits over roughly a dozen years include Joker, Longlegs, Babylon, Judas and the Black Messiah, Ghostbusters: Afterlife, The Birth of a Nation, The Addams Family and its 2022 sequel, Americana, Goodrich and the series Kin.
  • Creative Wealth was the main financier of Bron Studios, which filed for bankruptcy and closed in 2023. Both had been prior targets of investor lawsuits.
  • A 2021 Southern District of New York suit by investor Hudson Private alleged misappropriation and non-repayment on 2017–2020 film loans, claiming Bron owed at least $14.3 million plus interest on films including Bombshell, Capone, The Survivor and Greyhound, and that Cloth made "various knowingly false representations."
  • The Ontario Securities Commission alleges that between 2013 and 2022 Cloth and Creative Wealth raised more than $500 million from over 500 investors in Canada and the US, diverted at least $70 million, and collected tens of millions in loan-facilitation fees. Final arguments before the Capital Markets Tribunal: August 4.

Central Casting Opens In All 50 States As Production Leaves The Hubs
Los Angeles shoot days fell 12.7 percent year over year while New Mexico drew $91 million and Illinois $47 million in second-quarter production spend.
CEO Summary
Central Casting, the 100-year-old background casting company whose name became an idiom, is open for business in all 50 states as of Thursday, having previously operated only in California, New York, New Jersey, Georgia and Louisiana. It will offer casting, payroll and compliance services nationwide, while keeping its full-service "premium" tier confined to the original five states. The move lands as 39 states plus Washington DC and Puerto Rico compete on film and TV tax incentives, with Illinois and New Mexico drawing $47 million and $91 million in second-quarter production spend.
Why This Matters
The two-tier structure limits Central Casting's own casting-director oversight to the original five states. The new nationwide markets, including tax-incentive destinations such as Texas, Oklahoma and New Mexico, get only the lighter "production-driven" lookbook tier, with support available but not directing the process. That gap means the company's full-service coverage has not yet caught up to the incentive-driven relocation its own nationwide expansion is responding to.
Specific Implication
A production shooting outside Central Casting's original five states should confirm which service tier applies, since the company's own casting-director oversight is reported to apply only in California, New York, New Jersey, Georgia and Louisiana.
The Facts
  • Central Casting is open in all 50 states as of Thursday, July 30, expanding from California, New York, New Jersey, Georgia and Louisiana.
  • Nationwide services: casting, payroll and compliance. The "premium" tier, with company casting directors on every step, remains limited to the original five states.
  • Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and others get the "production-driven" tier: hiring off a casting-director lookbook, with support available but not driving the process. Multi-state productions can run a hybrid.
  • Toni Avalos, VP of casting, Central Casting: "Production is no longer confined to a handful of markets, and our clients are increasingly looking for casting solutions that can move with them."
  • 39 US states plus Washington DC and Puerto Rico now offer film and TV tax incentive programs.
  • California remains the top production-spend site per ProdPro, with New York, New Jersey and Georgia still powerhouses. Illinois drew $47 million and New Mexico $91 million in Q2 2026 production spend.
  • FilmLA reported a 12.7% year-over-year decline in Los Angeles County shoot days for the most recent quarter, with most of the 170 projects awarded expanded California tax credits still to come.

The Paramount Pause Opens WBD Poaching Season
Amazon hired HBO marketing executive Pia Barlow while she was still under contract through October 2027, and WBD is now suing Amazon for poaching.
CEO Summary
Paramount Skydance's agreement to pause its $111 billion WBD acquisition until the antitrust suits resolve, or June 2027, has left more than 35,000 WBD employees and showrunners including Bill Lawrence, Mindy Kaling and Chuck Lorre in contractual limbo. Amazon has already hired HBO marketing executive Pia Barlow, still under contract through October 2027, and WBD is suing for poaching. Quinta Brunson moved her overall deal to Disney the same week Warner Bros. TV locked John Wells into a new pact.
Why This Matters
The pattern in this reporting is that proximity to incoming CEO David Ellison, not contract term or past output, is functioning as the operative retention currency at WBD. The merger's open-ended timeline makes that shift possible. With U.S. scripted originals at a 10-year low of 444 titles, WBD talent and executives face a shrunken buyer pool. They also face a rare window where uncertainty about who will run the company gives them room to test the market without immediate consequence.

WBD executives and talent currently under exclusive contracts have grounds to field outside offers during the pause. Active poaching (Amazon/Barlow) and departures (Brunson) are already proceeding without penalty to those who leave.
The Facts
  • Paramount Skydance's agreement to pause its $111B WBD acquisition until 12 state AG suits and the WGA case resolve (or June 2027, whichever is first) has left more than 35,000 WBD employees, plus showrunners Bill Lawrence, Mindy Kaling and Chuck Lorre, in contractual limbo.
  • Amazon's Prime Video hired HBO marketing exec Pia Barlow (still under contract through Oct. 31, 2027) as head of original series marketing; WBD sued Amazon for poaching, alleging Amazon is "in the process of attempting to interfere with the term employment contract of at least one other WBD executive." HBO EVP of drama Francesca Orsi was separately reported as a target to become No. 2 to Prime Video's Peter Friedlander.

Warners also pursued Ryan Coogler after his Disney deal lapsed, but he signed with Netflix (Disney had balked at overhead costs and guarantees).

Sources say both are seen as closest to Ellison's thinking on the merged company.
  • A manager quoted: "You're 100 percent taking those meetings if you haven't met with Ellison yet... either you take the job or you use it as leverage." A studio insider: "More reps are testing the marketplace to see if there's interest."
  • Total U.S. scripted originals hit 444 last year, a 10-year low — sources note fewer buyers exist even as executives have more reason to test the market, calling every seat "rented."

Matt Stoller Puts Paramount's Odds Of Losing WBD At 60 Percent
Stoller puts the odds of a block at roughly 60 percent, citing that the merger's financing runs through the Middle East, banks and Oracle, whose stock has collapsed.
CEO Summary
Antitrust writer Matt Stoller puts the probability that the Paramount-WBD merger gets blocked at roughly 60%, through legal or financing risk, noting the financing rests on Middle East capital, banks and Oracle, whose stock has fallen sharply. Paramount moved Beth Wilkinson into the lead litigator role over the weekend. Stoller predicted the state AG challenge in February, including its mechanics.
Why This Matters
Stoller's 60 percent estimate treats litigation and financing as two independent paths to the same outcome, which means the deal's survival is no longer solely a function of the antitrust trial. Even a Paramount win in court would not resolve financing exposure tied to Oracle's stock decline, since that capital source sits outside the litigation process entirely.
Specific Implication
Counterparties negotiating deal terms tied to WBD ownership, including overalls, housekeeping deals, or first-look arrangements, should treat the merger's outcome as unresolved through at least June 2027. That is the outside date set by the pause agreement.
The Facts
  • Antitrust writer Matt Stoller (BIG newsletter) told Richard Rushfield he puts the probability that the Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery merger gets blocked at roughly 60%, "either through legal risk or through financing risk."
  • On financing: "The financing behind this is coming from the Middle East, from the banks and from Oracle — and Oracle stock has really collapsed."
  • Paramount framed its decision to pause the merger pending the antitrust cases as a "significant win." Stoller: "It's a big loss for Paramount to do this, or a tactical loss. It makes them look stupid. It makes them look unprofessional." He adds the company is "kind of in shambles right now."
  • Paramount changed lead litigators over the prior weekend, moving Wilkinson Stekloff's Beth Wilkinson — who defended Microsoft in its 2023 Activision acquisition — into the top role.
  • The suits from 12 state attorneys general and the WGA have halted the merger; Paramount cannot close until the cases resolve or June 2027, whichever comes first.
  • Stoller predicted the state AG challenge in February 2026, including the mechanics: a judge orders the entities operated separately for up to 15 months pending trial.
  • He believes the WGA case adds material risk through testimony: "having writers like Mike Schur and Adam McKay, who are speaking out and saying, 'Look, I'm an important writer. I've seen how this works, and these mergers are a problem' — I think that's a very powerful thing for a judge to hear."
  • Stoller also notes what Paramount is not saying: "The one thing they're not talking about is what they're gonna do with the merged entity... They just seem excited about buying things."
  • He allows the other side: "There is going to be a trial. Paramount could very well win that trial."

Banijay's production revenue fell 11.9 percent in the first half, even as its sports betting unit posted 1.21 billion euros, nearly matching the entertainment arm's size.
CEO Summary
Banijay Entertainment posted half-year revenue of 1.37 billion euros, down 2.2%, with production revenue falling 11.9% and distribution up 10.5% on a single format sale. All3Media enters the numbers from Q3, following the merger that created an $8 billion-revenue producer with a 265,000-hour library. The group's sports betting unit posted 1.21 billion euros, nearly the size of the entertainment arm.
Why This Matters
The merger's near-term function looks more like capital return than production reinvestment. Shareholders collected an exceptional €400 million dividend and the group took on a €750 million refinancing loan in the same period the entertainment arm's underlying business contracted. That is a different signal than the library-consolidation story the companies are telling publicly, and one relevant to any counterparty judging whether Banijay's commissioning appetite will match its new scale in the near term.
Specific Implication
A counterparty negotiating a format sale or library licensing deal with Banijay Entertainment is now dealing with a combined library exceeding 265,000 hours under one ownership structure, split evenly between Banijay and RedBird IMI. That gives the company more scope to bundle titles across a transaction.
The Facts
  • Banijay Entertainment posted half-year revenue of €1.37B ($1.56B), down 2.2% year over year, attributed to "anticipated phasing in production and distribution." All3Media's financials are not included and enter from Q3.
  • Production revenue fell 11.9%; distribution rose 10.5%, "fuelled in particular by a format sale in the first quarter." The company expects a stronger second half with Q4 earmarked for significant activity.
  • Banijay Group's live events business grew revenue nearly 50% on the Winter Olympics and the FIFA World Cup.
  • At group level, H1 revenue was €2.58B, up 16.9% reported; adjusted EBITDA €502.9M, up 18.5%; adjusted net income fell 3.7% to €141.5M.
  • Earlier this month Banijay merged its entertainment arm with RedBird IMI's All3Media, creating what Banijay Entertainment chair Jeff Zucker calls the largest indie producer ever created, at $8B revenue.
  • Combined library exceeds 265,000 hours and includes MasterChef, Big Brother, The Traitors, Peaky Blinders, Midsomer Murders and Gogglebox.
  • Banijay Group received €801M from the deal, including €625M from RedBird IMI and a €176M pre-closing dividend. Banijay and RedBird IMI hold an equal split of the new Banijay Entertainment. Leadership: Marco Bassetti CEO, Jane Turton (ex-All3Media CEO) deputy CEO, Zucker chair.
  • Shareholders receive an exceptional €400M dividend (€0.93/share) following the deal. A seven-year €750M loan secured last month refinances All3's outstanding senior facilities and pays transaction fees and certain merger-related dividends.
  • The sports betting and gaming unit posted €1.21B, just behind entertainment, integrating Tipico (acquired last October) and buying French casino operator JOA.
  • Banijay Group CEO Francois Riahi: "2026 is definitely a transformational year for Banijay Group."

FIFA Moves To Sell A Stake In The World Cup, UEFA Threatens Boycott
FIFA aims to raise $4.2 billion from minority investors in a $20 billion World Cup rights entity, with JP Morgan advising and Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital reportedly approached.
CEO Summary
FIFA is creating FIFA Forward Enterprise, an entity housing the commercial rights to its men's and women's World Cups, valued around $20 billion, aiming to raise $4.2 billion from minority investors with JP Morgan advising; Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital has reportedly been approached. UEFA condemned the plan, saying the World Cup is "not FIFA's to sell," and its members are discussing a boycott.
Why This Matters
FIFA's redistribution pitch, more than $10 billion returned to its member associations, sits alongside a detail further down in the reporting: Infantino stands to personally profit as FFE's commissioner once his current term ends in 2031. That conflict of interest gives UEFA's ratification vote more leverage than a simple governance objection would, since members can condition their vote on structural terms rather than just the sale itself.
Specific Implication
A buyer of World Cup media rights for the next commercial cycle should treat the ownership structure as unsettled. FIFA states it would retain controlling shareholder status, but the plan requires ratification by a majority of FIFA members and UEFA has not ruled out a boycott. Either could alter the entity negotiating those rights.
The Facts
  • FIFA is creating FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a new entity housing the commercial rights to its men's and women's World Cup tournaments, valued at around $20B per various reports. JP Morgan Chase is working with FIFA on the structure.
  • FIFA confirmed the plan, said it would remain controlling shareholder, and said it hopes to raise $4.2B by "carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests."
  • Thrive Capital, the firm led by Joshua Kushner, brother of Jared Kushner, has been approached about investing per reports. Deadline says it contacted Thrive for comment.
  • UEFA issued an unprecedented condemnation: "This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross... The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell."
  • UEFA members are meeting to discuss their response, with a World Cup boycott reported as one serious option on the table.
  • FIFA President Gianni Infantino stands to personally make millions by becoming FFE's commissioner after his expected third term expires in 2031, per The Times. FIFA claims more than $10B would be redistributed to its 211 member associations following the deals.
  • UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham: the World Cup is "not a product," and "once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out." Former FIFA president Sepp Blatter also condemned the plan.
  • Context: of the eight quarterfinalists at the recent U.S./Canada/Mexico World Cup, six were UEFA members and Spain won. JP Morgan financed the failed 2021 European Super League. The 2030 tournament is set for Spain, Portugal and Morocco with games in South America.
  • FFE would likely need ratification by a majority of FIFA members; no vote timing announced.

'The Odyssey' Passes 'Oppenheimer's Domestic Lifetime In 13 Days
The Odyssey is set to cross $330 million domestic in 13 days, the same total it took Oppenheimer 595 days to reach.
CEO Summary
Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is expected to cross $330 million domestic by end of day Wednesday, its 13th day of release, matching a total Oppenheimer took 595 days to reach. That makes it Nolan's third-highest domestic grosser and already Matt Damon's biggest film in a leading role. Its third weekend is projected to ease at most 50% against Spider-Man: Brand New Day's arrival.

The Oppenheimer comparison is a nominal-dollar comparison, not a comparable-admissions one. Ticket prices and premium-format availability have both risen since 2023, so reaching the same total faster does not by itself mean The Odyssey has outsold Oppenheimer on tickets. The raw days-to-total framing elides that distinction.
Specific Implication
A distributor or promoter evaluating an event-cinema or stage-to-screen booking with a built-in audience can point to Hadestown's performance-triggered extension as a precedent for extending a limited engagement based on early results rather than a fixed release plan.
The Facts
  • Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer took 595 days to finish at just over $330M domestic. The Odyssey is expected to cross $330M+ by end of day Wednesday, its 13th day of release.
  • Second Monday charted $14.7M; Tuesday tracking to $16M+, for a running domestic total of about $320.1M.
  • Crossing $330M makes The Odyssey Nolan's third-highest domestic grosser, behind The Dark Knight ($534.9M) and The Dark Knight Rises ($448.1M).
  • It is already Matt Damon's highest-grossing film in a leading role at the domestic box office.
  • With Spider-Man: Brand New Day arriving (tracking to a possible ~$200M North American opening), The Odyssey's third weekend is projected to ease by at most 50%, to roughly $45M.
  • Bleecker Street's Crosswalk and LD Entertainment's Broadway-capture film Hadestown was No. 2 Monday at $2.2M, tracking $1.4M Tuesday, running total just under $14M. Originally scheduled for a five-day run, it has been extended into a second weekend across 1,560 locations.

CopySight Raises $3M To Make An AI Copyright Score The Industry Standard
TheWrap's own test flagged a Gemini-generated "space knight" image at 88% similarity to the Mandalorian and 85% to a lightsaber, with attribution to Disney.
CEO Summary
CopySight, which scans AI-generated images and video for copyrighted elements and returns a similarity "Copy Score," raised a $3 million seed round led by Mucker Capital. CEO Artem Petrov says more than half the major-studio market is testing the tool, and the goal is for insurers to accept the score when indemnifying studio projects. Netflix's Ted Sarandos said this month that GenAI workflows were used in roughly 300 titles.
Why This Matters
Petrov's claim that more than half of major studios are testing CopySight is unverifiable since he declined to name any of them. The tool's real leverage point, insurers accepting the Copy Score as indemnification proof, is described as a goal rather than an existing practice. A studio citing the score today is relying on a vendor's self-reported adoption number and an insurance standard that does not yet exist.
Specific Implication
A studio or producer using generative AI in production can point to a quantified similarity score, once accepted by insurers, as part of the documentation needed to indemnify a project. CopySight's parallel provenance tool, which logs human involvement at each production step, is also relevant to any effort to establish copyright ownership over an AI-assisted asset. The Copyright Office's current position is against protecting machine-only output.
The Facts
  • CopySight, a startup that scans AI-generated images and video for faces, logos, memes and design elements and returns a "Copy Score," announced a $3M seed round led by Mucker Capital, with Taisu VC, Flint Capital and Yellow Rocks! participating.
  • It simultaneously launched CopyScore V2, adding AI-generated video scanning and more specific scans.
  • Score bands: 0-49 low similarity (clear), 50-74 moderate (human spot check advised), 75-100 high (review strongly advised).
  • In TheWrap's own test, a Gemini image generated from the prompt "a space knight holding a laser sword on the backdrop of a desert planet" was flagged at 88% similarity to the Mandalorian and 85% to a lightsaber, with attribution listed as creator George Lucas, company Disney.
  • CEO Artem Petrov: "If you're a studio and you create content, you want to own it. But AI-generated content is legally homeless." He says the goal is to have insurers accept the Copy Score as verification when offering indemnification on studio projects, and to have it hold up in court.
  • Petrov says more than half the major-studio market is testing the tool, with roughly 350 smaller studios and AI creators on the platform and 100,000 checks run since a January launch. He declined to name studio customers.
  • Doug Shapiro, former Turner Broadcasting chief strategy officer and BCG senior advisor, is an advisor and investor: "Increasingly, we're getting to the point where AI is embedded and nobody's going to know what is AI and what isn't AI. How do you prevent inadvertent infringement?"
  • Context cited: Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said on the company's earnings call this month that GenAI workflows were used in roughly 300 titles; Amazon touted three AI-assisted animated series in May.
  • CopySight is also building a provenance tool that logs human involvement at each step of an AI-generated asset, aimed at helping studios justify copyright protection on the output.

Atari Licenses Ten Game Properties To Universal

Atari, partnering with Entertainment 360, gave Universal Pictures the right to develop ten classic game properties for film, including Asteroids, Centipede, Missile Command and Pong. Universal's ten-property license with Atari followed the studio's purchase of a spec screenplay by Matt Reilly and Carl Hampe, built around Atari IP, which the story identifies as the catalyst for the wider catalogue deal. A rights holder with a dormant, undeveloped trademark catalogue may find that a commissioned or spec script demonstrating a viable take generates a broader licensing deal faster than shopping the underlying rights alone.

Agatha Christie Estate Posts Record $44M Revenue
AMC Networks holds 64% of Agatha Christie Limited through RLJ, but voting is split 50-50, with the Christie family holding the casting vote on estate matters.
CEO Summary
Agatha Christie Limited posted revenue of nearly 33 million pounds ($43.9 million) in 2025, the highest in its 40-year history, up 24%, with pre-tax profit of 20 million pounds. Netflix, BritBox, ITV, the BBC and 20th Century are all developing from the catalogue simultaneously. AMC Networks holds a majority economic interest through RLJ, but voting is split 50-50 with a family casting vote on estate matters.

The £33 million total does not just beat 2024. It beats the estate's prior all-time high of £26.7 million, set in 2018, by more than £6 million. It supports segmented, non-exclusive licensing as an economically working model rather than a compromise structure.
Specific Implication
A buyer negotiating rights to Christie material should account for the estate's non-exclusive licensing structure, in which multiple broadcasters and studios hold concurrent development rights segmented by format and territory. The buyer should also account for the family's retained casting vote on estate decisions, which operates independent of AMC Networks' majority economic stake.
The Facts
  • Agatha Christie Limited posted revenue of nearly £33M ($43.9M) in 2025, the highest in the company's 40-year history, per accounts filed at the UK's Companies House and analyzed by Deadline.
  • That is up 24% on 2024 and beats the previous record of £26.7M set in 2018.
  • Pre-tax profit was £20M, up from £13.7M in 2024. CEO James Prichard declined to comment.
  • The company attributed the result to increases in "publishing, TV distribution and licensing revenues," citing the Netflix series Agatha Christie's Seven Dials and the upcoming BritBox adaptation Tommy & Tuppence.
  • It said library programmes "also had strong sales performances," especially in the U.S. Evergreen properties include ITV's Poirot and Marple adaptations.
  • New projects are in development with 20th Century, the studio behind Kenneth Branagh's Poirot films (Murder on the Orient Express, A Haunting in Venice).
  • The BBC is developing a Poirot adaptation, Hercule, starring Edward Bluemel, co-produced by BritBox, with a three-season commitment per Deadline.
  • Ownership: AMC Networks holds a significant stake via RLJ Entertainment Holdings LLC. AMC owns 83% of RLJ, which holds 64% of Agatha Christie Limited. Voting rights are split 50-50, with the Christie family holding a casting vote on estate matters.

U.S.-based visual effects workers across Star Wars productions, including The Mandalorian & Grogu, Ahsoka and Star Wars: Starfighter, have organized with IATSE and will bargain a first contract with the studio. The Dying Cable Bundle Is Now the Sharpest Antitrust Problem in the Paramount-WBD Merger
The combined company would hold more than 50 cable networks and over a quarter of basic cable revenue, an issue the DOJ never raised when it cleared the deal.
CEO Summary
Deadline reports that cable-network concentration, not film, has become the sharpest antitrust problem in Paramount's $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The combined company would hold more than 50 networks and over a quarter of basic cable revenue, and Judge Martinez-Olguin's TRO rested on Paramount's "false assumptions" about the cable licensing market. The DOJ never raised the issue when it cleared the deal.
Why This Matters
The combined company would hold more than 50 cable networks and over a quarter of basic cable revenue, a concentration issue the DOJ did not raise when it cleared the merger. Judge Martínez-Olguín's TRO found that Paramount's argument on pay-TV negotiating power "rests on false assumptions regarding activity in the market for licensing basic cable channels to distributors." Charter reported losing under 1% of its video subscribers over the past 12 months, an improvement on prior periods. LightShed's Rich Greenfield cites that as evidence against Paramount's position that the combined channels are complements rather than substitutes in a declining, low-leverage market. He notes that Paramount separately tells investors the combination makes the portfolio more of a "must-have" for distributors.

Procedural postureTRO extended; Paramount skipped the preliminary-injunction hearing and elected to go to full trial; trial date not yet announced

Both cannot be true."

Who is defendingChief Legal Officer Makan Delrahim, former head of the DOJ antitrust division, who led the government's suit against AT&T-Time Warner

LightShed: Paramount's Own Public Record Is the Biggest Risk to Its $110B Warner Bros. Discovery Deal
Ellison called a Netflix-Warner deal "the death of the theatrical movie business" in December, then Paramount's own TRO filing cited Netflix's theatrical releases as proof the market is competitive.
CEO Summary
LightShed argues the biggest courtroom risk to Paramount's $110 billion WBD acquisition is Paramount's own public record. David Ellison said in December that a Netflix-Warner deal would be "the death of the theatrical movie business," then Paramount's TRO filing cited Netflix's theatrical releases as proof the market is competitive; chief legal officer Makan Delrahim reversed himself on whether YouTube belongs in the market definition within four months.
Why This Matters
Lead counsel Jeffrey Kessler cited Apple as an independent theatrical competitor during the TRO hearing, when Apple in fact releases films through major studios such as Warner Bros. on F1. That is the kind of factual misstatement opposing counsel can use to question the credibility of Paramount's broader competitive-set argument at trial. It compounds the exposure LightShed already flags in Ellison's and Delrahim's own contradictory public statements.
Specific Implication
A deal priced against a combined Paramount-WBD should account for the standstill period running to June 2027 or a final ruling, whichever comes first. Paramount's own contradictory public statements are now part of the litigation record, and LightShed identifies them as a distinct closing risk.

Jul 16, 2026, Paramount's own TRO opposition filing (Docket 114): "large streaming-oriented studios, including Netflix, have begun strategic theatrical releases" — cited as evidence the market is competitive

Talent and producers working in late night, news, or satire formats at a broadcast-licensed network are operating under a live, unresolved license-review process whose timing the filing directly ties to specific editorial content. Ofcom's overall finding, Netflix at 26% versus the BBC at 25%, sits within the range Ofcom itself attributes partly to a methodology change from the prior year's 28% to 23% result. Third-party funding of broadcaster content reached a record £748 million, which Ofcom notes increasingly comes attached to the streaming partner's full rights ownership.

A producer negotiating third-party UK co-production funding should confirm the rights-ownership terms attached to that record £748 million pool before assuming its availability is unconditional. The Ankler Argues AI Mockbusters Will Draft Off Studio Marketing Spend, Starting With The Odyssey
Musk floated backing a Mel Gibson AI Odyssey with $100 million, arguing Grok could draft off Universal's $250 million production and $125 million marketing campaign.
CEO Summary
The Ankler's Erik Barmack argues AI-generated mockbusters will draft off studio marketing spend, starting with Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, after Elon Musk suggested Grok could generate its own version and floated backing a Mel Gibson AI Odyssey with $100 million. The thesis: AI does not need a better film, only the demand signal Universal's $125 million campaign creates. This is a columnist's analytical read, not reporting on a funded project.
Why This Matters
This is a columnist's analytical argument, prompted by Musk's stated interest in an AI-generated Odyssey and his floated $100 million backing of a Mel Gibson version, not a report on a funded or in-production project. Barmack's thesis is that an AI version does not need to outperform Nolan's film creatively. It only needs to draft off the attention generated by Universal's reported $125 million marketing campaign. Barmack estimates production costs could fall toward the low thousands of dollars per title based on the prior economics of Netflix-era mockbusters. The underlying Odyssey text is public domain, which removes any licensing negotiation as a barrier to an AI-generated competing version.
Specific Implication
Because the underlying story here is public domain, the elements an AI-generated competitor cannot replicate are the terms most worth securing in a deal built on public-domain source material. Those elements are a specific actor's performance and likeness, a named director's attachment, and any additional controlled IP layered onto the adaptation.

Musk's stated objectionNolan's casting, specifically Lupita Nyong'o as Helen of Troy and Elliot Page, and the hiring of nonwhite actors including Himesh Patel
Barmack's counterThe Odyssey is mythology, not a historical document. "There is no historically accurate Cyclops." Its survival across 3,000 years comes from continuous reinterpretation, from Joyce onward
Grok scale citedTens of millions of users, with some estimates above 100 million monthly active across integrations, plus millions of paid subscribers via X Premium
Core thesisAI does not need to make a better Odyssey. It needs only to draft off the marketing spend and cultural attention that Universal's $125M campaign generates
Public-domain argumentThe public domain becomes "the largest open-source story library in history": potentially thousands of versions of the same foundational stories rather than a handful of major adaptations per decade
PrecedentAI-generated Bible content has already proliferated online. Netflix's mockbuster era worked at a few hundred thousand dollars a title and could work at a few thousand
Distribution pointMusk owns both the generation engine and X, giving him a built-in audience and marketing channel that studios spend billions cultivating

The structural shift is from resale to inclusion. Peacock was already sold a la carte on YouTube's Primetime Channels at $10.99. Folding it into Premium at no additional cost converts it from a retail product into carriage inventory, meaning NBCUniversal is now monetizing distribution reach rather than a direct consumer relationship. That is a cable-era wholesale posture rebuilt inside a platform it does not control. The party that owns the subscriber file, not the party that owns the programming, sets the terms of the next renewal.

Rights holders negotiating sports carriage with YouTube or NBCUniversal should treat this deal as a precedent for live sports access being obtained through a distribution and bundling agreement rather than a standalone rights auction.

What comes with itNFL, NBA and MLB live sports plus Law & Order, Saturday Night Live and Love Island, and, per LightShed, a full season of Sunday Night NFL games.
Other componentsRenews NBCU's distribution on YouTube TV; adds Peacock Premium (with ads) to YouTube Primetime Channels and renews Peacock Premium+ (ad-free) there; brings NBCU sports content to YouTube; brings YouTube offerings to Comcast Xfinity and Xumo; bundles Universal+ and Hayu internationally in select markets.
Production elementNBC Sports will stream some live events on its YouTube channels, and NBC will serve as production partner for select live events on YouTube.
Pricing contextPeacock Premium standalone is $10.99/month, often discounted. YouTube Premium is $15.99, with a $8.99 Premium Lite tier and a $26.99 family plan. LightShed notes it is not yet known whether YouTube will raise the Premium price before the early-2027 launch.
Comparison to prior dealsPeacock was already sold à la carte on YouTube Primetime Channels at $10.99, and is an add-on across Roku Premium Subscriptions and Amazon Prime Channels. LightShed's point: the YouTube Premium arrangement is the first where Peacock is included at no extra cost rather than sold alongside.
Peacock's positionTurned a profit for the first time last quarter. Has struck bundles with Apple TV, Prime Video and Roku over the past year, and hosted Starz as an app within its own platform.
QuotesComcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh: the deal "reflects our strategy of partnering with industry leaders to drive sustained growth for NBCUniversal." YouTube CEO Neal Mohan: "redefine what a modern entertainment subscription can be."
Analyst readLightShed (Greenfield, Ross, Kelley) note YouTube did not bid aggressively for a package of NFL games for 2026-27 (all five went to Netflix), and argue this deal gets YouTube far more sports, including a full Sunday Night football season, than licensing individual games would have.
