Canal+ Commits €1 Billion to French and European Film Through 2032, and Keeps Its Six-Month Window
Canal+ will commit nearly 1 billion euros to French film through 2032, more than double the 480 million euros pledged for 2025-2027, and keeps its six-month window.
CEO Summary
Canal+ agreed to invest nearly 1 billion euros in French and European films from 2028 through 2032, up from 480 million euros under the prior three-year pact, and keeps its six-month post-theatrical window. Netflix and Prime Video, held to a 17-month window, are challenging France's financing-for-access system at the Council of State.
Why This Matters
Both sides of the fight are affirming the same premise: the window ladder is a priced asset. Canal+ paying up to keep its slot while the U.S. streamers litigate for a better one means the dispute is over rates, not the system. Saada's own lobbying comparison, a nine-month window obtained for a €35 million theatrical investment, treats months of exclusivity as inventory with a published price per rung. That converts French window access from a regulatory condition into a negotiable line item any sufficiently capitalized buyer can bid on.
Specific Implication
A filmmaker with a documented past conflict with Canal+ should expect that history to factor into the company's assessment of a project, by Saada's own account, separate from the project's merits.
The Facts
The dealCanal+ reached a five-year agreement with French cinema organizations to invest nearly €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in French and European films between 2028 and 2032.
The increaseThe prior three-year agreement committed €480 million from 2025 to 2027. The new figure also absorbs obligations tied to OCS, the rival pay-TV group Canal+ bought in 2023, which had its own pact to invest at least €60 million between 2021 and 2023.
The windowCanal+ chairman and CEO Maxime Saada said the group will continue offering subscribers films six months after theatrical release, preserving its position in France's media chronology.
What the chronology doesFrance links a broadcaster's financial commitments to how soon it can access theatrical releases. Canal+ pays the most and waits the least.
The challengersNetflix and Prime Video have appealed to France's Council of State to challenge the financing and release-window system, which makes them wait 17 months for newly released films. Their argument is that their investment levels should entitle them to earlier access.
The comparison Saada is usingSaada has lobbied for an even better window for Canal+, pointing out that Disney+ obtained a nine-month window with a €35 million theatrical investment.
Saada's framingCalled the agreement "historic," wrote that French cinema "deserves to be supported, financed and championed," and noted Canal+ has backed the sector for more than 40 years.
The political backdropNegotiations ran through a period of open conflict with the French film industry over the influence of Vincent Bolloré, Canal+'s largest shareholder. A Cannes petition accused Bolloré of a fascist agenda; Saada told a producers' luncheon Canal+ would no longer work with signatories, drawing blacklisting accusations and thousands more signatures, including Javier Bardem and Mark Ruffalo. Maoyan want-to-see registrations passed 252,000, ahead of every other tracked imported title, and Oppenheimer took over 30% of its RMB452 million China gross through Imax alone.
Why This Matters
The dependency runs toward the studio. Imax China is coming off a first half of declining revenue and profit that Manwaring attributes to a soft local slate. A commitment approaching the entire network is therefore the exhibitor repairing its year with one import, not a concession granted to the distributor. That inverts the usual China allocation leverage: on this title, the format owner is the party that cannot afford a modest run.
Specific Implication
For a film with Imax China contributing over 30% of gross, as on Oppenheimer, participation structures that report only a blended total gross would obscure the format-specific contribution. Format-level reporting is the more accurate basis for backend calculations on titles with comparable concentration.
The Facts
The planImax China CEO Daniel Manwaring told Variety he expects "a very large majority of our entire network, if not all of our network" to play Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey in its first week, out of a network of nearly 800 screens. The film opens in mainland China Aug. 14.

Format precedentOppenheimer grossed RMB452 million ($66.8M) in mainland China, of which Imax alone contributed RMB137 million ($20.2M), over 30% of the total. Manwaring calls the pattern "the Nolan effect, or the snowball."
Early regional readImax's box office share in Hong Kong and Taiwan has topped 30% in both markets, with combined receipts approaching half a million dollars.
Business contextImax China's first-half results showed declines in both revenue and profit, which Manwaring attributes to a soft Lunar New Year slate and a dry April and May, particularly for local-language titles. John Wells Extends His Warner Bros. Television Overall Deal Through Mid-2030, in the Middle of a Pending Merger
Wells' three-year extension runs through mid-2030, signed while WBD's ownership under the Paramount merger remains unresolved past 2027; The Pitt drew 25 Emmy nominations this year.
CEO Summary

The deal covers all platforms including external streamers; Wells currently has The Pitt at HBO Max and two series at Netflix. The Pitt drew 25 Emmy nominations this year, the most of any series.
Why This Matters
The shape of the deal is what makes it merger-proof. Because the overall binds Wells to the studio as a supplier rather than to any owner's platform, a change of control above Warner Bros. Television changes his counterparty without changing his market. Output keeps flowing to whichever buyer pays. For the studio, locking a supplier whose prior deal was said to reach nine figures through mid-2030 while the company is being sold reads as preserving the asset's value in the shop window.
Specific Implication
A multi-year overall deal signed during a pending merger should specify what happens to the term if the sale extends past the deal's close. Wells's 2019 deal offers the precedent: strike-suspended time was added to the back end rather than absorbed into the original term.
The Facts
The dealJohn Wells re-upped his overall deal with Warner Bros. Television, marking 40 years with the studio. He continues developing original series under John Wells Productions.
TermPer The Studio System's deal record, updated July 27: a three-year extension starting next year and running through mid-2030. Terms undisclosed.
ScopeAll platforms, including Warner Bros. Discovery's HBO and HBO Max, external streaming services, and U.S. broadcast networks.
Prior deal valueThe Studio System's record notes his 2019 deal was "said to reach into nine figures." That deal was suspended in September 2023 during the WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes, with the suspended time expected to be added at the end of the term.
Current slateThe Pitt (HBO Max), which he executive produces with R. Scott Gemmill and star Noah Wyle, now in Season 3 production; Netflix's Untamed starring Eric Bana; and Netflix's Unaccustomed Earth, adapting Jhumpa Lahiri, debuting later this year.
PerformanceThe Pitt earned the most Emmy nominations of any series this year: 25 for Season 2, including 13 in acting categories, after 13 total for Season 1 in 2025.
Track recordER, The West Wing, Shameless, Maid, Third Watch. Over 300 Emmy nominations, 70 Emmy wins, seven Peabody Awards across four decades at the studio.
The studio's quoteWarner Bros. TV group and WBD U.S. Networks chairman and CEO Channing Dungey: "John Wells is an iconic storyteller whose work continues to leave an indelible mark on our culture… we are immensely proud that he has called Warner Bros. home for 40 years."
RepresentationWells is repped by CAA and Hansen Jacobson Teller.

CEO Summary

Netflix does not own its biggest reality franchises; Too Hot to Handle and Love Is Blind sit with Fremantle and Kinetic Content. Why This Matters
The ownership win came from salvage, not development. Lock Upp was a proven format stranded by the collapse of ALTBalaji and the absorption of MX Player, which let Netflix acquire outright ownership of tested IP at a price cold development never offers. The arbitrage worth watching is in orphaned formats from failed regional streamers. Ekta Kapoor's account of rejecting two other offers shows the sellers of such formats are choosing buyers on stewardship, not just price.
Specific Implication
A format owner negotiating with Netflix should expect the service to push for ownership of the underlying format rather than an exclusive production license, given Shergill's stated intent to develop formats Netflix owns.
The Facts
The disclosureNetflix India VP of Content Monika Shergill told Deadline the service is developing Netflix-owned unscripted formats for India: "We are working on a couple of very interesting, big global formats, which are Netflix formats, and they will be coming to India." She declined to name them.
Why ownership mattersNetflix does not own Too Hot to Handle or Love Is Blind. It holds exclusive international production deals on both, but the underlying format rights sit with Fremantle and The North Road Company-owned Kinetic Content respectively.

Scaling in-flightEpisode output was raised from five per week to six on "audience demand and overwhelming success," running through the Aug. 5 finale.
Format travelAsked about a second season or an adaptation outside India, Shergill declined to confirm either but said: "The format is getting a lot of interest internally. I cannot confirm either of those questions, but since it's doing so well, I think it has a long life."
Provenance of the showLock Upp began in 2022 on ALTBalaji, the now-defunct Balaji Telefilms streamer, and on MX Player, recently subsumed into Prime Video India. Netflix revived it with hosts Farah Khan and Riteish Deshmukh.
Creator viewCreator Ekta Kapoor said she rejected two other offers to go with Netflix, citing support beyond financing: "sense of ownership is mutual, and respect is mutual. If I make a show for Netflix, I know that Netflix won't abandon me midway, because it's not doing well."
The YouTube wrinkleNetflix struck a co-exclusive deal for Season 2 of Samay Raina's YouTube show India's Got Latent, which Shergill calls a "great experiment" and a potential precursor to similar agreements, with "both platforms, Raina and his audience all responding positively."

Sean Astin Says He Made $250,000 on a $2.9 Billion Trilogy and Had to Sell His House
Astin says he earned about $250,000 across a trilogy that grossed $2.9 billion and had to sell his house; Orlando Bloom made $175,000 for the same three films.
CEO Summary
Sean Astin told The Guardian he had to sell his house after earning roughly $250,000 across the Lord of the Rings trilogy, which grossed $2.9 billion worldwide. Orlando Bloom has said he made $175,000 for the same three films. The trilogy was shot back to back, and the franchise is returning with The Hunt for Gollum; Astin is not confirmed for it.
Why This Matters
The teller is the structural fact. Astin is the sitting president of SAG-AFTRA, whose board resolved days earlier to condition its merger position on enforceable guarantees. The actor who lived the gap between a franchise's grosses and its cast's paper is now the official who writes the union's demand that studio promises be binding. Anecdotes like this one are functioning as negotiating exhibits, not nostalgia.
Specific Implication
An actor entering a multi-film block shoot, where all installments are filmed before release, should negotiate escalators or backend terms into the original contract. The between-film renegotiation point available on a sequentially released franchise does not exist in that structure.
The Facts
The quoteSean Astin told The Guardian: "There was a disconnect between the attention that I was getting and how much money we had. It was not a lot of money! In fact, I had to sell my house because I negotiated such a small amount on the trilogy."
The numbersAstin has previously said he earned roughly $75,000 per film, about $250,000 across all three. Orlando Bloom said on The Howard Stern Show in 2019 that he was paid $175,000 for the trilogy.
What the films earnedThe Lord of the Rings grossed $2.9 billion worldwide between 2001 and 2003.
The structural causeAll three films were shot at once. As Elijah Wood put it to Business Insider last year: "Because we weren't making one movie and then renegotiating a contract for the next, it wasn't the sort of lucrative scenario that you could sort of rest easy for the rest of your life."
The studio's rationaleWood said New Line Cinema took a "real gamble" filming all three at once, and to mitigate the financial risk the ensemble was offered "not massive salaries."
What the cast got insteadWood: "The benefit of that was that we were also signing up for something that was going to be a part of our lives forever."
Where Astin is nowSays he is "very comfortable financially now." He is also the current president of SAG-AFTRA, which on Saturday resolved to oppose the Paramount-WBD merger absent enforceable U.S. production guarantees.
Why it is live againThe franchise is returning with The Hunt for Gollum, directed by Andy Serkis, and a new film co-written by Stephen Colbert. Astin is not confirmed for either. Asked whether he would fight for better pay: "Goddamn right."

In the same frame, Disney's live-action Moana sits at $228.2 million worldwide on the same $250 million budget, with The Ankler putting its theatrical-window loss at $150 million or more.
Why This Matters
The layoff and the milestone are consistent rather than ironic. Pixar's other 2026 release, the original Hoppers, opened well and did not hold, and that is the datapoint the headcount decision prices. Sequels at this scale succeed on brand and do not require the development infrastructure originals do, so the unit is being resized to a franchise-output business. The territory mix shows how durable that business is, with China contributing only the fourth-largest haul, behind Mexico, on a title that cleared a billion anyway.

The gap between Toy Story 5's performance and Moana's loss on matching $250 million budgets gives Disney a documented basis for narrowing which animated titles receive live-action treatment going forward. That basis is independent of the layoffs at the unit that produced the sequel hit.

A High-Quality 'Odyssey' Bootleg Ran to 2.1 Million Views on X Before Takedown, and the Box Office Did Not Move

CEO Summary
A high-quality copy of The Odyssey reached 2.1 million views on X in about two and a half hours on July 25 before Universal's takedown landed and the account was suspended. The film took $87 million domestically the same weekend, with 70mm Imax showtimes sold out into September.
Why This Matters
The defense that held was the product, not the process. What this release sells, a premium-format presentation booked months ahead, has no pirated substitute, so the leak competed only with the portion of demand a stream could ever satisfy. The enforcement detail cuts the same way. The remaining clones were crowded out by mislabeled Rickroll files, meaning platform noise degraded the bootleg faster than legal process did, a defense no rights holder can contract for.
Specific Implication
This case provides one data point showing no measured box office effect from a high-reach piracy incident during a premium-format tentpole's theatrical run. Studios weighing content-security restrictions against leak exposure can cite it as a comparable.

Shapiro: Advertising Is Having a Golden Age and a Gilded Age at Once, and AI Attacks It From Three Sides
Seventy-five percent of global ad growth from 2020 to 2025 went to four companies; brands that stop advertising see sales fall about 16 percent after one year and 25 percent after two.
CEO Summary
Doug Shapiro argues advertising is having a golden age and a gilded age at once: U.S. ad spend is approaching its highest-ever share of GDP, while 75% of global ad growth from 2020 to 2025 accrued to Google, Meta, ByteDance, and Amazon. Nearly 60% of new streaming subscribers chose ad-supported tiers in Q1 2026.
Why This Matters
The two halves of the argument carry a pricing consequence when read together: a market growing at its fastest rate since 1983 is still compatible with premium video capturing almost none of the increment. An ad-tier strategy priced off the headline market rate therefore assumes a spillover the concentration data does not support, and the beneficiaries of the record market are platform ecosystems, not sellers of premium inventory generally.
Specific Implication
For deals priced against subscriber counts, the shift toward ad-supported tiers is a factor to account for in negotiating terms, since subscriber totals alone increasingly diverge from what a title earns a platform.

Why This Matters
The contractual gap is the story. The premium was priced then rather than at the original signing. Del Toro's framing of the requirement as protecting "the beauty and the redeeming power of art" points to the leverage that made it enforceable. Catalog value tied to a living filmmaker's endorsement gives that filmmaker terms power no original paper granted.
Specific Implication
AI-use terms for future remasters, conversions, or reissues are worth specifying in catalog agreements at signing, since this case shows such terms otherwise get negotiated separately, and at added cost, decades later.

Why This Matters
California's bar on non-competes leaves the fixed-term contract as a studio's only retention mechanism, and the relief WBD seeks goes further than enforcing one agreement. An injunction barring Amazon from hiring any WBD employee under a term deal before expiration would rebuild a class-wide non-compete through tort law in a state that abolished them. That remedy, not the single marketing hire, is what makes the case worth watching.
Specific Implication
Executives at Warner Bros. Discovery currently under term employment agreements, and any counterparty in discussions with them, should treat the contract's end date and any pre-hire notice obligations as active legal exposure while this suit is pending.

A Former Studio Distribution Chief Makes the Case for Variable Ticket Pricing, and Warns Exhibitors Not to Let the Ordinary Auditorium Rot
The interview subject ran domestic distribution at a major studio from 2019 into this year and now advises a theatrical analytics firm he founded in 2010.
CEO Summary
A former president of domestic distribution at a major studio, now a consultant, is publicly arguing that theatrical's flat-ticket convention is obsolete: premium pricing where scarcity supports it, cheaper tickets for low-demand screenings. He also warns exhibitors not to fund premium-format upkeep by letting ordinary auditoriums decay.
Why This Matters
The argument arrives from an interested party. A theatrical analytics business sells exactly the demand modeling that variable pricing would make mandatory for every distributor and exhibitor, so adoption of the proposal would expand the market his firm serves. That does not make the supply-and-demand case wrong, but it means the pitch should be read as the opening move of a commercial campaign. Anyone evaluating it should separate the diagnosis, which is arguably sound, from the prescription, which routes through his product category.
Specific Implication
Participation and back-end definitions tied to gross or per-admission pricing should be reviewed for whether they hold up if ticket pricing becomes variable by screening rather than fixed. This source is actively advocating that shift from within the industry.
The Facts
  • The interview subject ran domestic distribution at a major studio from 2019 until earlier this year, after prior runs at two other studios. He is now an independent consultant and a board member and advisor to a theatrical analytics firm he founded in 2010.
  • His warning to studios and exhibitors as the box office heads toward its strongest year since Covid: do not get cocky.
  • On premium formats: "If they want a premium experience, the industry should be able to offer them premium experiences." Premium screens drove the opening-weekend grosses on the summer's dominant release.
  • On the risk: theaters must not prioritize upkeep of premium large-format screens over the quality of ordinary auditoriums. "Going to the movies is an elective, out-of-home choice. And as such, the industry cannot afford to have one of their experiences be bad in order to force customers to go to something better."
  • On variable pricing, his central proposal, analogized to premium versus upper-deck seats at a ballpark: "Supply and demand dictate that if you have limited supply and great demand, you should be able to charge more. If you have less demand on the regular experience, perhaps a lower ticket price might make sense (for those screens), which might spur additional moviegoing and remove price being a barrier from going to the movies."
  • On the flat-price convention: a documentary of the conversation itself would carry the same ticket price as the summer's biggest release, "and that doesn't make an awful lot of sense to me."

A Documentary Subject Sends Netflix a Cease-and-Desist Over the Trailer, Two Days Before Premiere
Netflix says the featured trade was placed in May 2025, before any Nevada court order; Kalshi counters the screenshot is fabricated, citing 'bet slip' wording its platform does not use.
CEO Summary
Prediction-market app Kalshi threatened Netflix with a defamation suit over the trailer for The Prediction Games, a documentary premiering Sunday, claiming footage implies trades made in violation of a Nevada court order. Netflix says the featured bet dates to May 2025, before the order, and Kalshi's own chief executive participates in the film.
Why This Matters
The letter's real audience is unlikely to be Netflix. Kalshi's legal survival rests on being regulated as a commodity-trading platform rather than as gambling, with multiple states suing to enforce gaming law against it. Trailer imagery of traders celebrating winnings in Las Vegas is therefore not a publicity problem. It is evidence-shaped footage in an active regulatory fight. The cease-and-desist reads as record-building for those proceedings, which explains why a company whose own chief executive sits in the film would attack the marketing cut rather than the documentary.
Specific Implication
Subject cooperation secured for a documentary's principal photography does not extend automatically to how footage is used in a separately produced trailer, based on this dispute arising despite the subject's on-camera participation in the finished film.
The Facts
  • Prediction-market app Kalshi threatened Netflix with a defamation suit over the trailer for "The Prediction Games," a documentary premiering Sunday on the streamer.
  • The dispute is over trailer footage showing traders celebrating Kalshi winnings from the recent World Cup final while partying in Las Vegas, after a court order requiring Kalshi to block sports-related markets in Nevada following a Nevada Gaming Commission suit.
  • The letter, obtained by CNN, claims the trailer contains "misleading statements portraying trades being made on Kalshi in violation of a court order." Kalshi says it is complying with the order.
  • Netflix's response: the event was filmed last weekend in Vegas, but the most prominent trade depicted was placed in 2025, long before the order. The featured trader "showed us a screenshot of his bet that was made in May 2025, prior to any Nevada court order," a Netflix spokesperson told CNN.
  • Kalshi further claims the screenshot itself was "fabricated," pointing to terms like "bet slip" that do not appear on its site, which avoids gambling terminology.
  • The company's chief executive participates in the documentary.
  • Kalshi is regulated as a commodity-trading platform rather than as gambling, but multiple states have sued to enforce gaming laws against it.

Counterparties negotiating around the transaction should read the timetable as elastic in only one direction: later.

Any overall deal or first-look tied to either company should define change-of-control triggers by a specific date rather than by "closing." The court has stated the deal cannot close before August 17 and has not set a firm date beyond that.

That reverses the usual crossover arrangement, in which the US studio holds the rights and licenses the home market. The adjacent note that another major Indian tentpole is already dated for spring 2027 indicates studios will be competing for this supply on distribution terms alone, with no equity to lever.
Specific Implication
Producers of Indian tentpoles evaluating international distribution structures can treat Ramayana's November performance outside its core diaspora markets as a specific data point once results are reported.
The Facts
  • Sony Pictures has signed on as international distributor of Ramayana, a two-part Indian epic produced by Prime Focus Studios.
  • Sony handles release in all territories outside India. Dharma Productions releases in India.
  • Visual effects are by DNEG, the Oscar-winning house under the same Prime Focus umbrella as the producing company. The score comes from two Oscar-winning composers.
  • Ramayana is the first Indian production to carry the "Filmed for Imax" label, as Imax pushes into Indian cinema.
  • Release is set for November, timed to Diwali in India. A new trailer dropped Thursday as part of a San Diego Comic-Con panel.
  • Screen International corroborated the Sony international deal the same day.
  • Adjacent context from the same reporting: another major Indian tentpole is dated for spring 2027.

Prime Video Adds a Games Tab, and Amazon Says MGM IP Is the Pipeline
Amazon's gaming GM said it holds rights to the next Bond game and is reviewing other MGM IP for the tab, launching with Hogwarts Legacy and EA Sports FC 26.
CEO Summary
Amazon embedded its Luna cloud-gaming service inside Prime Video for Fire TV users, adding a Games tab alongside Movies, TV Shows, Live TV and Sports, with launch titles including Hogwarts Legacy and EA Sports FC 26. Amazon's gaming GM said the target is casual players, that "there's a bunch of MGM IP that we're looking at right now," and that the ambition is Prime Video as an entertainment platform rather than strictly streaming video.
Why This Matters
Ampere's sizing puts the entire cloud-gaming category at about $700 million in 2025 consumer spending, 0.3 percent of global games spending, which means the Games tab cannot be a revenue story on any near horizon. Its function is contractual positioning. Amazon is establishing the practice of moving film and television IP into interactive use while the category is too small for anyone to fight over. The rights precedents will therefore be set years before the money that would make them worth contesting arrives.
Specific Implication
Talent or rights holders with franchise IP at Amazon MGM Studios should confirm whether interactive and game-adaptation rights are covered separately from the film or television grant of rights. The company has stated an active review of MGM IP for game development.
The Facts
  • Amazon embedded its Luna cloud-gaming service inside Prime Video starting today for Fire TV users, adding a "Games" tab alongside Movies, TV Shows, Live TV and Sports. Launch titles include Hogwarts Legacy, EA Sports FC 26 and Clue.
  • Amazon's GM of gaming framed the target as casual players, not console gamers: roughly 3.5 billion people play games worldwide against about 300 million consoles and gaming PCs. "Your PlayStations, your Xboxes, your Steam and PC players tends to be really well served already. I might even argue over-served."
  • On content strategy: "big IP, familiar IP, approachable IP with relatively simple game mechanics are really resonating." Tomb Raider arrives in February.
  • On owned IP: "Obviously, we'll have the rights to the next [James] Bond game, if there is a sequel of the Bond franchise, there's a bunch of MGM IP that we're looking at right now."
  • On the platform ambition: "you need more on Prime Video, thinking of it more as an entertainment platform versus strictly a streaming video platform," with future "games or interactive experiences that are really designed to complement or extend engagement with video IP."
  • Context from Ampere Analysis: pure-play cloud services including Luna Premium generated about $700M in consumer spending in 2025, roughly 0.3% of global games spending. "Years away from becoming a more mainstream activity."

QVC Hosts Vote 80% to Join SAG-AFTRA, With AI Likeness as the Stated Driver
Hosts presented a supermajority petition to management on June 10, and SAG-AFTRA filed for the NLRB election five days later; the drive proceeded while QVC Group was in bankruptcy.
CEO Summary
TV hosts across QVC, HSN and Omni Channel voted 80% in favor of joining SAG-AFTRA in an NLRB election tallied July 23. Per the union's petition release, the primary motivator was AI, specifically the use of hosts' image, voice and likeness without informed consent or fair compensation. The drive proceeded while QVC Group was in bankruptcy.
Why This Matters
The petition's framing of the job as "live social shopping, combining salesmanship, storytelling and entertainment" is jurisdictional drafting. It maps commerce hosting onto performer work so the unit fits naturally inside SAG-AFTRA rather than a retail union. That wording, more than the vote margin, marks AI likeness as the wedge capable of pulling previously non-union on-camera categories into performer-union coverage. Consent and compensation for a captured likeness apply identically whether the camera points at an actor or a seller.
Specific Implication
On-camera commerce, endorsement or brand-ambassador talent outside a union structure can cite this vote's stated rationale as a sourced precedent when negotiating those terms directly into a contract. The rationale on record is informed consent and fair compensation for image, voice and likeness use.
The Facts
  • TV hosts across QVC, HSN and Omni Channel voted to join SAG-AFTRA in an NLRB election tallied Thursday, July 23. 80% voted in favor.
  • A supermajority of hosts presented a petition to management on June 10, 2026 seeking voluntary recognition. SAG-AFTRA filed the NLRB election petition on June 15 (SAG-AFTRA release).
  • Per SAG-AFTRA's petition release, the primary motivator was artificial intelligence, "particularly the use of their image, voice and likeness without informed consent or fair compensation."
  • Secondary demands in the petition: transparency and equity in compensation, clearer standards for career advancement, a stronger voice in decisions affecting their work, and greater job security "as AI continues to reshape the industry."
  • The hosts' petition frames the work as "live social shopping, combining salesmanship, storytelling and entertainment across broadcast and digital platforms."
  • SAG-AFTRA's national executive director welcomed the unit and said the union had encouraged management to recognize it voluntarily and avoid a costly NLRB process.
  • Contemporaneous reporting notes the union drive proceeded while QVC Group was in bankruptcy.

L.A. Q2 Shoot Days Fall 13% Even as Incentivized Projects Hit 38% of TV Drama Volume
TV drama shoot days fell just 6.4 percent, with incentivized productions now 38.3 percent of the category; feature films logged only 443 shoot days, down 20 percent, mostly independents.
CEO Summary
L.A. on-location production totaled 4,711 shoot days in Q2 2026, down 13% year over year. TV drama held up best, down 6.4% with incentivized productions now 38.3% of the category's shoot days, while reality fell 40%, comedy 43%, features 20% and commercials 21%. Feature films logged 443 shoot days, mostly independents. Mayor Bass is pushing for an uncapped credit that includes above-the-line spend, plus a federal incentive.
Why This Matters
The quarter-over-quarter pattern carries the real information. The rebounds from Q1 concentrated in credit-eligible categories, with TV drama up 55 percent from Q1 and reality recovering from its Q1 floor after only recently gaining eligibility, while the annual base kept shrinking. Read together, the incentive is functioning as the marginal scheduler of what shoots in Los Angeles, deciding which projects land there quarter to quarter without arresting the structural decline. The program is defending share of a shrinking base rather than growing it.
Specific Implication
Productions being quoted in Los Angeles should factor travel, housing and per-diem terms into the initial quote rather than a later negotiation. Categories outside the state incentive's current coverage have posted four consecutive quarters of year-over-year decline.
The Facts
  • L.A. on-location production in Q2 2026 totaled 4,711 shoot days, down 13% year over year and down from 5,121 in Q1.
  • Television, the largest category, rose 34% from Q1 to 1,607 shoot days but fell 28% year over year. Reality accounted for most of the annual drop.
  • TV drama was down only 6.4% year over year and up 55% from Q1. Incentivized productions now account for 38.3% of shoot days in that category.
  • Feature films: 443 shoot days, down 20% year over year. 33% were state-incentivized. The features filming were mostly independent.
  • TV comedy: 57 shoot days, down 43% year over year. FilmLA notes most local comedy is stage-based and therefore outside its permit data.
  • TV reality: 676 shoot days, down 40% year over year but up from 463 in Q1. Reality only recently became eligible for the state credit.
  • Commercials: 543 shoot days, down 21% year over year.
  • "Other" (stills, student films, docs, shorts, online, music and industrial): 2,118 shoot days, down from Q1 but up 10% year over year.
  • 170 projects have been awarded credits under the revised California Film & TV Tax Credit Program to date, including 41 new film projects announced in July. Recipients include studio animation, studio features, and independent films.
  • THR's reporting on the same FilmLA data puts the year-over-year decline at 12%.
  • L.A. Mayor Karen Bass is pushing for an uncapped credit that includes above-the-line spend, plus a federal incentive.

UK Regulators Face a Test Case on Whether Representation Can Be Sold as a Service
A 2023 email said the agency 'only represents' actors who 'regularly train and attend our classes'; one employment-law partner called the messages grounds to suspect a Regulation 5 breach.
CEO Summary
A Deadline investigation reports that staff at a prominent British children's talent agency told prospective clients, in messages spanning 2021 to 2025, that the agency prefers to sign talent through paid acting classes run by a commonly owned stage school. UK law bars agencies from making work-finding conditional on the purchase of other services; three lawyers consulted called the messages grounds to suspect a breach. The agency strongly denies wrongdoing and has engaged an external consultant. Enforcement sits with the Fair Work Agency.
Why This Matters
What makes this a genuine test case rather than a scandal is the paper trail. Written messages accumulated over years, corroborated by a dozen students and parents who understood paid lessons as the price of consideration, give a regulator the documentary record these cases usually lack. The Fair Work Agency's enforcement model is inspect, then fine on failure to remediate. The probable output is therefore not a penalty against one firm but a compliance standard the whole child-talent sector must adopt wherever training and representation share an owner.
Specific Implication
A representative who also sells training, classes, or "pipeline" access as a stated condition of signing should be evaluated against Regulation 5's bar on conditioning work-finding services on other purchases, or the equivalent rule in the relevant jurisdiction.
The Facts
  • A Deadline investigation reports emails and messages spanning January 2021 to October 2025 in which staff at a prominent British children's talent agency told prospective clients the agency prefers to take on new talent through paid acting classes run by a commonly owned stage school.
  • Quoted messages include a 2023 email saying the agency "only represents" young actors "who regularly train and attend our classes," and a 2022 message saying actors "need" to attend a course to be considered for a new voice-work division.
  • UK law prohibits entertainment agencies from charging upfront fees; they may only earn commission on client earnings. Regulation 5 of the Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 bars agencies from making work-finding services conditional on the use of other services.
  • Three lawyers and two industry experts consulted by Deadline said the messages were grounds to suspect a Regulation 5 breach. One employment-law partner: "It seems pretty open and shut, and I can't see any exemption within the regulations." A media-law partner: "access to work should not be used as leverage to pressure actors, performers, models or other work seekers into paying for add-ons."
  • A dozen current and former students and parents told Deadline they understood paid lessons were necessary to be considered for representation.
  • The agency's spokesperson "strongly denied" that representation was "ever been contingent upon the purchase of training services," denied "allegations of deliberate wrongdoing, unlawful conduct or systemic misconduct," and said an external consultant has been engaged to review processes.
  • Enforcement sits with the Fair Work Agency, which can inspect agencies and fine those that fail to remediate. It declined to comment on the specific agency but said it would examine relevant complaints.

A24 Dates a Venice Title Into a Six-Wide September Frame
Primetime moves from its Venice slot to a nationwide release four weeks later, joining five other wide titles dated September 25, including a Marvel re-release and a DreamWorks animated film.
CEO Summary
A24 will open Primetime nationwide on September 25, 2026, days after the film took its Venice Film Festival slot. The film, a documentary filmmaker's narrative feature about the making of a 2006 network newsmagazine franchise, is produced by its lead actor through an owned production company. Five other wide releases are already dated for the same frame, including a Marvel re-release and a DreamWorks animated title.
Why This Matters
The composition of the frame matters more than its count. Bleecker Street's Victorian Psycho and Roadside Attractions' Crawlers are dated the same day. Primetime's real competition is therefore not the superhero re-release or the family title. It is two other specialty films chasing the same adult audience in the same rooms. The fast turn out of the festival also converts Venice itself into the marketing campaign, a structure in which a soft festival reception cannot be contained, because the nationwide booking commitment precedes the verdict.
Specific Implication
When a specialty distributor describes a release as "wide," the screen count and marketing spend should be confirmed in writing rather than assumed, since a wide release and a platform release carry different commitments under the same label.
The Facts
  • A24 will open Primetime nationwide on September 25, 2026, days after the film took its slot in the Venice Film Festival lineup.
  • The film is directed by a documentary filmmaker making a narrative feature; its lead actor also produces through an owned production company. Subject: the making of a 2006 network newsmagazine franchise.
  • Other wide releases already dated September 25: Paramount's Heart of the Beast, Disney/Marvel's Avengers: Endgame Encore, DreamWorks Animation's Forgotten Island, Bleecker Street's Victorian Psycho, and Roadside Attractions' Crawlers.

Patreon Cuts 20% of Staff, Citing 'Profound' Changes in the Creator Economy
Patreon's podcasters generated $629 million in revenue last year, up 33 percent, even as the company cut 93 employees, its largest layoff since a 2022 cut of 80 people.
CEO Summary
Patreon is laying off 20% of its employees, 93 people, its largest cut since 2022. CEO Jack Conte told staff the core business remains strong but the platform must respond to "profound" market changes, flattening the org chart and redirecting teams toward core creator and fan experiences. The company said in April its podcasters generated $629 million in revenue last year, up 33%.
Why This Matters
The precedent is the tell: the 2022 cut also reduced the creator partnerships team, the function that touches creators directly. A staff note that denies one cause, AI, while leaving the actual market changes unnamed suggests the pressure sits on Patreon's own economics rather than on creator demand. The cost of a restructuring framed this way lands on the human support layer between platform and creator.
Specific Implication
A creator whose revenue runs primarily through Patreon's direct-subscription model should confirm what account-support level the platform can still provide after the restructuring, before renewing any exclusivity commitment.
The Facts
  • Patreon is laying off 20% of its employees, 93 people, with at least 16 weeks of severance.
  • CEO Jack Conte said in a note to staff that the "core business" remains "strong and consistent," but the platform must respond to "profound" market changes this year affecting how Patreon navigates the creator economy.
  • Conte: "We need to adjust our cost structure to ensure that we remain a stable, dependable rock for our creators as we work toward our long term ambition."
  • Internal changes include flattening the org chart and redirecting teams toward "improving core creator and fan experiences" and "helping creators grow their audiences and businesses."
  • Conte addressed AI directly and said it is not the reason for the cuts: "We are not making the above changes because we believe AI replaces humans."
  • Patreon hosts a wide range of entertainment podcasts, including several fronted by well-known film, comedy and lifestyle figures.
  • In April the company said its podcasters generated $629 million in revenue last year, up 33% year over year.
  • This is the largest cut since 2022, when Patreon let go 80 employees, about 17% of staff, and reduced its creator partnerships team.

A Management Company Rebuilds Its Podcast Network as a Video-First Business
The relaunched network reaches 50 million monthly impressions and 66 million social followers, launching with a creator podcast carrying 160 million-plus lifetime views, under parent company Night.
CEO Summary
The Roost Podcast Network is relaunching as Podium, a video-first business, two years after being acquired by talent management and media company Night. The network reaches 50 million monthly video and audio impressions and 66 million social followers, and launches with the signing of an established creator podcast with 160M+ lifetime views, handling its distribution, audience development and brand partnerships.
Why This Matters
Night's corporate structure is the story. The same company now spans Night Talent, Night Labs, Night Studios, Night Ventures and Podium. A manager negotiating a creator's network deal can therefore sit on both sides of the table when the network is its own. The commission-based alignment that justifies management economics does not survive that position intact, whatever the individual terms turn out to be, because the company's return on a signing no longer runs solely through the client's earnings.
Specific Implication
A creator evaluating a deal that combines management and distribution under one company should get written clarity on show IP ownership, audience data ownership, and brand revenue splits before signing.
The Facts
  • The Roost Podcast Network is relaunching as Podium, a video-first business, two years after being acquired by talent management and media company Night.
  • The network reaches 50 million monthly video and audio impressions and has 66 million followers across social media.
  • It launches with a signing that brings an established creator podcast (160M+ lifetime views) onto the network. Podium handles distribution, audience development and brand partnership.
  • Night, founded 2015, now spans Night Talent, Night Labs, Night Studios, Night Ventures and Podium.
  • Night's founder and CEO: "When Night acquired The Roost in 2024, we saw a company that understood something the rest of the industry was just waking up to: That podcasting is video-first, personality-driven, and powered by fandom."
